- - - - THE BAIRNS A' AT REST. There was din, as ye ne'er heard the like, 'Mang our bairns the nicht roan' the fire-en' ; A' were busy as bees in a bike; A' were blithe as the birds in the glen. Wl_at Wl' castles and kirks built Wl' stools, What Wl' rhyming at spellings a' roun', What, wi' playing at, ball and at bools,-* But there's peace now, they're a' cuddled doun. Now, the bainas are asleep, and a calm Has fa'n roun' like a soft gloaming shade, And a kind hand unseen sheds a balm O'er their wee limbs in weariness laid. On their fair chubby faces we see Sic an evenly sweetness o' rest, That ye'd doubt but they'd borrow'd a wee Frae the far awa' realms o' the blest. Like wee birds in a nest do they cow'r, By ilk other so cozy and kin'' • 0, their bed's like a rose-bed inflow'r, And our glances o' love oh it shine. 0, awa' wi' your glairy gowd crown, Free the cunning cauld fingers o' Art: But, hurrah for the bairns that hae grown Like a living love-wreath roun'Lthe heart! Ha, let's wheesht.t .As we warm In their praise, We micht waken some flaxen-haled loon: See, already shot out frae the claes Just as lithe a wee limb's in the toon ! Hap It o'er, hap it o'er. Bonnie bairn, Whaur awe' may that wee. footle pace? The rich gait o' the world's ill to learn. And fair fortune is fickle to chase. • There are hid 'neath these lashes so long, The full een that are stars o' the day; There lies silent the nursery song, On these lips fresh as mornings in May'; And there beats in these bosoms a life More o' promise than spring-buds are giv'n, That must meet the world's favour or strife, And shall make them or mar them for heav'n. Will ye guard them, ye angels o' Peace. In this haven, in the curtains o' nicht? Will ye guide them when dangers Increase, Heaving out In their day-ocean fight? For 0, whaur, frae the barnie so wee To the bairnie the biggest of a', Is the ane we'd first part sal', and see To a bed in the monis; taen awe'? * Marbles. t Whisper. I The grave. JaarEs NEILSON, in Good Words.

Most people are like eggs—too fall of themselves to anything else. Dr. Franklin says," The eyes of other people are the eyes that ruin us. If all bat myself were blind, I should neither Want a fine house nor fine furniture." Good. manners is the art of making those peonle say with whom we converse. Whoever makes the fewest per- lion uneasy is the best bred in the company. To be happy at home is the ultimate result of all ambi- tion, the end to which every enterprise and labour tend, and cf which every desire prompts the execution. Profanity never did any man the least good. No man is richer, or happier, or wiser for it. It commends no one to society; it is disgusting to the refined, and abominable to the eoedr Would you be exempt from uneasiness, do nothing that you know or suspect to be wrong. Would you enjoy the purest pleasure, do everything in your power which you are convinced is right. We can easily manage if we will only take, each day, the buzlen appointed for it. But the burden will be too heavy far us if we add to its weight the burden of to-morrow before we are called to bear it.

A man may conceal his name, his age, the circumstance., Of his life' but not his character. That is his moral atm- sphere, and is as inseparable from him as the fragrance of the rose from the rose itself. In the glance of the eye, in the tones of the voice, in the mien and gesture, character dis- closes itself. Woareo's CONSOLLTIoN.—There exists in the consolation given by a woman a delicacy which has always something motherly, far-sighted, and complete; but when to these 'words of peace and hope are joined the graze of gesture, that eloquence of love which goes to the heart, and particu- larly when the benefactress is beautiful, it is impossible to resist. TEE MUSIC OF A CHEERFUL HEART.—When the poet Calton' inquired of his friend Haydn how it happened that biz church music was always so cheerful, the great com- poser made a most beautiful reply—"l cannot," he said, make it otherwise. I write according to the thoughts I fed. When I think upon God my heart is so full of joy that the notes dance and leap, as it were, from my pen, and since God has given me a cheerful heart it will be pardoned me that I serve him with a cheerful spirit." firseepe!_ WILBERFORCE AND 12115 NAG.—No Man loved a yoke Getter than the late BishOp- "Wilber- force, and among others of a practical kind the following is told of him :—The coachman of his brother, the Archdeacon of the East Riding of Yorkshire, having bought a saddle-horse for the Bishop's daughter, , Canis up to London with it. On his arrival he reported himself to the Bishop, who, with that almost childlike plea- sure in fan which endeared him so greatly to his own people, Said, "Now, W.,1 want you to go out and borrow one of the largest and finest dray horses in London, and to-morrow morning, at eight o'clock, parade it before the dining-room window." W. entered into the spirit of the thing, and TM parading the dray-horse in Eaton-square at the appointed time, when the Bishop led his daughter to the window, say- ing, "Oh, my dear, here is W. with your nag!" At a trial in the Court of Queen's Bench between two publishing houses as to an alleged piracy of an arrangement of "The Old English Gentleman" T. Cooke was subpcenaed as a witness. On cross-examination by Sir Jas. Scarlett the counsel rather flippantly said—" Now, sir, you say that the two melodies are the same, bat different. What do you mean, sir ?" Tom promptly answered, "I said that the notes in the two copies were alike, but with a different ac- ice lt."—Sir James: "What is musical accent?" Cooke: My terms are a guinea a lesson. sir." (A loud laugh.)— 51.: -James (rather ruffled): "Don't mind your terms here. I ask you what is musical accent? Can you see it ?" —Cooke: "No."—Sir James: "Can yen feel it ?"—Cooke: "A musician can." (Great laughter.)—Sir James (very a,grily): "Now, pray, sir, don't beat about the bush; but tdi his lordship and the jury, who are supposed to know nothing about it, the meaning of what you call accent."— Cooke: "Accent in music is a stress laid on a particular note, as you would lay a stress on any given word for the purpose 61 being better understood. If I were to say,' You are an ass,' it rests on ass; but were Ito say, You are an ace,' it 'rests on you. Sir James." Reiterated shouts of laughter by the whole court, in wilich the' Bench joined, billowed this repartee. Silence being obtained, Lord Den- ham, the judge, with much seeming gravity' accosted the chap-fallen counsel. "Are you satisfied, Sir James?" Sir James (deep red as he naturally was) had become Searlett in mire than name, and, in a great huff, said, 'The witness may go down." EABLY EDITIONS OF THE BlBLE.—Abant 1455 the first prated work (of any magnitude) was issued from the press of Gutenberg and Fast in the same city. This work was a magnificent edition of the Latin Bible, commonly known as the Mazarin Bible because a copy was found in the library OfCardinal Mazarin. Within twenty years of this date the invention had found a home in more than a hundred Euro- pean cities, and by the end of the century more than a thousand preilses were at work. The first book which is ex- .'. plicitly stated to have been printed in England is dated 1477. In the same year was first printed (probably at Bologna) a leotion of the Hebiew Bible, the Psalter. In 1488 the entire Hebrew Bible was printed at Soncino, near Cremona. This edition was followed within a brief period by many others, some of which leave little to be desired as editions of the extraordinary text. The Greek Testament was not printed until 1514. The earliest Greek Grammar (by Constantine Lascaris) appeared in 1476; the earliest Lexicon in 1480. The first Hebrew Grammar that appeared in print (1503) was written by Pellican, at the age of 25; three years later a Grammar and Lexicon by the celebrated Reuclilin were given to the world. It has been calculated that more than ten thousand editions of books or pamphlets were published between 1470 and 1500; of the Latin Bible alone as many as ninety-one editions had been issued before the close of the fifteenth century.—The Bible Educator.

FLOWERS ON TnE BREAKFAST TABLE.—We hear a good deal about dinner table decoration; but an earnest effort as regards flowers should be made also with the breakfast table. Things that look well by night are all very well in their way, but give us the things that bear the light of the morn. lug on a nice tablecloth. The Briton will never care about flowers till they come nearer to him—we mean the average Creature, who has been trained so long with his few yellows, reds, blues, greys, &c., in lines and circles. People who love flowers will have them on their tables, of course, even if they have in London to buy the wretched in the shops; but, considering the opportanites for the growth of hardy and beautiful flowers, and for collecting such things in the hedgerowa, possessed by dwellers in the country, it is sun. Pricing they do not more often use them on their tables. Getting the fair forms of many strange and beautiful flowers ,voweerlt saneeilyrbtheeen inetyheiksitnhge best way to make converts. We more of this subject, owing to ce tam n white or cream-white flowers seeming peculiarly beeutiful on the white ground of the tablecloth. Every ga-dener should do his best to encourage the cutting of fi )wers in every way that he can, barring such few rareties or zees:ties as he wishes to keep for set-d. A. supply equal to that of twenty plant houses can be get from an open square in the kitchen garden or any other piece ot healthy ground devoted to the culture of the finer hardy things best fitted fer cuttirg only. The smallest country place could afford a spot of ground to grow flowers for cutting. In large gardens it should be made a feature of, and we venture to say that it would be as much enjoyed for its beauty as even the best p irt of the flower garden. From this and the general open gaed.n collections—the woos, be.lefero we, and copsea—every charm of flo.vel life might he culled in abundance, from-one end of the year to the other_efor the embellishment of our homes and table, where flowers the most choice and elegant in form sboold be brought near the eye, not in coarse, un- considered jumbles, but each thoughtfully placed where it would lock best, and such a quantity as hest to show its The reason why so niany are unable to take Cocoa is that tha varieties commonly sold are mixed with starch, under the plee of rendering them soluble; while really making them think, heavy, and indigestible. SCIENTIFIC NOTES. • M. Cacault has detailed some experiments made by him in photographing on hard faience at Colombes. They were baked upon enamel at a single heat in a temperature about equivalent to that of boiling varnish. The results were very beautiful. It is stated in the last report of the Thames Conservancy Board that the river above the intake of the water com- panies is practically free from sewage contamination, and the public are informed that whatever organic matter chemists may detect in the water must ,have its origin in sources other thin sewage. .An extensive list of posthumous compositions by the late violinist Vieuxtemps is in course of publication by the Parisian firm Brandus et Cie. It includes two violin con- certos in G and A minor, a concerto for violoncello, thirty- six studies, and a number of miscellaneous pieces for violin, and two string quartets. THE ECLIPSE or 1833.—The Italian Minister of Public Instruction has agreed to the proposal made to the Govern- ment to participate in the international scientific expedition to the Marchese Islands, in 1883, to obserye the solar eclipse which will take place in May of that year. Professor Tac- chini, director of the Astronomical Observatory of the Col- legio Romano, has been entrusted with the necessary pre- parations, and will go to London to purchase various instru- ments for the study of the important phenomenon. • The Rev. W. Houghton is engaged in the examination of the stomachs of various sea fishes, with the view of deter- mining the food of the respective species in cortnection with their distribution and migrations. With this object he has recently been out in the North Sea in a steam•trawler, and taken notes of the contents of the stomachs of several fish. He thinks it probable that the search for food is one of the chief causes of the migration of certain fish, and that the nature of the food consumed influences the quality of the flesh as an article of diet. Crustacea appear to enter largely into the food-list of many fishes, the smaller kinds, such as Entomostraca being the favourite food of whitebait (young herrings), whose little stomachs are often fall of these minute creatures. Mackerel are also fond of smallernetacea, a microscopic exami oation of their stomachs frequently re- vealing their presence, as also that of quantities of the larval forms (zoea) or crabs; the rich quality of their flesh, like that of herrings, is perhaps mainly attributable to the nutritious properties of an abundant crustacean supply. The examination of the contents of the stomachs of fish in connection with their distribution and migrations is pro• bably the best way of obtaining reliable data, and an inves- tigation of this nature is not unlikely to lead to some prac- tical results. Mr. Houghton obtained in a surfece-net large quantities of crab.larvil in the North Sea, and numbers of &gine and Tomopteris, two aberrant forms of annelid life. THE Wonen's LETTESS —The International Postal B areau at Berne has lately issued a statistical report concerning the International Postal Union in the year 1879. It deals only with the postal intercommunication of the 25 chief coon - tries belonging to the union. The figures are colossal, and we know that they have much increased during the two years and a half which have passed since. The total num- ber of letters, Ltc., carried amounted in roand numbers to 8,280,000,000, of which 4,900,000,000 were letters and post- cards, being about an average of 13,500,000 daily. The other objects carried included newspapr3 and other printed matter, patterns, drc. Europe. the sm sliest quarter of the globe, was credited with 5,624,000,000 of postal objects; America comes next with 2.366,000,000; Asia had 205,000.000; Australia, 73,000,000; and Africa is last, with 12,000 000. Reckoning the total population of the earth at 1,400,000,000, these figures would give an average of 5.9 postages per head, of which 3 5 would be letters and post•carde, and 2.4 printed neater, Szc. England is set down for 1.587,000,000 postages ; Germany is next with 1,200,000,000. But in the matter cf post-cards, Germany comes first with 223,000,000; while England had only 114,000,000. The average postages of letters and post-cards per bead of population give 363 for England, 232 for Swit- zerland, 16 6 for the Low Countries, and 159 for Germany. ilt is not surprising to find that the lowest grades in the scale of postal communication are occupied by Servia,

NOTES *ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- I CULTURE, eze. The gamekeepers of Nairnshire have killed 4,000 rooks and 1,000 wild pigeons. The Buenos Ayres Exhibition has been closed, the accounts showing a deficit of £20,000. Five hundred and fifty-nine vessels during the past 12 months cleared with breadstuffe from California for Europe, Ceoetown and Australia. ee From all parts of European Turkey it is reported that the harvest is, on the whole, superior to any that has been gathered for the past ten years. Earl Bective's Red Rose of Eildon, of the Poppy branch of the American Red Roses, has just produced a roan heifer calf by Grand Duke 31st, 38,374. A shepherd on the farm of Blairnairn, near Helensbuegh, found, in an almost inaccessible place, the carcases of ten sheep. It is believed that they were killed by lightning during the storm on the previous Sunday. A single root of five potatoes of the Elephant variety was last week accidentally unearthed by Mr. C. Gelton, of Cabs- tor, and, though far from mature in growth, was found to weigh 4?elbs. Two of the tubers were 18oz. each. Harvest commenced at Brickhill Farm, Bedford, on Mon- day week. Oae of Messrs. Howarth? Simplex String Bind- ing Machines was used, and it did its work in a masterly way, cutting 91- acres of wheat, and tying it up well, in eight hours, thies fully accomplishing the work of eight or ten men, and leaving nothing for the horse rake—a great consideration. Mr. Robert Holloway, the most prominent Clyesdale im- porter and breeder of the Western States, has met with a severe loss in the death of the noted Clydesdale stallion, Jonnie Cope, which occurred at Monmouth, 111., July 23rd. The disease was "pink-eye." The horse was imported to the United States by Mr. Holloway in 1875, and was con- sidered the largest horse in America, and one of the best of his size. Earl Fertescue has this season been using one of Neilson's hay-drying machines, which has been a success. The rick of the noble earl was about thirty tons in weight, and, after a short caseation of pumping, the heat of the rick went up, but upon the machine being again used the heat was brought down 22 degrees in 23 minutes. Neilson's system has also been used by Mr. Martin, of West Backland ; by Mr. I. F. Smyth, of Westland Pound, and several other farmers of Devonshire—a county hitherto not over famous for being well to the fore in agricultural progress. PROFESSOR RUSKIN AND HORTICULTURE.—At the Coal- ston Horticultural Society, on Wednesday, Professor Ruskin was a successful exhibitor in both fruit, flowers, and vege- tables, taking 13 first and 10 second prizes. At the Ulver- ston Horticultural Exhibition Professor Ruskin annually gives £5 to be distributed amongst the cottagers taking the largest number of prizes, the amount in value being given in rare seeds, hand-glasses, or other garden requisites. This year there were 14 prizes, the highest being £l. The prize is intended to foster a love of gardening amongst the cot- tagers of the town. SEIZURE Foe EXPRAO2DINAUY.TITHES.—An auction sale under distraint took place on Saturday at Crockenhill, Kent, to recover extraordinary Aithes on fruit grounds in the occupation of Mr. W. Smith. The inventory was a "hand- some red cow in full profit, first calf," which was sold by the authority of the Rev. A. Welch, the Vicar of St. Mary Cray. The sale took place in an open field, where there were assembled a drum and fife band, a large number of the villagers of both sexes, as well as farmers of the neighbour- hood and also from Sussex. The auctioneer, Mr. Allen, was a great deal chaffed for what was termed the "dirty" job was doing, and one of the crowd sheeted out that he aught to be boycotted. Mr. Albert Bath said that that would defeat the object his friends had in view, for as Mr. Allen had the right to make one bid he might exercise that right, and then Mr. Smith would be the loser. After some rather strong language against the "parson," and sar- castic remarks respecting the auctioneer, Mr. Bath pur- chased the cow, which was exhibited with coloured ribbons, for £l6. Expoter or HORSES.—One of the choicest and most valu- able collections of Shire-bred horse ever exported is now about leaving this country for the United States. Mr. J. H. Truman, of the Stock Yards, Chicago, has been in Eng- land some two months, during which time he has bought over fifty of the best Shire-bred stallions, mares, and fillies to be found In England. These are to be shipped in the course of two or three days' and cannot fail to give oar friends over the water a mot favourable impression of the size, strength, and quality of the Snire-bred horse, and of its adaptability for work on the farm when young, and for heavy town traffic when arrived at maturity. Amongst the mares and fillies are Some p articularly well-bred and pro- raTsing animals. Thebuying of these has been attended with considerable tronble,as the owners of our best strains of blood very wisely decline tel part with their mares or fillies except at a very high price. Mr. F. H. Stericker, of Picker- ing, has just sent out eleven valuable young flake horses, consigned eo C3,p,ainW.R. Jo-dan, of the Bremmer Home importing Company, of lowa, United States. They were chiefly Cleveland bays. A RIBBON-BORDER OF POPPIES.—TraVellen by the Great Western Railway to Reading, as they come near to the town, pass along at the north-westerly end of Messrs. But one long and broad band of varied colour, not lines, as In the case of the rainbow, but mingled together, particularly strikes the eye, and many a wonder must be expressed as to what particular flower this huge band represents. Mr. G. Gould, Trenches. There ara two branches of the house. The Ear' the superintendent, attends to explain the experiments at of aancarty owns in the Preston station on Monday and Thursday afternoons, at Galway 2.4,010 acres. Hayward's Heath on Tuesdays, at Hassock's Gate on Wed- Roscommon 1,454 nesdays. and at Billinghurst by appointment, addressed to him at Withdeane Home Farm, Preston. The hon. secre- tary (Major Sergison), accompanied by Mr. J. H. Sclater, Mr. J. G. Blencows, and Mr. T. St. Leger, Blaauw, visited the experimental station, at Hayward'a Heath, and viewed, the crops, consisting of 'pate, swedes, and wheat. The prin-; cipal object of their visit, however, was to examine the yield; of wheat, that crop being cut and readiness for carrying. The object of tbehvheat experiment has been to ascertain the action of nitrogen in different farms, and to demone strata how a wheat crop fares when nitrogen is excluded from the manures applied. The results obtained have cleaq proved the value of nitrogen, for the three plots—or rather the six plots, for all the plots are duplicated--to which no nitrogen was applied are extremely poor, both in ear and straw. Of the three, the one that got no manure is the worst; but the other two, which got dung at the rate of five tons an ac re, as well as a mixture containing all the sub- stances ass ntial to plants, except nitrogen, are only slightly better. The remaining four plots had the same quantity of dung, sad werisimilarly treated with the mixture, receiv- ing in addition nitrogen in varied forms at the rate of 501bs. per acre. Of them the plot which received nitrogen in the form of nitrate of soda shows decidedly the better yield, being excellent alike in ear and straw. The duplicate plot shows a similar result. The plot which bad nitrogen applied by means of chalky soil saturated with urine has not realised the expectations of the association's chemist, but it Is superior to the plots from which nitrogen was withheld. Between the other two plots, the one treated with nitrogen as guano and the other with sulphate of ammonia, there is not much to choose, both having a good average yield. Much interest was evinced by the visitors in this crop, and much attention was also given to an experiment on swedes In which the steamed bone flour, to which Mr. Jamieson, the chemist, has drawn particular attention, was brought into use. The experiment in this case was to ascertain the ac- tion of phosphorous and nitrogen in different forms in a root crop. Mengels were first tried, but proved a failure, and swed as were substituted. In six out of seven plots phosphor us was applied as half coprolite flour and half steamed be tie flour, superphosphate being used, we believe, at an additional cost of 23a. per acre (the coprolite and bone flow costi rig 265. per acre), in the one plot. The result is a universally excellent crop, the steamed bone flour and copro- lite yieldino, as far as can be seen, a copy fully equal to that secured by the more costly manure. Not one of the oat plants in the analytical department which seeks to as- certain whether any of the substances essential to plants are deficient in the soil can be described as more than an average crop; indeed, some of the plots are very poor. But the ex- periment here demonstrates most clearly the necessity for the application of nitrogen. Major Sergison conducted the party over the station and explained the different experi- ments.—Farmer.

Turkey, and Bulgaria. A I,.l"vir Carrot; PIANT.—A new vatiety of cotton plant has been brought to light in America, where great things are expected of it. It is the product of the hybridisation of the cotton plant with the common okra—both of them in- digenous to Florida, where the new plant has been reared. The hybrid, which attains a height of about two feet, has the stalk of the okra and the foliage of the cotton, but the flower and fruit are said to be quite unlike those of either Iparent. The flower, of which each plant only bears one, is as large as the magnolia, and nearly as fragrant. It, like the cotton bloom, is white for eeveral days after it opens; later it becomes pale pink, and finally red, "when it drops, disclosing a wonderful boll." For about ten days the boll resembles that of the cotton plant, when its growth, "as if by magic," increases wonderfully, and it finally reaches the size of a large cocoanut. Theo, the lint or cotton down ap- pears, of which each boll produces about two pounds of a Effie long staple, superior to the Sea _bland cotton. The , great advantage Which this cotton possesses is in the ease I with whi,l the bolls can be gathered, an unskilled picker being able to collect 600 or 700 pounds weight in a day. A still farther advantage consists in the absence, or rather the , peculiar disposition of the seeds, which, instead of being , mixed with the lint, lie at the bottom of the boll. There are only four or five of these seeds, which resemble persi- mum seed, and can be easily shaken out as the boll is ' plucked, so that the cotton requiu.s no ginning. The saving , in exoense occasioned by the reduction of labour both in picking and ginning are likely to cause this hybrid cotton to supplant the true gossypium, even if its produce were not of the superior quality attribated to it—Colonies and India.

Total 25,464 „ with a rent-roll of e 11,142. Lord Ashtown has in Yorkshire 6,336 acres. sight Irish Counties 14,17„

Total... ..50,543 „ with rent-roll of £23,202. We shall see presently by what sinister means the peerages were obtained. Mr. Henry Trench has also 10,760 acres in six Irish counties, with a rent-roll of £4,714. The Trenches therefore hold between them more than 80,000 acres of land in Ireland, every inch of which has been acquired during the last three hundred years. It is hardly necessary to remark that the Trenches are not an Irish family, hut belong to that numerous class of adventurers who, in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, "undertook" the ex- ploitation of the sister island. They profess to be of French extraction, being descended from a Protestant refugee who settled in Northumberland about 1575. According to one account, Frederick Trench settled in Galway in 1605; according to another, in 1631. Not long before, the who'e of Connaught had been the scene of most frightful cruelties, which were perpetrated by the English upon the unhappy inhabitants. Writing of the year 1577, Mr. Fronde says : , " When the people were quiet there was the rope for male- factors, and death by natural law for those whom the written Ilaw would not touch. When they broke out there was the Iblazing homestead and death by the sword for all, not for the armed kerne only, but for the aged and infirm, the nursing mother, and the baby at the breast." Writing of Ithe year 1552, the Four Masters say :—" Neither the sanc- tuary of the saint nor of the poet, neither the wood nor the Iforest valley, the town nor the lawn, wfis a shelter from the Captain (Brabazon) and his people, till the whole terr o ry was destroyed by him." Such was the condition of Con- naught a few years before pe first Trench made his appear- ance there. Frederick Trench is said to have purchased I the extensive estate of Garbally, in County Galway. Irish !estates were certainly cheap in those days ;but Northumber- land was not then a mone-i-making county, and I am at a loss to conceive whence these Huguenot refugees could have obtained the purchase-money. However, whether they obtained a direct grant, or bought cheaply from those who had so lately received a grant of confiscated lands, matters I very litt'e. The great-grandson of this Frederick Trench, Richard by name, married the heiress of David Power, of County Gal- way. As the Clancarty branch of the Trench family now nail themselves Le Poer Trench, I presume that the Powers were descendants of the Roger Le Poer who accompanied StroAbow to Ireland, and was a large gainer by the earliest of the many confiscations that have taken place in the island. By this marriage Richard Trench's estate was con- siderably increased. His son was created Baron Kilconnel in 17,97, and his eldest son sat in the last Irish Parliament, voted for the Act of Union on condition of receiving certain psomised rewards. Almost immediately after the Act had passed the father WM made a yiscount, and the year follow- ing he was advanced another step in the peerage as Earl of Clancarty. That name has been recently made familiar by a popular play, and therefore I may as well explain in pass- ing that the Earldom of Glancartv held by Donotrgh McCarty, the hero of Mr. Tom Taylor's drama, had become extinct. The new Earl, however, was descended, through the Powers, from a sister of Donough McCarty. The sons of the first Earl of Clancarty of the new creation were all born with a silver spoon in their mouths. The eldest, who voted for the Act of Union as Member for Countz Galway, obtairLed his own reward, apart from the reversion of his father's new title, in the shape of an appointment as one of the Commissioners on the affairs of India, and subse- quently of the sinecure of Irish Postmaster General. He was afterwards appointed Ambassador to Holland, and, on his retirement from that easy post, obtained a modest pension of £2,000 per annum. For a man who never displayed any remarkable abilities, he certainly was successful at the trade of politics. The second son of the first Earl was brought up to the Church, and became first Bishop of Elphin, and afterwards Archbishop of Tuam and' Bishop of Clonfert. Though he had in the two latter dioceses only 3,000 Protestant families to look af!er, he received the enormous annual income of

WOOD cLurrica FOR LADIES.—There is in wood-carving a fine field for the employment of ladies. For instance, if I had been a younger man, and inclined to extend my busi- ness, I could have given, I dare say, constant home-work to half a dozen ladies. In this ceiling, which we were talking of just now, I require several hundred feet of flat moulding, which will be wholly turned out by my boy and myself. I am too old to begin new ways, and yet I don't care to give up so long as I can do enough to keep me from rusting. But I know that ladies are often employed in this manner. They cannot, of course, do the heavy joinery in making up the furniture, nor can they plane and prepare the work. Bat they carve better than men; indeed, at first they carve too well, finishing their work with a delicacy and refinement quite out of keeping with old work. Now if my chisel hap- pens to slip a little I know that it deo not matter, and do not fret over it. All the tools required are a small iron clamp, to hold the work steady, and a few fine chisels and gouges. -Balf•a-sovereign would buy them all, and practice would do the rest. In the neighbouring county town, an architect, who has devoted much time to the study of old oak, has a class of ladies to whom he is teaching carving, and I have no doubt that it will, where necessary, be a lucra- tive occupation—far different from the stamp swindles one so often hears of as advertised in the newspapers.—CasseNs Fa m'!/ Magazine.

£17,326. His eldest son went into Holy Orders, and was, of course, welLprovided for, his father having numerous good livings in his gift. The next son of the first Earl became an Admiral; two out of his three sons were also quartered upon the Irish Church. The next son was in Holy Orders, and became Archdeacon of Ardagh, with three fat livings, whose united annual value was £2,206; his eldest son became a pluralist in that diocese of Tuam which proved such a mine of wealth to the fortunate Trenches.

Let us now turn to the other branch of the family, of which Lord Ashtown is the head. The younger son of the first Trench who settled in Ireland went into Holy Orders, and became Dean of Raphoe. He, or one of his immediate descendants, appears to have acquired lands in the County of Galway. A little later, Frederick Trench acquired lands in Tipperary by his marriage with the heiress of Francis Sadleir.. Of his sons, the third became Dean of Kildare; his eldest son, in turn, being quartered on the Irish Church. Frederick Trench's eldest son was M.P. for Portarlington, and afterwards the first Lord Ashtown. The Act of Union, it will be remembered, was passed by one vote in the Irish House of Commons. That vote was the vote of the Member for Portarlington. How was it gained? There had been previous rumours that the Ministers had entered into negotiations with him, but that his conditions were too exacting. As a certain class of voters hang back till near the close of the poll, so with Mr. Trench. He even went so far as to rise in his place and declare that he should vote against the Ministry. Cooke and Castlereagh conferred a short time together, and then Cooke went and sat down by the side of Trench and had a short conversation with him. A few minutes afterwards, Trench had the unblushing audacity to rise, and, amid the disgust of the House, declare that he had thought better of the subject since he had unguardedly expressed himself, and was now prepared to vote with the Ministry. As Sir Jonah Barrington says, "scarcely was there a member of any party who w, s not disgustad. . . • . Mr. Trench's venality excited the indignation of every friend of Ireland." A few months after' Mr. Trench become Lord Ashtown. With regard to the Ashtown estates in Yorkshire, I need only remark that they have been acquired by marriage with the Olivers, who derived them in the same way from the Gascoignes, a family to whom the famous Chief Justice Gascoigne belonged. Lest the Spectator should again ask Cui bono ? I will ask the question myself, and endeavour to answer it. Here is a family which, as late as the reign of Elizabeth, was un— known in Ireland; it now owns more than 80,000 acres of Irish soil. It has had no other means of acquiring this large property than by the exploitation of the Irish people or by marriage with other houses of the same class. Its gains by the Irish Protestant Establishment may be reckoned by hundreds of thousands, I might almost say millions. And, like oiler great Irish landlords, the Trenches have the right to evict from their holdings the descendants of those who by their labour and energy have given to the soil of Ireland- the value which it now possesses. The demand of the Irish tenant farmers is for fixity of tenure, that so tong as he pays his rent no one shall be able to dis- possess him of his holding. If the greater portion of the soil of England was held by men of another race and another creed, who had fastened upon the country within the last three hundred years, is it not-very likely that Englishmen would make a similar demand? The Norman merged into tlie Englishman centuries before most of the families that now rank as great Irish landlords set foot in Ireland. The English people can never thoroughly understand the Irish Land Question until they look at it from the Irish standpoint.

FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE: A telegram from Zanzibar announces the sudden death of Bishop Steers. The telegram merely announces the fact, stating that he died on Sunday, from apoplexy. The epidemic of cholera, which has caused a great number of deaths among the inhabitants of the Philippines, is said to be increasing. In one province alone 4,000 natives have died from the pest. The recent negotiations with Burmah are now said to have been regarded at Mandalay as a solemn farce. In the opinion of a Calcutta correspondent of the Times," unless we were prepared to make extravagant conceisions to the King without requiring any reciprocity on his part, the failure of the mission was foredoomed before it started:" INSURRBCTION IN COI/EL.—The news of the insurrection in Core is confirmed by a despatch from Yokohama. The Queen ,and 13 Ministers of State were killed. The King was spared, but the heir-apparent and his betrothed, both children, were poisoned. The uncle of the King is reported to have seized the throne. MunuEn or SECOCOENI.—The Durban correspondent of the Times telegraphs :—" News portending the probable result of the new policy in Zululand comes from the Trans- vaal. Secocoeni, who was vanquished and captured by Sir Garnet Wolseley and restored to the Boers, has been filled with his son and 14 followers by Mampoer, the chief put into his place by the English Government." Talk is cheap, but Emperors do not usually indulge in bellicose utterances unless they have some object in view. What, then, can be the Czar's object in saying to five hun- dred officers who were recently promoted that he hoped they would know how to fight valorously for their country and defend the honour of Russia? Who are they to fight, and by' whom is Russia's honour threatened? Contradiction is given by the Haytian Legation in Paris to the rumour recently circulated regarding the alleged existence of revolutionary agitation in Hayti.. Intelligence published on the 21st ult. in New York, stating that a fire had occurred at Port-au-Prince, daring which several shops had been plundered by the populace, is also declared to be incorrect. On the contrary, perfect tranquillity con- - dunes. Terrible outrages have been committed by Hindoos on their Mahornetan neighbours at Salem, in the Madras presi- dency. The orgies in which the "mild Hindoo " indulged are said by an observer on the spot to recall the worst days of the Mutiny. A large number of arrests have been made, and the Malsometan population of India will expect to see vigorous justice done. The riotsare attributed to " religious " feelings. The Peruvians still obstinately refuse to make formal , submission to the Chilians, and a desultory warfare is being carried on, in which the Peruvians suffer much loss. On a recent occasion 400 of them were killed. Reports from ' Santiago state that Chili has determined to increase the army of occupation, and by measures of the utmost severity compel the Peruvians to submit. M. Paul Bert, whose strange appointment as Minister of Worship in the Gambetta Cabinet caused a great sensation at the time, has contrived to render himself specially obnoxious at Berlin by a speech in which he Charged Prince Frederick Charles with having issued a proclamation in 1870, in which he described the French as" a band of brigands that ought to be exterminated." The official organ of the German Government declares the statement "an impudent falsehood from beginning to end." • TOURNAMENT 01, BEAUTY.—An "International Tourna- ment of Beauty" has been held at Buda•Pesth, at which 150 ladies presented themselves as competitors and filed past the jury, a committee of municipal councillors. Prizes or certificates were awarded to the ten who were judged to be most beautiful. The first prize, a diamond bracelet, was awarded to the daughter of a Hungarian civil servant, Cornelia Szekely, who is described as being remarkably beantaul, with an ideally perfect Grecian profile. It is intended that the proud owner of the bracelet shall be photo- graphed, *and that her likeness shall be sent to every illus- trated paper in the world for reproduction. We hear occasionally of the punishment of some " anti- Semitic " ruffians in Russia. In the government of Kieff

twelve rioters have been convicted an sentenced to severe terms of imprisonment. M. Louis Kossuth has expressed his views very strongly with regard to the agitation. The illustrious patriot, in conversing with a deputy of the Hun- garian Diet, expressed his surprise that the manifestations in Hungary so hostile to the Jews should be able to strike such deep roots, and declared the anti-Semitic agitation to be nothing but humbug, and a trade carried on by certain persons for the purpose of profiting by the passions of the thoughtless, and for fishing in troubled waters. The" anti- Semitic" is by no means the only agitaticu to whie'l this I accurate description would apply. HOSTILITIES ON TUB TURCO-GREEK FRONTlER.—Hosti- lities have suddenly broken out on the Turco-Greek frontier. According to the Greek account the Turkish troops attacked the Greeks all along the border from Zorbas to Degaus, and after the fighting had continued all day the Greek losses were four killed and ten wounded. The Turkish story, how- ever, is quite of a different character. According to it the Greeks attempted to seize disputed territory at Karalik Dervend, on the frontier of Thessalv, but were repulsed with heavy loss, while on the Turkish side only eight were killed. It may be assumed, therefore, that so far as the , fighting goes each side is convinced that it was attacked and repulsed the other. The Greek 'telegram says a thousand troops have been sent to the frontier, and the Turkish ac- count states that the Greek Minister and the Turkish Premier are conferring on the matter. It is to be hoped that the friendly interview will render the further use of pdwder and shot unnecessary. FRENCH POSTAL AND TELEGRAPH SERVICE.—M. Coch ery has published the statistics of the French Postal and Tele- graph Service. The total number of letters which passed through the post in 1881 was 1,350,000,000. In 1877 it was but 865,000,000. Newspapers have risen from 219,000,000 to 354,000,000; other printed matter from 161,000,000 to 297,000,000. and so on. Post cards have not increased. They numbered 32,800,000 in 1877, and 32,234,000 in 1881. It must be remembered that the French inland post card, like the foreign one, costs a penny, and that the inland letter unit is three-halfpence, so that the saving by pest cards is but small. The service for collecting bills, started in 1879, has increased in the values of the total sums collected from 6,700,000 f. to 48,800,0001. The Parcel Post Service, opened in May last year, has also given very satisfactory results. The number of parcels forwarded in May was 349,600; in August it was 410,100; in November 666,700; and in December 808,700. ROBBERY BY REVOLUTIONARY LEADERS.—An official statement of the Vienna police was published on Friday relating to a robbery committed on the 4th ult., at the house of a shoemaker named Merstallinger. The author- ities had received information that the robbery was carried out by the followers of the local Radical party, in order to increase the funds of the• association. A portion of the stolen property was discovered in the residence of a :leader of the revolutionary party, and the remainder at the houfes of workmen connected with the revolutionists. A quantity of correspondence has also been seized, by means of which the authorities had succeeded in arresting other Socialists implicated in the robbery. The officials had, with the infor- mation received, traced the cause of the crime to the editorial elepartment of the local Sooial Democratic paper, but they had been unable to discover any actual intentions of the party in the reasons aseigned in the correspondenoe for the robbery.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

The whole of the fitters and machinemen employed at Messrs. Dickenson's engineering works, Sunderland, struck on Monday, their object being to obtain the dismissal of an unpopular foreman. On Tuesday, an incident occurred in Bolton which shows the depressed state of trade in the town. A tradesman advertised for a light porter at 18s. a week, the applicant to apply personally. The steeet in which the advertiser's business is situated was literally besieged with all sorts and conditions of men. About two hundred presented them- selves.

The Central News says some serious disturbances are threatened at Barking. One of the foremen at Messrs. Levy's jute works was recently discharged. He was a favourite with the Irish employs, and four hundred of the Irish women employed refused to work after his dismissal. They now march up and down before the works, carrying a flag, and endeavouring, to prevent others from working. A strong body of police have bean sent into the district. " WEEKLY-RETURN OF BILLS OF SALE AND FAILURES."— In the week ending August 26, 1882, there were 847 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 73 over those of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted numbereft 154, a decrease of 50. The totals for portion of year to Aug. 26. 1882, are bills of sale registered for England and Wales. 31,818, a decrease of 1,163 • the failures gazetted numbered 7,091, a decrease of 709.—Extract from Stubbs' Mercantile Gazette. A GREAT STRIKE AVERTED.—The executive committee of the Durham Miners' Association received reports on Saturday by which it is known that a strike of the hands employed at Messrs. Peace's collieries has been prevented by the action of the committee. The men, 20,000 in number, had decided to give in their notices. The extent of their demands was—first, that a joint committee of representa- tives from each colliery of the firm and an Equal number of representatives of the latter should be formed to try com- plaints and grievances which cropped up from time to time, and also that the employers should pay. ss. per week to each man injured at the collieries. Both these demands were refused, and the result was a determination to strike. On Friday mght two members of the executive committee visited each of the collieries, and pointed out that the strike, with- out the leave of the association, was a direct breach of the rules. The reports show that in each instance the men had agreed to abrndon their intention, and to forward their grievances to the executive committee, to be dealt with in a constitutional way. THE LABOUR MARKET.—The labour market has entered on few important changes, but in the North of England an extensive strike of miners has, it is hoped, been averted. Some sections of workers, however, specially joiners on the Clyde, still remain unsettled, and at Sunderland the glass bottle makers are still on strike. At Birmingham the staple trades continue generally well employed, and at Barrow, Sheffield, and other centres of the iron trade there is good employment. Harvest operations throughout the country are progressing satisfactorily, but in Cheshire some deficiency of the ordinary immigrant labour from Ireland is reported. In South Wales both the iron-and steel works are fairly em- ployed, and a commencementehas been made at Cyfartha. In the textile trades a somewhat more healthy tone prevails, and at Huddersfield, Leeds, and other Yorkshire centres. manufacturers are, as a rule, fairly busy. Large undertakings in various parts of the country are still in want of navvies
4ANfoni

and when the harvest is over there should be plenty of work for stroll.- and willing workers. The army requirements are being systematically laid before labourers and other suitable recruits. In London pauperism shows a slight increase, but the miscellaneous trades are on the whole well employed. At New York the emigration commissioners have been officially reconstituted. Meanwhile most of the larger larger labour strikes have been settled. Chinese labour is still finding its way through British Columbia. In the Argentine Republic prospects are reported good, and in Queensland there is a good demand for female servants.- Labour _Yews. THE WEATHER AND THE CORN TRADE.-The Mark-laze Express says :-" More or less delay has occurred through- out the country in connection with harvest work on account of unsettled weather, but as yet there does not appear to have been much harm done. In earlier districts the greater portion of the wheat crop is in stack, and a fair average of spring corn and pulse has been cleared. The prolonged cheek to harvesting operations has influenced trade some- what, but in most provincial exchanges prices of English wheat continued to decline, and quotations come is. to 25., and occasionally 3s. lower from the previous week. In London, however, the influence of foreign trade prevented any quotable change. Millers are not eager buyers of the new crop, for the simple reason that the bulk of it so far has been too soft to grind. Country flour is too scarce to be cheaper. New malting barley continues to make 355. to 40s. Oats and peas have not been offered in sufficient quantities to establish values. The yield of the crop ap- pears to vary greatly, and with regard to wheat it is com- mon to hear of one or two sacks per acre leas than expected. Trade for foreign wheat off the stands in London remains almost at a deadlock. Foreign flour firmer." Tile Farmer says :-" The improved weather keeps trade slow. Sup- plies are heavy of wheat, flour, and oats; otherwise small. The condition of new English wheat is often unsatisfactory, which makes value is. lower. Best foreign wheat keeps 'firm. New American is 6d. cheaper. Flour is generally neglected at prices asked. Malting barley unchanged. Feeding sorts and 0V.73 rather cheaper; demand fair. Value of beans, maize, and peas unaltered. Market opinion keeps on the side of buyers. Speculation dormant." THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADE MANCHES- TER, WEDNESDA,Y.-There is still very little movement either one way or the other in the iron trade of this district. There has been little or nothing doing to actually test the market. For delivery equal to Manchester Lancashire Dig iron is still quoted at 465., Lincolnshire at 475. Gd. to 495., and Derbyshire at 435. 6d. to 50s. per ton less 2A-. Finished iron makers throughout the district are reported to be well supplied with work, but the orders going out appear to be more for shipment than for home consumption. For manu- factured iron prices are steady at about £6 7s. 6d. for bars, £6 15s. to £6 17s. 6d. for hoops, and £8 7s. Gd. to LS-123.6d. for sheets delivered equal to Manchester or Liverpool. Founders are fairly well engaged on heavy work, and in the engineering trades there is still work in hand to keep most branches fully going, although in some departraents new orders are not coming in very freely. An increased business doing continues to be reported generally throughout the coal trade. Any enlargement of the demand is chiefly in the better qualities of round coal for home-fire purposes and in caals for gas making purposes. The demand for other classes of fuel for iron making and steam purposes remains much the same as of late. In one or two exceptional cases a slight advance on the price of best coals is contemplated with the close of the month, but there is no general upward movement at present. The average prices at the pit mouth are without material alteration, an may be given as under: -Best coal, Bs. to Sc. 6d.; seconds' 6s. to 75.; common round coal, 45. 9d. to ss. 6d.; burgy, 4s. 3d. to 4s. 6d.; good slack, 3s. 6d. up to 43. in some cases; and common, 3s. to 3s. 3d. per ton. A tolerably good business is being done for ship- ment, and this branch of trade has shown increased activity during the week. Sellers, however, are not able to realise better prices, and delivered at Garston or Liverpool steam coal can still be bought at 63. 61. to 75., and seconds house coal at Sc. 3d. to Bs. 63. per ton.

div.head: "OUR OLD NOBILITY,'
div.p: "OUR OLD NOBILITY,'
THE STATE OF IRELAND.

A Swineford telegram states that on Tuesday night an extensive search for arms was made in the neighbourhood of Foxforcl by a strong force of constabulary. Many houses were visited. No arrests were made nor arms found; but documents of a treasonable character were seized in two houses. •

The 16 prisoners in custody for the Maamstrasna massacre were brought up on remand Jon Saturday in Galway gaol, before Mr. A. Newton Brady, R.M. Sub-inspector Gulkins appealed fora remand of 13 of the prisoners for a week, on the ground that further time was required to complete the case against them. The application was granted. Three of the prisoners were discharged. An agrarian outrage is reported from the townland of Corr, county Tyrone, not far from Dungannon. A farm of land from which a tenant was evicted was taken possession of by a man named William Hamilton. It appears from the reports to hand that the premises have been visited by a large body of armed men, Is ho carried off the crops and _put them into bogholes. William Terrie, a butler, and his an Richard. toth of Upper Exchange-street-, were charged on 'Wednes- day by twe Terrie's children with the murder of their mother Ellen, aged about 50, on Tuesday night, by kicking her in the stomach, and causing hemorrhage. She was found dead, and covered with blood. An inquest was held, and the accused brought before the police magistrate. In an article on " Mr. Parnell's Policy," the Spectator comments on the absence from his speeches of any con- demnation of the outrages in Ireland. Our contemporary says that after reading Mr. Parnell's " smooth " speech in introducing the Labour League, it," felt that the Irish peo- ple could not be much to klaine if they did assume " that the member for Cork •• does not go out of his way to inveigh against crime, just because, as he finds it advantageous to his movement, he likes to find excuses for it- in his own breast."

The Prevention of Crime Act has been put in force by the j magistrati s at Millstreet—a pre-eminently 'disturbed " neighbourhood—against a man named Mullane who had intimidated and boycotted a farmer. A gang of men of whom Mullane was the leader assaulted a fanner named Donoughue and his ,rife on the public road, and the proof of identity being complete the accused was committed for six months with hard labour. The power of appeal given in the Act was of course taken advantage of, and Mullane is at liberty on bail. MORE OUTRAGEs.—lntelligenee was received on Saturday at Carrick-on-Shannon of a daring outrage near Cloone, co. Leitrim. As a Boycotted man named Bernard Galloghy was standing outside his own door in the eerzning, two shots were fired at him by a cohple of men. Gelloghy rushed in- to his house, seized his gun, and fired after them, and, the patrol arriving immediately afterwards, he was escorted to Mohill to lodge information. The assailants escaped, and no arrests had been made. The police patrol from Bailie- boro, co. Cavan, on Saturday night arrested two young men, one a commercial traveller, the other a son of a well-known merchant in county Armagh, in the act of searching a hoise for arms. They had visited several houses in the neighbourhood, threatening the inmates and firing shots, and then taking away with them any arms they could find. THE. LIBEL ON A DUBLIN JURY.—Mr. E. Hamilton writee to the St. James's Gazette, under date of Friday :—" I now enclose you a return showing the exact amount of spirits dice drunk by each of the jurcrs in the case of Crown v. Hynes, taken from the jurors' affidavits. The beer, gin, and whisky was drunk chiefly by the bailiffs and police, who had, of course, to be provided with refreshments at the hotel. An affidavit from each member of the jury will be submitted to the Lord Lieutenant this (Friday) afternoon, which will effectually put an end to the slanderous calumnies which have been promulgated by the enemies of justice against us. In addition there was drunk one bottle of champagne between four, Mr. Barrett, Mr. McConkey, Mr. Reis, and Mr. Wardrope. The total shows :—Beer 3, claret tSt. Este-ahe) 131,, sherry 7, spirits 51-. Two of the jurymen are total abstainers." A CLERGYMAN ARRESTED.—The Rev. Mr. Usher, incum- bent of Baltinglass, county Wicklow, has been arrested on a charge of firing a revolver. Baltinglass was a stronghold of the Land League, and the Rev. Mr. Usher has been repeatedly urging upon the authorities the alarming dis- loyalty of the rebels and the near approach of an insur- rection. It is needless to remark that for the protection of his life against the rebellious population in whose midst he dwells he always earries a loaded revbiver. A disturbance occurred on Saturday night, which is represented on the or.e side as being an attack on the rev, gentleman by the rebels, resulting in his providential escape. Details are absent from this version of the occurrence, but on the other side the fol- lowing account is given, which appears to approach more closely to the actual facts :—On Saturday night, at ten o'clock, a fracas occurred on the bridge of Biltingless between a man named Fennellv and the- Rev. Mr. Usher. After some conversation, Mr. Usher was observed to draw a revolver, whereupon a man named Flinter, who came to make peace, ran away, followed by the Rev. hle. Usher. it is stated that a shot was fired by the rev, gentleman, but missed, and that he still followed and fired a second shot. Flinter then met him face to face, whereupon, it is stated, the Rev. Mr. Usher fired a third shot, which also missed. People crowded around and gave up Mr. Uusher t• the police, who let him go home without search. Mr. George O'Toole, a prominent shopkeeper and Land Leaguer of the town, had information sworn against Mr. Usher, and the latter was arrested. THE CONSTABULARY AGITATION RENEWED.—The dis- affection among the Irish constabulary has broken out anew at Limerick. Six ocestables wilt), it is supposed Is a punish- ment for their part in the recent movement were ordered to new stations declined to proceed, and received their dismis- sal. About 100 others announced an intention of resigning unless their comrades were re-instated, and ininerous other threatened resignations speedily followed as telegrams were forwarded to Cork, Londonderry, Waterford, Belfast, and other districts calling on the force generally to support the Limerick men. The Lard Lieutenant was eventually me- morialised, and Colonel Bruce arrived in Limerick on Mon- day. He told the six who had disobeyed orders that their resignations would not be received; and that if they did not leave for the north by the seven o'clock train on .Tues-

day they would be liable to four months' imprison- ment for disobedience. He gave them some time to reconsider their conduct. They did so, but adhered- to their original determination, and the rest threa- tened to resign in a body if any punishment was attempted. An explanation, however, contained in an official circular published in Limerick on Tuesday as to the cause of the order for the removal of the six sub-constables has pro- duced a good effect. It appears that the order was issued, not to punish them far their share in the strike threatened some weeks back, but because they had recently refused to share their quarters at New Pallas with a number of soldiers who were on duty there. All the sub-constables who had tendered their resignations have, at the request of •the Inspector-General, withdrawn them, and the men generally now seem contentea with a respectful memorial to the Lord- Lieutenant praying for the reinstatement of their late com- rades.

div.head: LIBERALISM IN WEST CHESHIRE.
div.p: LIBERALISM IN WEST CHESHIRE.
SPEECH OF MR. G. W. LATHAM.

On Friday evening a public meeting was held in the Town Hall of Nantwich in connection with a movement which is now on foot for the establishment of a new Liberal Club in that town. The only accommodation for the Liberal party in the shape of a club at present existing in this old Cheshire town are two or three rooms in the Town and it has been decided to leave these and to erect more suitable premises. Mr. Philip Barker occupied the chair at the meeting, and was supported by Mr. G. W. Latham, Mr. J. Tornkineen, Mr, W. Johnson, Mr. Thomas Wood, Mr. Thomas Pierce, Mr. J. Jackson, Mr. Lisle, Mr. J. Matthews, Mr. F. Walker, Mr. Parratt, and others. There waa a large attendance.
The HON. SECRETARY (Mr. Ambrose Jones) read letters of apology for uon-attendance from Mr. Fox-Bristowe and Mr. W. R. Kennedy, of Liverpool. After a brief address from the chairman,

Mr. G. W. LATHAM, who was received with cheers, moved :—" That this meeting possesses unabated confidence in her Majesty's Government, and hopes in the next session ' it will be able to pass bills for the benefit of the agricultural interest, the reform of the land laws, the household suffrage I in counties, a redistribution of seats and other desired mea- sures." He believed the majority of whole nation agreed iin their love and respect for Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) If Mr. Gladstone really was the guiding star of England, the , people must do all in their power to maintain him in office (cheers), and the only way of doing that was by returning Liberal members to Parliament. (Cheers.) It was important that the people of Nantvrich and West Cheshire should do their duty in this respect. He saw the other day that one of the hon. members for West Cheshire was kind enough to talk about an arrangement which he, his cousin, and his uncle had entered into, by which there should only be one Tollemache left to represent the comity, and in doing this ha seemed to think that he had done a very liberal thing. He (Mr. Latham) thought that the days of arrangements were over; he thought that the hon. member should have recollected that the power of voting was in the hands of the people, and was no lenger_conined to the landowners and their tenants, who were subservient to them. Ik was for the people to decide who should be elected,and not the landlords of West Cheshire. He would not tell the Liberals of that dis- •' trict that they must return Mr. Tomkinson at the next elec- tion, because he knew that in spite of all the Tollemaches they would do it t but he would tell them that they must return a second Liberal candidate, for it would be a sorry I triumph if they reduced that division of the county to a political nonentity. Mr. J. Tomkinson, who met with a cordial reception, seconded the motion. Speaking of the House of Lords, he said while he recognised to the full the ability and eloquence of members of that house, he must complain that although three-fourths of the ability, public spirit, and legislative talent belonged to the Liberal party, the Conservative leader could, when necessary, whip up a certain namber of young peers, who as a rule, took little or no interest in politics, and by the aid of their votes could frustrate the in- tentions of the other side. One of their own order had strongly advocated a reform of the House of Lords, so that no peers should take their seats until they reached an age of discretion—say thirty-five years. This seemed to him to be a fair and reasonable proposition. (Cheers.) The motion was carried with acclaniation. Mr. Wm. ;MUNSON' moved, and Mr. FRED WALKER seconded, the following motion, which was also carried "That this meeting recognises the value of the past services rendered by the Nantwich Liberal Club, and the importance of extending its usefulness; and therefore is of opinion that suitable premises should be secured • for carrying out its ob- jects, and that a joint stock company should beformed for that purpose." A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceed- ings.

div.head: CETYWAYO IN LONDON.
div.p: CETYWAYO IN LONDON.

On Saturday morning King Cetywayo admitted Mr. Thos. Bell, of Manchester, to an audience, and discussed with him the subject of the industries of that city. He listened with much apparent interest to a description of the Manchester manufactories and warehouses, and both he and his chiefs exhibited great delight when Mr. Bell showed them a new cotton blartket of striking colour which his firm are making for sale to the native tribes of South Africa. During the interview Cetywayo produced his own best blanket, which proved to be the production of a Kendal or Yorkshire loom. On Monday morning the Rev. A. Maclagen, for some time %missionary in Africa, had another interview with Cetywayo, in Melbury-road, when the reverend gentleman gave the King several suitable presents. The King after- wards signed the following letter, which he gave to Mr. Maclagen :—" I should be very glad if the Society for Pro- moting Christian Knowledge would give me copies of any books or other publications in the Zulu language, br any works in English, which might be useful to missionaries if translated into Zulu.—Signed, CirrYwAYo. Cetywayo, who remained indoors all Monday, went to Kew Gardens on Tuesday morning. The people soon be- came aware of his arrival, and so pressed against him that he left. The afternoon was spent indoors.

The first meeting of the Irish Land Corporation was held on Wednesday, at Lord Ardilaun's house, Dublin, under the presidency of the Marquis of Waterford. Arrangements were made for opening forthwith a branch office in College Green, Dublin.

AN ENCOUNTER BETWEEN Two PlKE.—Those gentlemen who formed a pike angling party to a well-known pike. water, one of the best fishing places in Sherwood Forest, on the borders of North Notts, witnessed the other day a strange and interesting battle between two large pike. It seems on one of the party making a cast with a live bait on, a fine fish at once seized it. No sooner had he done so than another equally fine one made a dash for the bait as well. Instantly a furious battle began between the two fish. Snapping at each other about the head and neck, the two worried one another very like two bulldogs. Twisting and coiling themselves, and darting about, now and again leap- ing up out of the water a foot or more, the struggle went on for fully three minutes. The fight would have lasted longer had not one of the gentlemen attempted and nearly suc- ceeded in getting one of them into his landing-net. This ended the battle, but the affair lud been so deadly that the water was tinged with blood, and both fish appeared much Injured about the head and shoulders. The fish were about a yard long, and probably about 121bs. each.—Land and Water.

div.p: M ISCELLANEOUS. 0- ------ ......,___. The Welsh S---'''----"'Cl-'''----'er-'-- into • ;un3ay Closing Act came operation in tome parts of the Principality on Sunday. The reports • how t 1 t , a persons craving drink did not grudge the trouble e„ a journey to districts which have not yet fallen under . he previsions of the new law. °n Saturday night, whilst Sir Julius Benedict was con- iiieting a full rehearsal of his new cantata " Graziella," atr nlingham Town Hall, he was seized with a fainting fit, ...Ind had to be removed, the rehearsal being abandoned. Sir Julius is reported to have since recovered. b The second formal proclamation of the holding of the _ vest°, Guild Merchant was made on Saturday, at noon. ' the Market-place steps of the Town Hall. The Guild ofoee Mayortilderrnan Edmund Birley) was attired in his robes ' 'steAlr. Bradlaugb, M.P., speaking at Oldham, on Sunday, • L;ncienaned in severe terms England's action in regard to ZigYPt. He asserted that the war was undertaken on be- . "if of the bankers of London, Paris, and Berlin, and that , bo reference was made to real British interests or to the a People of Egypt. 4- match for the swimming championship of England •• took" place on Hollingworth Lake on Saturday. The corn- • Petitors were Willie Beckwith, of London (the champion), and James Finney, the champion of Lancashire. Beckwith . ”°ll by about 20 yards. The course wee a distance of • One mile. Pre, p , -.AI RATES AND PAUPERISM.—A return issued from roc I'," statistical department of the Local Government Board . I.`,l°Nys that the amount expended in the 647 unions of Eng- ‘ttlld and Wales on the in-maintenance of paupers during li• 4°e. half-year ended Lady-day was £963,882, and in outdoor eeel,lef £1,287,156—a total of 2,251,038. As compared t w'th the corresponding period of last year, this aumunt re- poit.' • Presents a decrease of 19 per cent. .1 THE DUKE OF ALBANY AND THE PRESTON GUILD.—It 3 ofncially announced that His Royal Highness the Duke of lAlbany • , a will not be able to pay his promised vieit to the 1 1 .unild celebration at Preston. The Mayor of Liverpool has ,°...,ceired an intimation on the subject, in consequence of 2:410h certain preparations contemplated there to give the . "Itinguished visitor a welcome have been abandoned. The lkgreatest consternation has been produced in Preston by the latelligenne• ' The cricket match between the Australians and the Eleven ' of England was concluded on Tuesday at the Oval. At the 6 eornmencement of the day's play both sides had finished the - ,first innings, the Australians having scored 63, and the Eng- ,tah Eleven 101. On going in again on Tuesday morning - the Australians succeeded in sceriug 122, and as the English team,.. in their second innings only made 77, the match was "on by the colonists by seven runs. ~ GREAT TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION —A great teetotal uenionstratioe was held at the Crystal Palace on Monday, nnder the presidency of Cardinal Manning, when the Len- d°o branches of the League of the Cross held their annual ..f..ete. Nearly 20,000 persons attended, including deputations many large towns. Cardinal Manning delivered an laddress, after which a large number took the pledge efi . !naSSe. . DREADFUL BATHING FATALITY : THREE YOUTHS "ONVNED.—A lamentable catastrophe occurred on Monday bear Ilfracombe. Four youths from India under the care of ,-gt,bardians have been sojourning for a few weeks past at 'roYde. On Monday, in the temporary absence of their 11 , tat., they made their way to the shore and bathed. A - ground sea was running, and soon after entering the -. three of them were swept off their feet by a wave and carried away. The fourth could swim, and attempted to rescue his companions, but had a narrow escape from. Sharing their fate. Their bodies have not been recovered. BRUTAL MURDER IN MANCHESTER.—An inquest was held 4.00 Tuesday at the Manchester Workhouse, Crumpsall, touching the death of James Barrow, Si furniture porter, 50 ' of age. The deceased lived in Whitworth-street, tte, opposite to Michael Allen, a hawker. On the tat July a quarrel took place between the men and they fought. Allen, after getting the worst of the encounter, all into his house, and in ten minutes afterwards came out 'th a poker, with which he struck Barrow violently on the ea, ri. Barrow fell, and as he lay on the ground Allen-struck nal two or three heavy blows on the head. His injuries ansed his death on the -26th inst. A verdict of "Wilful urder " was returned against Allen. TEE REV. Mn. GREEN IN Ijis PRISON. Dr. Pusey ,rites as follows to the Times: —The character of the Rev. ;dr. Green has been so entirely misrepresented, as if he wil- ally remained in Lancaster Gaol, "keeping the door locked °n the inside," that it occurred to me that the following c`ceount of his condition from one who saw him lately might ,°llen the eves of some who would not jest at suffering : ~Augurt 24.—Mr. Green says in a letter which I had a few ' 'aYs ago, 'I do not know of any ray_efe_light whatever to ;.boourage me to hope that the morning is breaking. Day °Y day I scan my letters, like the servant who went again 'and again to look for the cloud over the sea, and each day there _is nothing.' Mr. Green was once a fine-looking plan; r is not so now ; he looks wasted and gaunt, although his tare is good. The room in which he is locked up looked to tile like a very large dungeon, with a huge fire. Ile must ae uncemmonly strong to have stood the trial so well; if he nad been delicate he must have died. He talked pleasantly: 0t a 1 word of self. He must be a very good man: certainly " Is a brave one." , „,..A. Ban BEGINNING.—A youth named William Hodge was charged at the Southport Police Court, on Monday, ?ith stealing £3O from his employer, a local ironmonger. le was sent with the money to the bank, but absconded iirith it to Liverpool, where he bought a steerage passage to W Tork, and fitted himself out for life in the States by ,",urohasine• a revolver, some ammunition, and a tobacc "' o Pe. Meese necessaries once obtained, however, his avail- able capital was reduced to a single copper coin as he had returned some cheques forming part of the stolen property to his father, whom he informed of the Transatlantic ex- Mition. Acting on this information the police at once owed and seized the lad on board a /teenier in the eereey. He was described to the magistrates as of respect - Able • erentage, and, his employer not pressing for a heavy -, he was sent to gaol for fourteen days, with hard

An :ish gentleman, who had arrived from Limerick that after- 'c'cln, and was waiting for the mail to London, entered the teneral waiting-room, and, feeling somewhat weary, ,411itretched himself at full length on one of the forms placed various parts of the room. In order to render himself r e,;3'nfortable he placed his Gladstone bag under his head to h'erve as a pillow. Whilst be was slumbering another anger entered the room, and he was observed by a young also waiting for a train, to commence tickling the lee Per with a small stick on the neck. He succeeded in liking him, and the owner of the bag suddenly got up and itted the room, leaving his property behind. Returning minutes later, the Irishman discovered.that the bag, - amongst other things contained a bench of keys, a Iree with three £lO and one a banknotes, also £4 in gold, A„ of dress, and a small case 3f medicines, had dis- ;reared. The young woman who witnessed the ;robbery thought the two men were frilnds' and that they ere perpetrating practical jokes. The thief is described as as about thirty ye..rs of age, and of a somewhat military ,pe.arance.
