div.p: Of 179,203 persons committed to prison last year, 30,840 could neither read nor write. A Glasgow correspondent telegraphs the statement that Mr. Gladstone will address his constituents in Midlothian this year, but the date is not yet fixed. The fire which broke out at Gvversyllt Colliery, two miles from Wrexham, on the 23rd inst., has now been got under sufficiently to enable workmen to commence removing the burnt material. A colliery explosion took place on Wednesday evening at Motherwell, near Glasgow, by which, according to the report, several men were injured, some so seriously that they are not expected to recover. It has been finally ascertained that the trial of Charles Soutar for complicity in the outrage at Dun Echt cannot be held at Aberdeen, but will take place at Edinburgh in November or December next. The Duke of Cambridge, who has been the guest of Prince Edward of Saxe Weimar since Saturday, on Monday in- spected the troops in Portsmouth garrison, concluding with a march past on Southsea• Comtnen. There were 4,500 troops on parade. On Saturday, Police-constable Jenkins, of the E Division was presented by the division with a handsome gold watch, in recognition of his bravery in jumping into the Thames from Waterloo Bridge and saving the life of Henry Chapman on the 14th July last. The business of the Southampton meeting of the British Association was brought to a close on Wednesday. The total number of tickets taken for the meeting was 1,253. Next year's meeting, to be held at Southport, will be com- menced on the 19th September. A box, addressed to a person in the neighbourhood of Inverness, was handed out from one of the passenger trains which arrived at Fort George in the course of 'Tuesday. When opened it was found to coqtain a living child, about twelve days old. The police are making inquiries into the matter. The Limerick Chronicle of Tuesday evening states that a respectable draper living in Main-street, Thurles, while making some alterations in his establishment, had occasion to remove a partition wall, and embedded in the centre he found a sum of over £4OO, made up of guineas, old notes. and silver coin. Sir W. Lawson ventured into the heart of Midlothian on Tuesday night to attack Mr. Gladstone on the Egyptian question. The hon. Baronet met, however, with a sing- ularly cold reception, and the meeting passed by a great majority a resolution thoroughly approving of the action of the Cabinet. There was an •exciting scene in Denbigh Police Court on Saturday, when four men were convicted for picking pockets at the railway station. One of them, a Glaswegian named Butler, had made a desperate resistance to arrest, and while in the dock he behaved in a scandalous and violent manner assaulting the detective who proved the case. Mr. Robert Whittaker' cotton spinner, Halliwell, was•on Monday fined by the Bolfon Magistrates £26, including costs, for running his mill twenty minutes beyond the legal hour. An inspector visited the mill at ten minutes to six o'clock in the evening and found the engine at work and fifteen persons employed, as alleged to complete an impor- tant contract. Mrs. Weldon was on Wednesday refused admission to the Birmingham Musical Festival, and she subsequently pro- ceeded to the police court, and asked a summons against one of the stewards for an assault alleged to have been com- mitted in preventing her entrance. The stipendiary referred her to a solicitor. Considerable excitement was caused by her proceedings. It is not expeCted that any leading member of the Government or the Opposition will be present at the Shef- field Cutlers' Feast this year. The occasion has been for some years steadily declining in importance. The bad taste shown by many of the Conservative guests in marking their dis- approval of the presence of political opponents has Lad much to-do with this result. A PRIZE FIGHT.—At Wednesbury police court, on Tues- day, Israel Jones and Edward Clare were charged with being principals in a prize fight. On Saturday afternoon the pri- soners fought in a field at Sedgley, in the presence of about 300 persons, for a heavy stake. A ring was formed, and the combatants fought until they were exhausted. The prisoners were directed to find heavy suretiee, or in default to be imprisoned for three months. A bricklayer named William Thompson was before the Hyde magistrates on Wednesday, on a charge of attempting to murder his wife. He induced the woman to return to his house, from which he had driven her by violence and threats. On Tuesday he went home drunk, and tried to cut his wife's throat with a table knife. The knife was dull, and fortu- nately no serious wounds were caused. The prisoner was sent for trial on the charge of wounding. PAUPERS AND RELIGIOUS SERVICES. Receetly the Bishop of Salford wrote to the chairman of the Bolton Board of Guardians, requesting that facilities might be afforded to inmates of the Workhouse to attend mass. The question came before the Guardians, and, on the motion of the Rev. S. Allen, it was unanimously resolved that the Roman Catholic inmates of the Workhouse be allowed to attend their own place of worship on Sundays. THE CHANNEL TIINNEL.—A farther inspection by the Board of Trade of the Channel Tunnel works took place on Saturday. The men now engaged on the works are only those who are actually necessary to look after the plant and machinery. Boring operations have been entirely suspended since the last application to the Court of Chancery. Col. Beaumont's compressed air locomotive engine, designed by that gentleman for the‘Channel Tunnel has arrived, but has not yet been lowered intn the tunnel. DEATH OF LADY HAVELOCK.—We regret to have to an- nounce the death of Lady Havelock, widow of Sir Henry Havelock, the captor of Lucknow, which occurred on Fri- day last at her residence in Kensington Irark Gardens. It may be remembered that a few days before the tidings of Havelock's death reached England letters patent to create him a baronet were directed. His widow, at the instance of the Queen, received the rank to which she would have been entitled if he had lived a little longer., and a pension of £l,OOO was bestowed upon her by Parliament. The Corporation of Birkenhead have adopted a bye-law which enables any peace officer to put a stop to the playing of bands of music in the streets of the a city of the future." The bye-law has been rebelled against, and a test case was brought before the Stipendiary on Wednesday. The defen- dant was the master of a school band, and he had refusal to desist from playing when it occurred to a policeman to order him to do so. Mr. Preston very promptly dismissed the summons, on the ground that the bye-law was inconsis- tent with the general law of the land, which permits the playing of music in the streets. SERIOUS THEFT OF BONDS.—Wednesday was settling day on the London Stock Exchange, and a daring robbery was perpetrated by some person evidently conversant with the method of condetcting business by memb,rs of the establishment. The person who committed the robbery had apparently learned that a firm of brokers bad to &liver a large amount of foreign bonds, and he presented bit-I:self at the office of the delivering firm, asking them for the bona, as they had to be sent up to the _West End and a cheque would follow. This being not an unusual cnstom the clerk was taken off his guard and banded over the bonds. The fraud was subsequently discovered on a person Iron% the delivering firm calling for the cheque. We understand the value of the bonds is at least £15,000.

SCHOOL .ACCOMMODATION AT BIRKENHEAD.—Notice is given by the Education Department that additional school accommodation for 2,o2o,children ismequired in the school district of Birkenhead—namely, for 1,160 children in Lower Tran:nere, 800 children in the Borough-road, near. Christ Church, Claughton' and for 120 infants between Park-road East and Bentinck-street—and that unless this additional accommodation is supplied, or is in course of being supplied with due despatch, within six months, a School Board will be insisted upon for Birkenhead. A school already exists in Bentinck-strea, which under a certified teacher would supply the wants of that district, and ,plans for a school for Christ Church, Clanghton, hays been approved by the Edu- cation Department. Whether, however, the additional accommodation in Tranmere can be so much as initiated within the six months is open to doubt, though the sup- porters of voluntary education will probably struggle bard b 5 avoid the creation of a School Board. THE ANTI-VICAR'S RATE WAR IN COVENTRY.—At Coventry Police Court, on Wednesday, 13 persons holding respectable positions, and leading members of the Anti- Vicar's Rate Association, were summoned for the non-pay- ment of the vicar's rate, in the parish of Holy Trinity. The ' case against Mr. Franklin was withdrawn the rate being paid, but Mr. Browett, who defended, desired it to be known that the rate was not paid by Mr. Franklin or by his desire or consent; he knew nothing about it until he received a receipt by post. Eleven cases were heard, Mr. Minister prosecut- ing. Mr. John Fairish, who defended, raised two points of law, but these were overruled, the magistrates deciding that he could not go behind the rate after it had been made and signed by the magistrates. There being no other defence except that of conscientious objection, the magistrates made an order for a distress warrant to be issued in each case. The court was crowded during the hearing, most of the Noncon- formist ministers in the city being present. ONE WHO HAS 66 SQUANDERED THOUSANDS."-011 SO tEr- day, at Lambeth, Edward Gillett, 83, attired in rags and in ' a filthy condition, and described as of "no home," was charged with begging in Hercules Buildings. The case was proved by a police constable, who stated that he had been informed that not long ago the prisoner inherited £3,000, which he squandered in a very short period.—Mr. Chance: Is that so, prisoner? Yes; and I have got another £l,OOO come.—Mr. Chance: And you admit haying squandered this large sum of money in a short time? Prisoner: Yes; it is quite true.—Mr. Chance: It is perfectly shockiny, to hear such a statement, especially when one sees the misery so often brought to light for the want of a few shillings. Are you, prisoner, willing to go to the workhouse for a week ? Prisoner: Yes. I hope you will not deal severely with me. , —Mr. Chance: You deserve little pity, and if you have, as you say, a further £l,OOO coming to you, I trust the lesson you have had will cause you to have your money placed in the hands of those who will lay it out for your benefit. The prisoner was then removed to the workhouse. Eprs's .COCOA„—GRATEFUL AND COMFORTING. By a

THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 2, The condemned convict Francis Hynes, lying in Limerick r ?T[ %T WAR IN EGY. PT. Gaol, still denies his guilt of the murder of Doloughty, but' he is stated to be resigned to his fate. The master cotton spinners of Bolton have declined to I grant the operatives a holiday next Wednesday to enable I them to take part in the trades' procession at Preston Guild. On Wednesday night, after returning home :from the I Theatre Royal, Hanley, an old lady, named Lucy Instone.l boarding-house keeper, living in Stafford-street, partook of a hearty supper of tripe, and shortly afterwards died. On Wednesday night, a fire occurred at a waste ware- house of Messrs. Stott, St. George's-street, Bolton. It was I caused by spontaneous combustion, and spread to two i upper storeys. The damage estimated by the firm at £5OO, I is fully insured. In a report issued on Thursday, the Select Committee of ! the House of Lords on the Irish Land Act state their inquiry is yet incomplete, and they rOcommend the re-appointment of the Committee next session, with a view to the con-1 tinuance of the inquiry. At the anneal special meeting of the Manchester, Liver- pool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society, held on , Thursday, at Preston, it was agreed to hold next year's I show at Liverpool. and to rait upon the mayor of the city in the coming December to ascertain what encouragement was likely to be offered. At the fortnightly meeting of the Haslingden Board of , Guardians, on Thursday, the clerk reported that the Local Government Board had sent the necessary order' for taking a poll of the ratepayers in the union on the subject of triennial electories, and that the voting papers would be delivered on the 19th September, and collected the following morning. Intelligence has been received by telegraph at Plymouth, of the fatal result to Lieutenant Porter, RE., of an accident he sustained a fortnight ago while on board a transport ex route for the seat of war. Lieutenant Porter was the only , son of Major-General Whitworth Porter, RE., of Plymouth, to whose family the death of a promising young officer has caused a terrible shock. The Dublin coroner, on Wednesday, held an inquest on a lady, named M'Nulty, found dead at her lodgings on the previous day. The deceased and her sister were left £2,000 each, but the money was all swallowed up in law proceed- ings, and both lived in an abject state of poverty. Their misfortune somewhat affected their minds, and both were under the hallucination that they were not sisters. At Middleton, on Thursday, George Wilson was charged with stabbing Edward Kay. The prosecutor stated that on the night of the-24th ultimo, after a dispute with the prisoner, the latter pulled out a pruning knife and ran it into his side. Dr. Sandford stated that the breast bone had intercepted the weapon, which would have otherwise caused death. The prisoner was committed for trial. Whilst the Salvation Army were marching through the streets of Bolton on Wednesday night with drums, tam- bourines, and cymbals, they were assaulted by a large mob of Irish, who hooted and jostled them, and attempted to wrest from them their musical instruments, pelting them with stones. Matters looked so serious at one time that many tradesmen closed their establishments, and eventually the police had to escort the army to their homes. On Thursday, a party of consta,bulary were dragging the canal near Leicester, on the banks of which a blood-stained hammer was found under extraordinary circumstances. Two boats passing' down the canal reported having seen a dead body in the water. The body, it is believed, is connected with the mysterious affair at Leicester Abbey, where the blood stains and marks of a struggle were found. The body has not been recovered.

An exciting scene was witnessed on Thursday morning at Portland Railway Station. A party of four lunatic con- victs were being conveyed-in charge of three warders to Woking prison, and on arriving at the platform, they made a rush at the officers, using as weapons everything that came to hand, and k;cking violently. A desperiie struggle ensued, lasting for a quarter of an hour, when the convicts were at lastovercome and placed in the train. It subse- quently trgEspired that they were lunatic,prisoners. Alter the performance of "Adrienne Lecouvreur," at St. George's Hall, Bradford, on Wednesday evening, Madame Sarah Bernhardt, whose impersonations of the title role had evoked the greatest enthusiasm, was taken seriously ill. Exhausted by the severity of her part she was taken with spitting of blood, and lost consciousness. Mr. Parkinson, surgeon, was in attendance for two hours before the actress could be removed to her hotel. On Thursday morning she was somewhat better, but unable to leave her bed. JOHN O'GROAT'S TO LAND'S giND ON A TRICYCLE.— Mr. Alfred Nixon, hon. secretary to the London Tricycle Club, writes to the Daily Chronicle:—lt may interest many of your readers to know that I have just succeeded in accom- plishing this long journey on my " Premier " tricycle, the first time it has ever been attempted on a tricycle, in 13 days 23 hours 55 minutes. I left John O'Groat.'s on Wed- nes3ay, August 16th. at 11 a.m., and reached Land's End, Cornwall, on Wednesday, the 30th, at 10-55 a.m. My machine weighs 051 b., and luggage (all of which I carried with me) bib. Distance, 095 miles. _ _ _ _

COURTS' COURT COSTS.—On Thursday the Act to amend the law relating to costs and salaries in county courts was issued. It is declared that no -person other than a solicitor of the Supreme Court shall be entitled to have or recover any fee or reward for appearing or acting on behalf of any other party in a county court. The Act is not to affect the right of a barrister to appear, or a solicitor recovering for such employment. Further a judge can now award costs on the higher scale, no matter what the amount recovered, or award the same to a defendant on a certificate that the case involved some novel or difficult point or a point of public interest. BOAT ACCIDENT: THREE LIVES ILOST—On Thursolay a fatal boat accident occurred near the South Pier, South Shields. A salmon boat, containing Thomas Coulter, John Galbraith, and William Baint, when engaged fishing got into broken ,water behind the South Pier and capsized, the whole of the men being drowned. The accident was observed by a man named Richard Elliott, who was on the pier at the time. He swam to Coulter's assistance, but the latter was entangled in the nets and held under the wate by the boat's mast, which had fallen upon him, and he was drowned. His body and that of Galbraith were recovered. The three men were married. There was a strong sea on at the time of the accident. A shocking affair occurred on Wednesday at Bradford. A man named Williams, a fishmonger, who lives in Man- chester-road in that town, keeps a number of cats. Yester- day one of these animals was greatly 'excited by an encounter with a dog, and rushing into the kitchen where William's little daughter, eleven months old, was seated, it attacked her in a savage manner. The father was attracted by the screams of the child, but he was compelled to kill the cat before he could get it away from the child, who is frightfully disfigured. It is doubted whether she will recover. The report of the Inspector of Reformatory and Industrial Schools, published on Thursday, states that the total num- ber of children under sentence of detention at the close of 1881 was 23,693, of which 19,037 were boys and 4,656 girls. The total number of scholars under inspection is 203, and the cost of maintenance £482,-602,0f which £263,053 was con- tributed by the Treasury. The inspector would like to see industrial sotools kept strictly for criminal cases, and educa- tional cases dealt with only in truant •or day industrial schools. If day industrial,schools and truant schools re- ceived more attention there woukt be a sensible decrease in the number of industrial schools and a considerable saving to the country even if the preaent rate of Government assistance was kept up.
PROGRESS OF THE CAMPAIGN.

Great progress has been made by Sir Garnet Wolselev since the defeat of the enemy on Thursday. The General has telegraphed that the defeat of the Egyptians on that occasion was mere complete than he had thought, and that they were completely routed. They fled in terror towards Zagazig, throwing away arms mad accoutrements as they went, and leaving many dead half-buried in the sand, while the corpses of others were thrown into the fresh water canal. Judging from the arms that have been picked up and the bodies that have been found, it appears that a very large proportion of the fugitive army must have consisted of prasuitry, who have been dragged into the field against theieCvill. On Friday, Sir Garnet found himself at the heal of thr whole of the First Division, backed by all the cavalry and sixteen guns, but the Egyptians had withdrawn their guns during the night, and on Sir Garnet advancing to battle the great difficulty of the British troops was to get near the Egyptians. Many of the infantry fled as fast as railway trains could carry them, and the cavalry retreated at full gallop. The British infantry had no opportunity of coming up with the foe, but the cavalry, under General Lowe, swept round to the enemy's rear and was in time to cut off the retreat of;the tail of the Egyptian force and to capture a number of railway trucks laden with provisions, five Krupp guns, a quantity of ammunition, and some Remington rifles. The fugitives were pursued to Mahsameh railway station, eight miles distant. THE CASUALTIES ON THURSDAY AND FRIDAY,

At Bradford (iVezt Riding) Police-court, on Thursday morning, Edwin Holmes, grocer and wine merchant at Keighley, and John M'Clelland, of London, were charged with forging a bank guarantee. It was stated on behalf of the prosecution that M'Cielland was, in 1677, the Keighley manager of the Bradford Old Bank, and Holmes was a customer of the bank. Holmes had a'secured overdraft at the bank of £l,OOO, but slightly increased it, and, when pressed for further security, M'Clelland sent to head quarters a guarantee for £5OO, which purported to be signed J. B. Myers, but was subsequently proved to have been written by M'Clelland himself, and, the prosecution alleged, signed by Holmes. The prisoners, who moved in the best society in Keighley, were remanded, being admitted to bail on-find- ing heavy surities. TIIE QUEEN'S DEPARTURE FOR SCOTLAND.—The Queen and Royal family left Osborne on Thursday evening, at half-past six o'clock, for Scotland, crossing the Solent to Gosport in the Royal yacht Alberta, escorted by the Elfin and Victoria. The weather was very rough, the sta being covered with mist and a heavy rain falling. The Alberta then returned to Osborpe, where she will remain until the Duke of Albany is convalescent. According to the latest accounts the Duke is not so well, but his condition does not create any alarm. The Queen's departure for Scotland is exactly a week after her usual date of quitting her marine residence, and ten days later than the puled originally determined upon. The principal reason for Her Majesty's delay is considered to have been the indisposition of the Duke of Albany. • I AN" INFAMOUS" DOCUMENT.---A case which in its re- suit affects probably thousands of persons in a bumble -station was heard on Thursday at the Burnley County Court. The "Singer" Sewing-Machine Company were the plaintiffs in an action against a Mrs. LiveAcy, who had bought a sewing machine from the Company, paying a certain sum at once, and promising a, weekly instalment of half-a-crown to clear off the balance. An agreement between the parties stipulated that if the price were not paid the Company had a right to seize the machine, even though the last instalment had been reached, and no remedy was placed within the reach of the purchaser, who in the agreement4or- felted any claim to recover money already paid. The Judge, on reading the document, said it was a " most in- famous" one, and promptly nonsuited• the Company, re- fusing to hear their legal representative or grant a case for a superior court. THE DWELLINGS OF AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS. A country rector writes to the Standard in the following plain terms on the dwellings of agricultural labourers:—" How can a man be expected to bring up his family with any sense of modesty when he, his wife, and sons, nnd daughters have tolive and sleep in two rooms; it is sickening to hear the pious horror with which some well-to-do-people speak of the immorality of the poor, of which they themselves, by their thoughtlessness or meanness, are the real cause. A landlord who allows men with families to have no better home than these two-roomed cottages is the first cause of every case of immorality which arises in that family." Is it not a pity plain speaking like this is not oftener heard from the pulpit instead of merely read in the newspaper? The Bishop of Manchester denounced these scandals to a Royal Commission nearly 20 years ago; but how little has been done'! Query, would it not have mended matters if occasionally instead of the lessons of the day the rural clergy had been ordered to read extracts from Dr. Fraser's report ? Pall Mall Gazette.
should b?, speedily beaten thev would n.) doubt be verifled, for in Egypt nothing succeeds like success, TETE INTENTION OF .TEIE ENENIY AT KAFR DO SVA R.

What may be the intention of the enemy at Kafr DJW.ir is still a mystery, but surprising activity is shown there. On Sunday night considerable reinforcements were seen to arrive, and early on Monday morning fresh tents were erected. Large numbers of the enemy have also been seen at Meks' where they have begun throwing up earthivorks. It is stated that the British think of cutting the dykes near the Meks Forts, and flooding the dry bed of Lake Mareotis, so that it will be impossible for the enemy to attack from that side. On the other hand, it is quite possible that the extra- ordinary activity of Arabi's forces may have for its object the prevention of a British attack. Judging, at all events, from the precipitate flight of Arabi's troops from Mahsameh, it can scarcely be supposed that they think of attack- ing the British entrenched position at Ramleh or the forts at Melo.

NEW EGYPTIAN MINISTRY. By the simple expedient of postponing consideration Le question as to the Chamber of Notables until peace and order have been restored, the difficulty in the way of the formation of an Egyptian Ministry has been removed, and the welcome announcement is made that the ministry lote been formed with Cherif as President and Minister of Foreign Affairs, and Riaz as Minister of the Interior. The imme- diate business before the new Ministry is to restore the Government of the Khedive throughout Egypt, and until that is done little progress can be made in other directions. The mere fact, however, that an influential and trustworthy Ministry has been formed will, when it becomes known, have an excellent effect in Egypt in turning wavering loyalty to the Khedive. We append the constitution of the Ministry :—Cherif Pacha, President of the Council and Minister for Foreign Affairs; Ifiaz Pacha, Minister of the Interior; Omar Pacha Lufti, Minister of War; Fakri Pacha, Minister of Justice; Haidar Pacha, Minister of Finance; Khaki Pacha, Minister of Public Instruction; Zeki Pacha, Minister of Wakfs; Ali Pacha Monbarek, Minister of Public Works.

A TURKISH COMMISSIONER WITH SIR *GARNET. A few hours after the announcement of the formation of the Ministry it became known that Sultan Pasha, with Fend Pasha and a staff of clerks, was to start immediately to join Sir Garnet Wolseley as the Khedive's commissioner, his special mission being to inform the natives that the object of the British expedition is to restore the 'authority of the Khedive and to free Egypt from military despetism. THE MILITARY CONTENTION. At the same time, the Egyptians will learn that the Sultan has agreed to send his troops to assist the British in restoring order in Egypt, and that he has proclaimed Arabi a rebel. The Turkish troops, it is true, have not yet arrived in Egypt, nor has the proclamation ef Arabi been issued, but on Sunday Lord Dufferin was officially informed by the Turkish Premier that the Sultan accepted the Military Convention on England's terms, and would declare Arabi a rebel as demanded. Should this promise be duly carried out, following, as it will, immediately upon the formation of the Khedive's Ministry and the despatch of his commis- sion to Sir Garnet's camp, its effect in Egypt should be highly favourable

div.head: TERMS OF THE CONVENTION.
div.p: THE TERMS OF THE CONVENTION.

The following are the terms of the Convention :-1. The Turkish contingent is to consist of from 5,000 to 0,000 men, and is to be subject to augmentation by common under- standing between the two Powers. 2. The movements and operations of the Turkish troops are to be regulated in accordance with previous agreement between the Turkish and English Commancters in Chief. 3. The Turkish troops will land at Aboukir, Rosetta, or Damietta. 4. To secure the requisite unity of action an English Commissioner will be attached to the Turkish contingent and a Turkish Com- missioner to the English headquarters. 5. The two armies will evacuate Egypt simultaneously, unless it should ha found necessary by common consent to prolong the Turkish occupation. The Turkish Government at the last moment waived its demand for the landing of troops at Alexandria. The English will have an imperative veto upon all move- ments of the Turkish troops. ARABI SUES FOR AN ARMISTICE.

A second edition of Thursday's Daily Chronicle gives the following from its Port Said correspondent, dated Thursday, 7-45 a.m. —" Arabi has asked for an armistice for eight days. Sir Garnet Wolseley has refused this, but offered one day. Nothing, however, will be doing for several days unless Arabi again forces our hand. Arabi thinks little of the affair of the 28th, his outposts Mug hardly farther than before the fighting. Arabi was recognised yesterday by Egyptians who were deserting to us. Troops are being brought to the front. Trains are returning daily to the front. The 72nd is at Mahuta ; Ismailia is refilling."
IMPORTANT ARRIVAL OF NEGOTIATORS AT THE CAMP.

The Daily News published a second edition on Thufsday with the following telegram, dated Ismailia,. Thursday, 4 a.m. :—" Sultan Pasha and the late Governor of Zagazig have come into the English camp, and wish to negotiate— at any rate, it is safd here they do—and great importance is attached to their visit. The former was President of the Chamber of Notables. Both are moderate men, though patriotic; and are probably convinced that it is useless to continue the war. The supposition at Ismailia is that, as we threaten the very heart of Egypt, it will not be surpris- ing if the country should submit. We do no count on the certainty of such a prudent course being adopted. The will of the fanatical element is strong. Amongst some classes Arabi still has the power of the sword to silence his critics. It is now clear that Monday's engage- ment was caused by the need of action on the enemy's side to keep his men in good spirits. Arabi himself is re- ported to have been present, and, though not in command, to have used all his persanal influence to encourage the emy to fight. Hence their obstinate advance, and the hard work they did in the night dragging away their guns which welled captured. Every effort is being made among the Egyptian infantry to screw them up to resistance, but without much siiccess. The Bedouins, horsemen full of fanatical desire and wili, continue the war; but the regulars are much discouraged. The Egytian Notables begin to des- pair of further resistance. Our sick and wounded have all been brought down from the front and carefully disposed of, either in the pilace hospital here or on board ship. The commisiariat struggles gallantly to send up supplies to the front; and now, that the railway is in working order our troops are better fed._ _

div.head: ADVANCE OF TROOPS. SAFETY OF MISSING OFFICERS.
div.p: ADVANCE OF TROOPS. SAFETY OF MISSING OFFICERS.

A second edition of the Daily Telegraph, published at 11 a.m. on Thursday, says :—"'Tlae following is an extract from a special telegram which we have received this morn- ing :—" Isucailia, Kassassin, Aug. 30. (Via Port Said, Aug. 31, 8.17 aan.)—All is now quiet, and the completion of the transport arrangements is awaited. Colonel Milne Home, who was reported to be missitag with several troopers of the let Life Guards, has arrived in camp all safe. It appears he was separated from our men with several others, who rallied sufficiently to keep off loose bodies of Bedouins. There are now seven troopers missing, and also Lieut. Gribble. It is to In regretted that a few of the wounded fell into the hands of the enemy, by whom they have been sadly mutilated. General Wolseley and the members of his staff nem yesterday returned to Ismailia. All the troops arc moving rapidly to the front, and a train has been taken as far as Kassassin. The water in the canal has been sinking for the last two days, and the smells are most offensive, but the troops wonderfully well. Of the sick and wounded, however, in the hespital near here there are, I understand about 300."
MI'SCELLANEOUS IrEms. On Saturday the line was restored from Suez to Chalouf. It seems that the Austrian boat's crew arrested at Aboukir have been released.

•The Kassassine Lock, on the Fresh Water Canal, is now in possession of our troops, and the water supply.continues fairly good. Two English °fliers who were sent into Syria to purchase ; animals for the expedition have been robbed of the money entrusted to them, and, it is feared, murdered. A favourable circumstance for the army is that it will now soon enter the delta of the Nile, where it will be relieved from the scorching heat of the desert. A special correspondent at Port Said states that a steamer arrived there ou Friday night with Turkish troops. The officer in command was not permitted to land the men, and in the morning he steamed away. From India we learn that a reserve is being formed to strengthen, if necessary, the contingent already in Egypt, and that the whole control of the Indian troops has been placed in the hands of Sir Garnet. It is announced in the Court Circular that the Queen was greatly gratified by the news of Sir Garnet Wolseley's success, and heard by telegraph with thankfulness of the safety of the Duke of Connaught. The German correspondents with the English Army state ' that they are very well treated, and surrounded by all pos- sible comfort. They complain, however, that the tele- graphic traffic is very narrowly watched by the staff officers. Sir Garnet sets an excellent example of activity and vigour. Taking advantage of the coolness of the night, he journeyed to Ismailia on Saturday evening, arriving there at ten o'clock, and after.six hours' work, left again at four on Sunday morning for the front. The value of the Fresh Water Canal was shown on Friday, when Admiral Seymour sent a pinnace with a 9-pounder gun up the Canal to help Sir Garnet to dislodge the enemy, and the Admiral was also organising a boat service by which supplies could be sent to the front until the railway was restored to working order. A correspondent at Alexandria telegraphs the refrisal, " doubtless for high military reasons," as the correspondent says, of Sir Garnet Wolseley to allow Lord Charles Beres- ford to accompany the British army as aide-de-camp to the Khedive, although his lordship's application was strongly supported by his Highness. Official denial is given to the rumour that Sir Garnet Woiseley has asked for reinforcements. Should, however, more troops be required, it is understood that they could be at once drawn from the Mediterranean stations, their places being filled from England; and a considerable additional force is also ready for despatch from India. A Constantieople correspondent informs us that the withdrawal of the orders by the Porte prohibiting the ex- portation of mules, pack-saddles, &c., for Egypt was due to ; strong representations and precise and explicit demands ; made by Lord Dufferin, who made no secret of his determi- nation not to allow such obstruction to be permitted. A telegram from Alexandria, states that the Bedouins in large force made an attack on Sunday, at Mex. They were repelled after a considerable amount of firing, one soldier of the 95th Regiment being killed and another wounded. At Ramleb artillery firing was kept up, and it
was rernarked that the enemy's practice has considerably improved.

An order was received at the Royal Arsenal, Woo:wich, on Wednesday, which appears to foreshadow a longer cen- tinuance of hostilities in the E.-Ist than had been anticipatel. This order referred to the sending out at once of the light siege train, which consists of 36 pieces. Intimation was also sent from the War Office to the Ordnance Department at Woolwich that provision would have to be made for the early despatch to Egypt of a balloon equipment. No serious fighting seems to be anticipated in the neigh- bourhood of Alexandria, and on Wednesday the brigade of Highlanders that has been stationed at Ramleh embarked on board transports for Ismailia, where there will be consider- ably more work for them to do. Another reconnaissance from Fort Meks shows that the enemy is stron !ly entrenched in that quarter, and well "sup Plied with heavy guns. News has reached the Khedive from Kafr Dowar that Toulba Pasha, the man upon whom Arabi chiefly relied in political matters, has died, and the general belief is that he has been poisoned, as he was regarded with much jealousy by some members of Arabi's staff. Arabi has thus been deprived of the counsel of both Toulba and Mahmoud, and consequently is now both in political and military matters largely dependent upon himself. Regret is now expressed that balloons have not been included amongst the British munitions of war, as by their Aid it would have been possible to have speedily and accu- rately ascertained the exact position of affairs. From a leading employe of the Canal Company, who had been in constant communication with Arabi, a correspondent learned that that chief some days ago formed a plan to retreat, if he were worsted, into Tripoli, after destroying Cairo as far as he might be able. Her Majesty is teken very great interest in the Egyptian war. On Saturday two officers of the Excellent, with a party of seamen, proceeded to Osborne House, taken with them a seven-pounder gun, together with Nordenfeldt, Gat- Hug, and Gardiner machine guns* Each of these weapons was fired in Her Majesty's presence, and it is understood that she took much interest in these, the, most effectual means yet devised of shooting a large number of men in a short time. The Standard also announces that the Queen has expressed personally to some of the colonels commandant of the Royal Marines "her sense of the admirable behaviour of the officers and men of the Royal Marine forces through- out the present campaign in Egypt. Her Majesty has taken the greatest interest in the doings of the Marines," and the Standard believes that at the Close of the operations some means will be found "for marking in a substantial manner the Queen's appreciation of the soldierly qualities displayed by the representatives of the corps throughout the present crisis."

div.head: AND THE PRISONERS.
div.p: AND THE PRISONERS.

The British casualties on Thursday and Friday are offici- ally stated to have been five killed, five severely wounded, and twenty-two less 'severely. There were, however, 41 cases of sunstroke, which is, perhaps, as small a number as could be expected, considering the arduous nature of the work to be done and the scorching heat of the sun. One correspondent says the marching was like being in front of a rousing kitchen fire for ten hours, and that his stirrup- irons became so hot that they burned his boots. Amongst the prisoners taken is Mahmoud Fehmy, who at the time of the military emute at. Cairo figured conspicuously amongst the rebellious colonels, and has held the rank of chief engineer and military adviser in Arab's army. He had doffed his:own uniform and put on that of a private, but his identity was revealed by another prisoner. It is said, too, that his son has also beeecaptured. Describing the capture of Arabi's chief advis2r, the Standard correspondent says :—" While General Drury- Lowe was surveying the village captured, a respectable man came up and entered into conversation with him in French. While they were talking an Egyptian .)fficer passed as a prisoner under an escort. The Egyptian officer exclaimed to General Drury-Lowe, "That 'llan y‘ou are speaking to is Mahmoud Fehmy, Arabi's second in command." The man was at cuss arrested, and was brought here in the evening. This capture is of very great importance. It appears that Mahmond went out from Tel-el-Kebir in a train: to recon- noitre, alighted, and ascended a hill. While he was absent the engine-driver caught sight of our soldiers, and at once put on steam and returned. Fehmy, with his servant, ignor- ant of the reason of the sudden retirement of the train, came down the hill and walked along the line into the village, where be expected to find Egyptian troops. Finding it oc- cupi.e2d by the English. be with great coolness and presence of mind walked up to the General and entered into conversa- tion with him and would probably have been able to retire unmolested ad be not been -recognised by the Egyptian prisoner. Next only to Arabi himself the capture is the most important which could have been effected. Mahmoud Fehmy is the most distinguished pupil which the military school of Cairo has produced. Before the troubles began he was Inspector-General of the Fortifications. When Arabi rose to power, be supported him warmly, and was by him named Minister of Public Works. He designed the lines of Karr Dowar and Tel-el-Kebir, going to the latter place nominally to give his advice to Raclal Bey, who commands the troops there, but practically he took the command out of the latter's hands. All the important telegrams which have fallen into our hands are addressed to Mahmoud Fehmy, and it is evident that he had despatched some wholly fabulous accounts of the fighting, since the telegrams both from Arabi and Cairo contained the most enthusiastic congratulations upon the victories which he had reported. He is regarded as the Nana ..3ahib of the Egyptian revolt. Fehmy says that no troops have come down from Kafr Dowar to rein- force those at Tel-el-Kebir." • AN ENGAGEMENT AT KASSASSIN.

Or. Saturday—that is, the day after the battle—the main bady of the strength of our infantry division was encamped near Mahuta (Guards' Brigade' Marines, Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry, York and Lancaster, King's Royal Rifle Corps). A cavalry division some 19 squadrons strong was at Mahr.arneh, and a small advanced guard composed mainly of Artillery was at Rros.s.ssin Lncl.s. On Sunday Sir Garnet Wolseley was reconnoitring beyond that place with the advanced guard, which had been completed by the march to the front of Hie Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry and the *York and Lancaster regiment. Sir Garnet appears then to have returned to headquarters at Ismailia, so that the commands would be, the advanced guard (21 battalions, 5 guns, mounted infantry and small cavalry detachment) at Kassassin under General Graham; the Cavalry Division, General Drury Lowe, at Mallsameh (Household Cavalry, 4th a.nd 7th Dragoons, 3rd Beneal Cavalry, 30th Bengal Lancers, the whole in two brigades, of which the first is under Sir Baker Russell) ; the First Infantry Division under General Willis at Mahuta.. The camp of the latter seems to have been at Abu Risheh, behind Mahuta. On Monday evening the advanced guard was attacked by a force of the enemy numbering eight battalions and 12 guns. General Graham was reinforced by the arrival of an additional bat- talion, and supported by the cavalry from Mahsameh. He then attacked the enemy in front with his infantry, while Sir Baker Russel's Cavalry Brigade charged them in flank, acting, of 'course, under the general direction of Major General Drury Lowe. The enemy was defeated with con- siderable loss, but succeeded, in the obscurity of the moon- light, in carrying off his guns. It is reported that Ourabi was himself present at the action. TI/0 English loss was inconsiderable. The following is Sir Garnet Wolseley's account of the engagement which is dated from Kassassin Lock, twenty-one miles west of Ismailia :

"General Graham, commanding this post, was attacked ye.sterday (Monday) evening by about 12 guns arid eight battalions. Our men behaved extremely well, and inflicted severe loss upon the enemy. At first Graham had but five guns and 2-t- battalions, a small detachment of cavalry and mounted infantry. Graham, being reinforced by another battalion, attacked the enemy in front, while the First Cavalry Brigade, under Sir Baker Russell, charged them in flank, sabring a considerable number. The caralry were well handled by General Lowe. General Graham's disposi- tions were all they should Lave be-en; and his operations were carried out with that coolness for which he has always been well known. Arabi Pasha was on the field during the action. The cavalry charged by moonlight, and were unable to secure the guns, which the enemy carried off in the night, but leaving all the ammunition on the ground. The list of casualties is heavy, but much lighter than at first supposed, the corrected list showing only five killed, and about forty wounded. As to the enemy's loss no correct estimate can be formed. General Drury-Lowe, however, says that the ground was strewn with the dead, and some accounts place the number at 2,000. It was fortunate for the enemy that the rout took place in the dark, otherwise the seven guns that formed the battery through which the Gotards charged, would assuredly have fallen into the hands of the British, and!many prislner3 might have been taken. Sir Garnet was at Ismailia when he heard of the fight, and be immediately set off for the scene of action.

GENERAL LOWE'S ACCOUNT OF THE ACTION AT KASSASSIN. , The folloiing is a summary of General Lowe's report on the cavalry action of. the 28th ittst. " Hearing in the afternoon that the enemy were ad- vancing to attack Graham at .KassaFsin I turned out with the Household Cavalry, 7th Dragoon Guards, and four guns of N Battery A Brigade Horse Artillery, and advanced to- wards the enemy's left. Remained some hours. Returned to camp at 4-30 p.m., finding that the enemy's attack was only a distant artillery ilre. About 5-30 I received a message from Graham that the enemy were advancing in force. I turned out again, and in compliance with Graham's request, proceeded to attack the enemy's left flank. We made a wide circuit, brought the guns into action, and Sir Baker Russell charged home with the Household Cavalry well led by Colonel Ewart. The enemy's infantry was completely dis- persed. The ground was strewed with his dead. The cavalry charged through a battery of .seven or nine guns, which would have been brought in had it been daylight. The enemy removed them during the night. The greatest praise is due to all ranks of the Household Cavalry. I may add on my own account that their excellent behaviour at all times is on a par with their gallantry in action. Most of the wounded brought to hospital here last night; the remainder will be here to-day. The enemy is throwing up works in front of Graham."

div.head: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN SUEZ AND ISMAILIA.
div.p: COMMUNICATION BETWEEN SUEZ AND ISMAILIA.

The most important item of news from Ismailia is the an- nouncement that a railway train has arrived there from Suez. An engine was taken from Alexandria and placed on the railway at Suez, and with nine trucks attached it ran through to Ismailia in five hours. Its freight included a detachment of men from the Euryalus and the Ruby, with a Gatling and a 7-pounder gun, and half of a company of Madras Sappers and Miners. The appearance of an engine on the railway is an event of the first importance, and at the front it is anxiously looked for. The Cairo line is open 'as far as Ramses, but there a great sandbank had been been thrown across it. This, however, is being removed, and very shortly the armed train which the blue jackets have fitted up, and had drawn to R tnises by horses, will be pushed on to the front, where it will be invaluable for recon- noitring. The Indian cavalry, too, are a great acquisition, and will relieve the heavier cavalry from England of much work for will& the Indian contingent is better adapted.

. - Deserters' stories may not be worth much, but if the statements of six officers who have deserted from Arabi are to be trusted, the troops who were ignominiously fleeing before the British on Friday must form a portion of his best troops. He was, in they say, at Ismailia up to Monday, and had twenty thousand of his best troops there, as well as artillerymen recently taken from Fort Aboukir. They also state that Arabi's extortions and oppressions are much re- sented by the Egyptian people, who are longing for the English to deliver them from his yoke, and that even at Cairo his popularity has vanished. div.head: COST OF CRIME AND POLICE IN
div.p: THE COST OF CRIME AND POLICE IN
LANCASHIRE.

Blue-books have acquired a proverbial reputation for their general want of interest, and it is possible that, acting in the spirit of the old saw of hanging a dog for its bad name, the public sometimes lose information of interest and importance from contemptuous indifference to this weighty class of literature-if it is literature. On the present occasion we propose to extract from the ponderous return of the "Judi- cial Statistics" for last year some information as to the extent and cost of crime in the county palatine of Lan- caster. The habitually criminal classes of the county so far as they are "known to the police" amount to 5,288 per- sons. They consist of 523 lads and 72 girls under 10 who were known thieves; of 2,195 men and 931 women over that age engaged in stealing; of 91 men and 35 women engaged in the reception of stolen goods,; of 215 males and 62 females under 16, and 1,247 males and 407 females over that age of whose honesty there were grave suspicions. Of the " business " haunts of the criminal classes, if we may use the term, there are 116 returned as places for the recep- tion of stolen goods. That 90 public-houses and 70 beer- shops should be affected by thieves and burglars is not perhaps surprising, but that 12 coffee-shops should be so patronised may strike teetotallers with surprise. Two of these anti-alcoholic but predatory taverns are situated in Manchester and six in Preston-the birthplace of teeto- talism. Is the temperance reformation affecting even the Ibt of the burglar? Adding to those already named 238 "other houses," we have a total of 621 establishments in the county known to be habitually used by thieves and depredators. The number of indictable offences not sum- marily disposed of amounted to 12,759. The influence of meteorology upon crime is a not unpromising subject for philosophical investigation, but the figures as to Lancashire do not vary greatly /or the different seasons of the year. The months of January, February, and March showed the maximum of 3,273 offences, but the minimum of 3,152 in October, November, and December is not far 'behind. The January quarter, when the burglar and his associates in crime might be hoped to be contemplating the "turning over a new leaf," is unfortunately the period when cri- minal activity is at its height. The exertions of the pollee appear to have been greatest in July, August, and September, when they apprehended 1,116 persons, and least in January, February, and March, when but 937 per- sons came into their clutches for offences of this description. It will be observed from these figures that when the criminals are the most active the police are most supine or most unfortunate. The total number of persons arrested for indictable offences was 4,209, of whom 2;887 were men and 1,322 women. Of these persons not less than 993 were discharged for want of evidence! From this it may be con- cluded that the admonition against excess of zeal is not always present in the policeman's mind. Of the 4,209 per- sons indicted 859 men and 383 women were known thieves, 286 were prostitutes, 17 men and six women were vagrants, 266 were suspicious characters, whilst 145 men and 42 women were habitual drunkards. From the details given as to those summarily dealt with it appears that the lesser offenders included 2,091 men and 873 women who were known thieves, 8,050 prostitutes, 985 males and 253 female vagrants; and 2,070 men and 491 women of suspicious character. No less than 9,362 men and 3,501 women are registered as habitual drunkards. Altogether 103,5(32 men and 27,452 women were dealt with under the summary jurisdiction of the magistrates. The nature of the offences committed by Lancashire criminals will be sufficiently indicated by the figures showing the numbers committed or bailed for trial. 444 were thus dealt with for offences aglinst the person, but more than one-half of these were charged with assault, 'whilst 25 were indicted for shooting ad maiming and six for murder. and three with endangering the safety of rail- way passengers. The violent offenders against property were 394 in number. The offenders against property whose thefts were not accompanied by violence were 1986. The malicious offences against property, including eight cases of arson, were 23 in number. There were 57 forgers and passers of false currency, and 97 persons were charged with "other offences," including 2T apprehended for riot, breach of the peace, and pound-breach," and 21 would-be suicides. It may be of interest to know that there were no cases of abduction, unlawful abandonment of children under two years of age, "breaking within the curtilages of dwelling- houses and steaiing ;", " stealing in dwelling-houses, persons therein being put in fear ; " of sending menacsing letters to extort money. Lancashire in common with the rest of England enjoyed a complete immunity from piracy during the year under review. These was in the county neither I cattle stealing or sheep stealing, nor theft of goods in pro- cess of manufacture. No attempt was made to set fire to , house or shop, "the persons being therein," nor was there any attempt to set fire to crops or heaths, to destroy silk, woollen the., goods in process of manufacture, or to destroy hop binds, trees, and shrubs growing, s,sc. No letter was sent threatening to barn houses. There was no forgery of bank notes, no high treason, no aiding of smugglers, deer stealing, taking fish in enclosed waters, sedition or rescue, and refusal to aid the peace 'officers. At all events, if any of these crimes and misdemeanours existed they passed un- detected. It may be remarked as showing the rela- tive criminality of the two sexes that in the five years 1877-81 there were 11,352 men and 4,322 women committed or bailed for trial, and that in the five years preceding the figures were-men 9,423, women 4,019. It would thus appear that the women of the criminal classes have been, to a certain extent, mending their ways. The number of prosecations daring theeyear was 3,750, and the total amount paid by the Treasury for such prosecutions at assiz,s, quarter sessions, and under the , Summary Jurisdiction Act of 1870 was .L 3,799 Gs. ld. The 1 police establishatent of the county is necessarily large. ' There is in the first place the Chief constable of the county, who has under his immediate control 1,215 men, but in addition to this each borough has its own separate force. Taking these into account the peace officers of the county may be said to consist of the chief constable of the county, 14 head constable of boroughs, 52 superintendents, 204 in- spectors, 332 sergeants, 3,183 constables, 38 "additional constables," and 94 detectives. The reign of law is thus enforced by 3,918 men, whose duties, however multifarious in character, are all intended for the preservation of the lives, peace, and property of the lieges of the Dachaes of Lancaster. The cost of this small army is of course large. Without going into the details of salaries, allowances, clothing, accoutrements, horses, station-houses, it may be well to state the total cost of each separate din:sic& of the police. s, d. Lancaster County Police Ashton Blackburn 9,745 1 9 Bolton Lancaster Liverpool Manchester Oldham .1,386 16 8 Preston Rochdale Salford Southport 3,075 4 1 Stalybridge Warrington Wigan 4,695 3 10

400,194 13 10 The gross tottl is certainly one sufficiently larze to attract the attention of the most careless observer, and tbongh the local ratepayer may rejoice in the fact that the Imperial Treasury contributes a sum of £161,353 S. W., the relief is more apparent than red, since most persons have to con- tribute to the national as well as to the local taass.— Manchester Gitordian.

A man named Joseph Burn; was c):nmitted for trial by Mr. Mansfield, on Saturday, for deliberately going OP window of a jeweller in Dale-strest, Liverpool, sma3l?:rumnl,:i sheet of plate glass with a stone, and snatching a brooch. Prisoner said he was starving at .the. time.

ITHE LIVERPOOL POST AND WORM lioliSE LITERATURE. It is always difficult to decide where liberality with other , people's money passes the line of justifiable expenditure. some little time ago several marble baths were fitted up i- the Birkenhead Workhouse, and though baths are, of course, very necessary things in such an establishment, the rate. , payers could scarcely be expected to warmly apprar,.! the e_ use of marble. The Warrington Guardians have this week _ had a question of expenditure before them which invol7n It . very small outlay, sod yet raises a point which is not easy to decide. The order book " contained an entry -for the purchase of the Graphic and the Illustrated London Yews,. and Mr. Longshaw objected to these purchases on the ground of extravagance. Mr. Woelfall remarked that the papers were fcr the officers, and if that were the case, it would at once decide the matter, for whatever question there may be - as to purchasing these papers for the paupers, there cla be no doubt that they should not be bought for the oftlee7s. The clerk, however, corrected Mr. Woolfall, and explained that the illustrated papers were for the inmates of the hospital, and even economists will scarcely like to deprive sick paupers of the entertainment to be gathered from the illustrated newspapers. Another Guardian, however, thought that the Graphic, the Illustrated London News, and. Punch were too expensive papers for the inmates of a Workhouse, and finally the matter was left to the fleese Committee. No one who has any knowledge of the weariness of life in a hospital will begrudge the inmates of the workhouse sick wards the relief that is- to be found in looking at pictures in newspapers or in reading -' the letterpress of the illustrated or comic papers, but in most places there are to be found those who take pleasure Irt supplying luxuries to the sick poor. If the good-natured, people who pour a steady stream of religious literature, not always the most fascinating of its kind, upon the poor, ' whether in or out of workhouses, could only realise the dulness of the lives of those in whom they take so muck interest, and endeavour to relieve that dulness by dis- tributing light literature and pictorial publications, their , periodical visits would be hailed with deeper joy. Wnen, - however, it comes to buying illustrated and comic papers, magazines, and other light literature for paupers with the hard earned money of ratepayers, who cannot afford such .4 luxuries for themselves, sympathetic guardians, who also feel strongly their duty to the ratepayers, find themselves ire a most unpleasant position.. The probability is that the ratepayers would not much obj-,,et to the purchase of the papers if they felt convinced that they were really for the use of the sick and the infirm, but they will strongly sus- pect the real object of the purchase to be the entertainment of the workhouse ofticials.—Liverpeel Post.

, . MRS. WELDON AND M. GOUNOD . . . Oa Thursday morning, consequent upon the fact becom:. . - ing known that Mrs. Weldon wourd, through counsel, make . another application for a summons for assault, the Birming- ham Police Court was crowded soon after the opening of the - - doors. Mrs. Weldon, who was seated immediately behind ~ e her counsel, Mr. Dominick Daly (Midland circuit), and he solicitor, Mr. lienunant, appeared to feel much grief, freer quently giving vent to tears during the half-hour she was waiting for her "case " to come on. Shortly after twelve ' , o'clock the learned counsel said he had respect- fully to ask the magistrates to grant Mrs. Wel- don the summons which she herself bad ap- plied for in person, but had been refused. Before . proceeding to do so, he wished strongly to complain of the offensive references which had appeared in the public prose respecting the lady. She had been described as a "woman,' . and there was really no foundation—(laughter)--no foune , dation for the statements that she intended to disturb the - - audience or interfere with M. Gounod. As a great lover of 1 - music she naturally desired to be present. There was no truth in the statement which appeared in a London paper es., . that Mrs. Weldon had a pistol in her pocket. (Laughter).' —The Stipendiary: Do you apply for a summons against the newspaper ?—Mr. Daly: No, sir.—The learned counsel proceeded to argue that the magistrates had no alternative but to grant a summons, an assault, not only technical, but , an assault with sodae slight violence, having been corn- - - ' mitted. Mr. Farmer, against whom he wished a - summons, placed both hands on Mrs. Weldon's • , , shoulders, and pushed her from the entrance.—The Stipene • - diary: Do you contend that the magistrates have no disuses tion with regard to granting or refusing your applicstion —Mr. Daly replied that he was sure the stipendiary was , lawyer enough and conscientious enough, sitting there as a - man and as a magistrate, not to put Mrs. Weldon to the - , expense of applying for a mandamus, which must inevitably , ' - - issue if the granting of the summons was refused.—After some discussion the stipendiary said he had no doubt some-. one did lay hands on Mrs. Weldon, but he could see no ' reason why he should give a different decision io that which , ' - , e he gave on the previous dg. She had, of course, a perfect -; right to apply for a mandamus if she chose, and he should .i. ~ have to answer it. Te _ - .- - • The grave has just closed over the mortal 'relr,eins of ' Edmund Jones, of Liverpool, one of the veteran-, or e.her -•- , . . Chartist agitation, who possessed extraordinary gifts of' f--- - ..... : natural oratory. Mr. Jones, tillo was of Welsh extraction, z- • --- settled early in his life as a basket maker in Liverpool, and , took an active part in both the Free Trade and Chartist , • ; agitations. When the Chartists had been led by the influence _ of Feargas O'Connor into violent courses, Edmund Jones • , used his singularly powerful gifts to restrain them from vairt attempts.at physical force, and after the arrest of Frost, Williams, and Jones at Newport, he, with great difficulty, restrained their followers from repeating a like foolish out- break. After the collapse of the Chartist agitation, Mr. Jones threw himself with his accustomed energy into the _ Co-operation and Temperance Movements, and his house at - Liverpool became the rendezvous of advanced -industrial politicians. About ten years ago his'sympathies were en- _ listed in the movement for the repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts, after attending a perblie meeting on the sub- . ject. Soon after he became the President of the Working Men's National League for the Repeal of the Acts; and, une , til he was laid aside by illness, he was untiring in his advo- cacy of the cause. Though deprived of the advantage. of - -._ even elementary education in his youth, his natural abilities - made him an accomplished orator, and the powers which he possessed were always placed freely at: the service of every . good cause that commended itself to his judgment. The _ survivors of the political struggles of his Youth are but few, but his loss will be regretted by many of the social reformers ' to whose cause he lent the strength of his eloettent tongue.

SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 2, 1882.

THE really hard work in connection with the Egyptian campaign may now be said to have com- menced in earnest, and, judging from the fighting qualities which the enemy developed on Monday at - Sassassin Lock, we should think the end of the struggle is not yet near. Ever since Sir Garnet Wolseley, with his army, seized the Suer Canal and obtained a footing at Ismailia, his progress has been almost uninterrupted, for at no point, except at Mah- sameh,did the Egyptian forces offer any serious obstacle to his victorious march. Even at Alahsanneh, it appears) a large proportion of the force which opposed Sir Garnet consisted of peasantry and raw recruits, and they were routed without much difficulty. The com- pleteness of their defeat on that occasion is shown by '.the fact that they fl-d in terror towards Zagazig, throwing awa`7 their arms and accoutrements asithey

On Sunday morning, Mr. T. Horrocks preached a tem- perance sermon in Lacey-street school-room. There was a large congregation, and Bro. W. Shaw, of Runcorn, conducted .the service. The collections realised £1 16s. RUNCORN AND TARPORLEY AGRICULTURAL SHOW.— The committee entrusted with making the arrangements for Tarporley Agricultural Show have decided that it shall be held at Runcorn, probably about the commencement of October.

DAIIESBURY BREWSTER SESSIONS. - The annual licensing sessions for the Daresbury division were held at the Sessions House, Daresburv, on Tuesday, the pre- siding magistrates being Messrs. E. Greenell and James Marson.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson presented his report, which stated that there 23 licensed victuallers, 2 beersellers, and 4 others who sell off the premises, making a total of 29; giving an average of 283 of the population to each license. One licensed victualler had been proceeded against during the year, a conviction being recorded against him. One beersaller had also been proceeded against, and had been convicted. Twenty-nine p2rsons had been convicted of drunkenness as against 23 the previous year. The case of Wm. Worrell, of the Letters, Whitley Inferior, who bad been fined 295. and us. 6d. costs for selling beer on unlicensed premises on May 30, 1882, was adjourned until the next licensing day. The justices also adjourned the consideration of the renewal of off-licenses until the next sessions.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson stated that there were no applications for new licenses. Rummy SHooriNG" CLun.—The usual monthly challenge cup competition took place on Saturday last on Runcorn Heath. Conditions, seven rounds at 200, 500, and 600 yards. Wimbledon targets and scoring. which he is capable with the view of striking a deci- sive blow at the main body of the Egyptians, of whose fighting capacity he has now had ample oppor- tunities of judging. Fortune seems to smile upon the General in his work. Mahmoud Fehmy, the chief of ArabPs staff, has been taken a prisoner. Under this officer's direction all the earthworks and

entrenchments at Kafir Dower, Tel-el-Kebir, and other strongholds have been constructed; and his loss must, therefore,be seriously felt by the enemy. Toulba Pasha, too, Arabi's chief political adviser, is reported to be dead, an is believed to have been poisoned. The Dictator is, therefore, without the assistance in both
political and military matters on which he was wont to depend. Again, Sir Garnet has not been hampered
with the presence of Turkish troops in Egypt, which it was supposed at one time would be a serious draw-
back; and, although the Turkish Convention with England may now be signed, and a contingent of the

Turkish army may very soon be landed at either Aboukir, Rosetta, or Damietta, the conditions, under which the intervention takes place are such that they can scarcely have any injurious effect upon Sir Garnet's movements. The Sultan has completely succumbed to the English demands in this matter, he has men'.

Woodlands ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT HATTON.—The man John Kirkham, who attempted to commit suicide by cutting his throat at Hatton on the 17th August, was brought up for trial at the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. E. Greenall, and James Marson.—Dr. Willett said that he was requested to visit the defendant on the 17th inst. On arrival at the defendant's residence he found that he had cut his throat with a razor, and was suffering from a considerable amount of prostration, consequent upon the loss of a great quantity of blood. His throat was not seriously injured, but had bled very profusely. Defendant told him that he had been suffering, for many days previous, from intense pain in the head. The loss of blood was a very salient change,and had perhaps saved the defendant from an epileptic fit.—The defendant said he was sorry he had cut his throat. He could not really help it, as he did not know what he was doing. It was a thing that he should not have done if he had known what he was doing. He had been suffering for a fortnight from illness.—The Chairman: You know it is a very wrong thing to cut your throat. Will you give us your promise that you will never attempt it again? Defendant replied in the affirmative.—Dr. Willett: He expressed the greatest regret a few days after- wards.—The Chairman-: You must be bound over to keep the peace, and you will have to pay the costs. BREACH OF TILE LICENSING ACT AT WHITLEY SUPEIROR. —William Worrell, an off-license holder at Whitley Supe- rior, was charged at Daresbury Petty Sessions with selling a quantity of beer which was drunk in the vicinity of his premises. William Lawson, George Cotterill, and James Thornton were charged with aiding and abetting the land- lord—Mr. G. T. Moore defended Mr. Worrall.—P.S. B lair said that in consequence of numerous complaints he had received, he went, on the 19th inst., in company with P.C. Daintith, to Whitley Superior. They hid themselves behind a hedge opposite the licensed premises. There were a number of men near the house, and he saw a man whom he took to be Lawson, about ten minutes to ten o'clock, go into Worrall'e shop and bring out a'half-gallon bottle and a cup. Lawson went to the men on the highway, and he heard him ask them to drink out of the cup. They then left their hiding place and immediately the lights in the house were put out. They heard someone shout " heigh up," and a deal ief whistling ensued, which was answered from Worrall's house. They went up to the men and found them with a half-gallon bottle and a cup full of beer.—P.C. Daintith corroborated.—Mrs. Worrell said that a man named Robert Buckley, and not Lawson, came to her house during the night and purchased four quarts of ale. No portion of the beer was consumed on the premises. She gave him strict nstructions to take it away from the house, which he promised to do. She did not lend him either the bottle or the cup.—Robert Buckley was called and he said he purchased the four quarts of ale. They drunk the beer off the premises, at a distance of 74 yards away.—The case was dismissed.

restoring order in Egypt, and, if he remains loyal to the compact, we need have nothing to fear. Our only object in interfering ourselves is to restore order, and
