SERMONS IT Surrox WEAVER. -- The Rev. Mr. Fitzpatrick, of Bolton, preached two sermons at Union Church, Sutton Weaver, on Sunday last. There was a large congregation in the morning, and in the evening the service was attended by upwards of 400 persons. The collections realised about £l6.

E ROCK SAVAGE PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.—Mr. T StringfellOw and Mr. James Dcbilon preached at this place of worship on Sunday last, and about £8 was collected to- wards the building fund. The chapel, which was opened a Ifortnight ago,. is almost free from debt. How A WESTON PIG DEALER GOT ROBBED. - At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Joseph Wm. Chorley, a young man, was brought up on remand, charged with stealing, on the 23rd ult., a bag and £2l, the property of John Capper, publican and pig dealer, Weston.—The cir- cumstances of the cass ,have been previously reported in The Examiner, and the evidence having been again given, the prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Knutsford Sessions.

THE SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK AT WIDNES.—Mr. G. H. Danby, cletk to the School Board, appeared at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to prosecute the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school, and they were dealt with as follows :—Margaret Raynor, Dennis Malone, Michael McDermott, and Martin Flanagan. Commitment orders were made against John Westhead, Patrick Cannon, and Adam Green, who had failed to pay fines imposed upon them.

AN A GGRAVATED HUSBAND AT WIDNES POLICE COVET. —At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Mr. W. F. Earle and Mr. F. lf. Gossage, Joseph Stanley, who appeared to be a flatman, pleaded guilty to assaulting his wife Eliza- beth. On the 220 ult., about eleven o'clock, the prisoner went home for his breakfast, and cursed his wife whilst she was preparing it. When he had eaten it he " thumped " her. He had been twice previously summ9ned by her, but each time she had 'forgiven him. Prisoner said he got aggravated and 'struck her whilst in a temper. lie did not do it wilfully. His wife threw a knife at him. Complainant denied this. Considering that the prisoner had already been in gaol six days, the Bench only sentenced him to seven days' hard labour.

Bnussvricx SUNDAY ScHoot TEAT.—The scholars and teachers of Brunswick Sunday school on Saturday last journeyed to Frodsham by a special train, leaving Runcorn about one o clock. Their ultimate destination was Mersey View, Overton Hills, and every arrangement had been made for spending an enjoyable afternoon, but rain descended pitilessly during almost the whole of the time, and shelter had to be taken in the large tea rooms. Interesting games and sports, including a football match, however, were to some extent indulged in, and a good tea was a very solacing item in the programme. To- wards evening many of the exculsionists p lid a visit to Dunsdale, the residence of Mr. John Simpson, the senior superintendent of the school, who kindly con- ducted them through the beautiful and well kept grounds, anct pointed out the various objects of interest. At the con- clusion of the visit the party thanked Mr. Simpson for his courtesy, and departed for the station, where the yciunger scholars had already arrived. Runcorn was shortly after- wards reached.

DAMAGE TO PROPETCTY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. W. F. Earle, Geo. Taylor and Henry Peters, boys, were charged with com- mitting damage to houses in Oxford-street, 'Widnes, the pro- perty of Ni'arrington Permanent Benefit Building Society. Mr. Edwin Woods, estate agent to the society, said there had been a great amount of damage done to their empty pro- perty in Widnes, and especially in Oxford-street, where there were 20 houses empty. He made arrangements nith Inspector Barnett to watch the property, and P.S. McGregor, who had undertaken the duty, saw Taylor break three or four panes of glass, and Peters one. A number of stones were sent. Taylor had committed damage to the amount of 53. and Peters Is. Bd. Taylor was fined ss. and costs total 18s Gd., And Peters was ordered to pay a fine of 3s. ad. and costs, total 12s. Bcl., and the magistrate said he hoped the parebts would flog them when they got them home.

STREET " LOAFING " TO BE PUT DOWN AT WIDNES.— James Parkinson, a young man, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. W. F. Earle and Mr. F. H. 4ossage, to answer a charge of obstructing the footpath at Widnos. P.C. Brown said that on Monday, the 21st ult., about seven o'clock, the defendant and a crowd of men were standing on the footpath in ‘Vaterloo-road. He requested them to go away, and they did so; but immedi- ately he went away Parkinson again stood on the footpath. Mr. Superintendent Barker said this conduct was very common in Widnes. Mr. W. F. Earle said this practice had been put down at. Prescot, and the 'tench would try to do the same at Widnes. Defendant was fined ss. and costs.— For having on the same evening obstructed the footpath in Anne-street West, James Moran and John Newall were each mulcted in a similar penalty. P.C. 203 proved the case. BREACH OF THE LICENSING ACT AT WIDNES: A PUBLICAN FINED.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Ses- sions, before Mr. W. F. Earle and Mr. F. H. Gossage, Edward Hughes was summoned to answer a charge of being drunk on the licensed premises of Joseph Rogers, and Joseph Rogers, landlord of the Ivy Green beerhouse, was charged with selling liquor to a drunken person.—Mr. Husband ap- peared for the defendants.—P.C. Brown said that on Monday, the 14th of August, he was on duty in Waterloo-road, in company with P.C. Coutts. About half-past six he sew the defendant Hughes and another man going along Wellington- street. Hughes was very drunk. The Ivy Green beerhouse was in the neighbourhoud, and the defendant Hughes and his co:opinion entered. Immediately afterwards witness and P.C. Coutts also went into the house, and standing at the bar was Hughes and his companion, each With a pint pot half full of beer before him. Witness asked the land- lady, "Who does this drink belong to ? " Hughes replied, "One of them is mine ;" and the landlady said she had served it. She said Hughes had just been paying her some money he osved her. Witness then said "This man is drunk, and I shall report you for supplying him with drink." At this point Rogers entered the bar, and wished to know " What's up." The constable informed him, and defendant Rogers said to his wife " Why did you serve him ? " Witness after- wards took Hughes to the police station, where Inspebtor Barnett saw him, and after his name and address had been obtained, he was allowed to go home.—By Mr. Husband:. Witness had to help Hughes to walk to the police station.— P.C. Coutts corroborated this account, and Inspector Barnett and P.S. McGregor gave evidence that Hughes was very drunk.—ln defence, Mr. Husband said he was instructed that Hughes was not very drunk; be was perhaps a little fresh, . but to all appearance he looked sober, and Mrs. Rogers had no idea that he was intoxicated. Mr. Husband spoke of the good character of the defendants.—Mrs. Rogers was called and said her husband had had the public house three years and she had partly been brought up in one. She noticed no !limas of intoxication upan Hughes, and had she done so, she would not have served him. He told her he had come to pay for some beer he had the previous week, and was quite rational.—Michael Timmins, labourer, said he was with Hughes all the afternoon on the day in question, and they bad only two pints of beer. He did not think Hughes was drunk. After a few minutes' conversation the Chairman said Hughes would be fined ss. and 7s. 01,costs. There WV no doubt Hughes ought not to have been served with the liquor, but as it was Rogers' first offence he would only be fined 20s. and costs 17s.

A Wm:mg BUTOIZER Comm=En FOR Tnin.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, a butcher named Richard Baxter was charged with having, on the 11th of August, stolen seven hooks, belonging to Robert Hirst, of Widnes-road, Widnes.—Mr. Swift, of St. Helens, appeared for the prosecutor, and the defendant was represented by Mr. Peters.—From Mr. Swift's opening statement it appeared that up to the end of last year the defendant was presumed to be in a good position, but he then had a visit from the sheriff, and his effects were sold under an exe- cution. At the time of the execution the defendant was a tenant of the prosecutor, having a lock-up shop situated in Albert-road under him. In that shop were a number of sliding hooks used by the defendant as a butcher, which were offered for sale by the, sheriff with other effects, and the prosecutor purchased 22, for which he paid £2 Ss. When the defendant, left the shop remained untenanted for six months, but at the end of July a man named Daniel Hirst went in. The hooks remained in the shop. On the 9th August the defendant, who was about to open a new shop, asked the prosecutor if he would lend him one or two of the hooks. Prosecutor refused. The following day, however, the defendant's daughter went down to the shop, and informed the tenant that her father had received the permission of the prosecutor to the loan of six books. He refused to let her have any, and defendant then went and asked why he 14ould not lend them. Next day, while the tenant was away from home, the defendant and his daughter went to the shop, and, without saving any- thing, took away seven hooks. The prosecutor hearing of this, went and had an interview with the defendant, who admitted he had taken the hooks, and refused to give them up, remarking that he would take other things.—The prosecutor gave evidence confirming this statement, and said the books were worth 2s. each. He had not given the prosecutor permission to remove them.—Daniel Hurst, the tenant of the shop, a butcher, and his assistant, a boy, also gave evidence bearing out the 'facts stated.—P.C. Orrnerod deposed to serving the summons upon the defendant, who said they were his own hcolls and worth ss. each.—Mr. Swift said his client had no vindictive feeling in the matter, and if the Bench thought the ends of justice would be met by so doing, the prosecu- tor would be satisfied if the hooks were returned and the costs of the summons paid for.—Mr. Peters addressed the Bench for the defence, contending that the defendant had no intention of stealing the hooks. He understood that tht prosecutor had aiven him permission to take the books.— The Bench decided that there was a prima fade case for the sessions and the defendant having been charged in the usual way, said Robert Hirst, the owner of the shop, said he could have six of the books!—The defendant was then committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions. He was admitted to bail in two sureties of £lO ea6h.

MAINTENANCE or CHILDREN AT RIINCORN.—John Clnens, a labouring man living in Bridgewater-street, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. C. Reynolds, charged with neglect- ing to maintain his family, whereby three children became chargeable to the common fund of the Runcorn Union.— Mr. T. Houghton appeared on behalf of the Guardians, and said the defendant had promised to take the children out of the workhouse and pay the amount owing, £ll 45., by weekly instalments of 12s. He therefore asked the Bench to adjourn the case for a month to see if he carried out his promise.—The case was adjourned. UNPROVOKED ATTACK ON AN OLD MAN AT WIDNES.— An elderly man, named James Brown, appeared before Mr, Earle and Mr. F. H. Gossage, at the, Widnes.Police Court, on Wednesday, to supriort a charge of assault against a young man, [-lamed John Riley, who had a bandage round his head. The prosecutor had a plaister over his left eye. Brown lives at Appleton. On Monday, while standing in the works where he is employed, the prisoner went up to him, and used some obscene and insulting Janguage. Brown advised him to go home, when be struck him seriously cutting his forehead just above the eye.—The pri- soner, who pleaded guilty, said he knew nothing whatever of the assault, as he wag drunk at the time.—lt seemed he had been previously before the court, and he was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour. RUNCORN AND DISTRICT (406) STARR BOWKETT BUILD- ING SOCIETY.—The first annual report and balance sheet of this society, which will be submitted to the members' meet- ing on Friday next, states that the number of share certificates issued during the year was 250, carrying thereon 542 shares. As a considerable number of the members have only joined the society during the latter half of the year, the amount of subscriptions was necessarily small, but the directors antici- pated from the present regular payments a much larger return for next year. Four appropriations were made during, the year, and Mr. 11. Johnson, Mrs. W. Handley, Mr. A. Riley, and Mr. J. Tonks, each became entitled to the use of £2OO. From the statement of accounts we learn that mem- bers' subscriptions amount to £455 155., which with £l5 153. OW. received for fines, entrance fees, commission, Sze., makes the total receipts £5Ol 10s. Oid. The formation expenses are put down at £62 155., and the working expenses for the year were £77 2s. 9d. Mr. J. Povah and Mr. W. Brookes, the auditors, certify the correctness of the ac- counts. The retiring directors, who are eligible for re-elec- tion, are Messrs. W. Armstrong, J. Poole, W. Booth, and R. Royle.

THE SALVATIONIST AND HEE NEIGHBOITE AT WIDNES. —On Tuesday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Mr. F. H. Gossage, Peter Byrne was brought up, on remand, charged with using threats to a married woman named Jane Priest- lev. It appeared that Priestley and her husband are mem- bers of the Salvation Army, while the prisoner is a Roman Catholic. They live in the same street, and the prisoner seems to have taken offence at his neighbours going to the Army. On Saturday the prosecutrix and her husband were at home singing hymns, when the prisoner burst into the house, and after using disgusting language, threatened to take the prosecutrix's life if she did not cease singing. He was bound over to keep the peace three months, himself in £lO and two sureties of .-05 each. Mr. Gossage remarked that the prisoner's conduct was censurable in the highest degree, and if ever he or a man named Gray, who had given evidence, were again brought up for threatening the woman or her husband, they would he dealt with much more severely.

LEC LIME dis 7 ASTI:IO2O3IY AT RUNCORN.-.Mr. John Leach, of Runcorn, on Wednesday evening read an excellent paper on astronomy before the members of the Young Men's Im- provement Class in connection with Brunswick-street Sunday school. After defining the scope of his paper, Mr. Leach dealt with the important discoveries made by the ancients and the theories adopted by them for the explana- tion of the celestial motions, .tarrounded as WQ WM at the present time with the. meridian splendour of the truth, it was almost impossible for us to realise the position of those brave pioneers of science who had to feel their way amid darkness and obscurity, and the patience and perseverance of those indefatigable observers of the heavens could not be too much admired. At a very early period they had become familiar with the general motions of heaven; the notion of the sun and moon, had as- certained the cause of those remarleable charges in the ap- pearance of the moon called her phases, bad discovered the fine planets which are visible to the naked eye, namely, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn; had determined the periods of their revolutions and the inclinations of the planes of their orbits to the plane of the ecliptic; had noted the irregularities in the motions of tile planets, were ac- quainted with their stationery points and retrogradations. They had also investigated with success the cause of those grand and imposing phenomena, solar and lunar eclipses, and were able to anticipate and predict their coming. The dis- covery of the cause of the eclipse of the moon was touched upon, and the researches of the celebrated Hipparchus, who is styled the Newton of antiquity, were explained. He it was, who 123 years before the Christian era, discovered the motion known by the term Precession of /he Equinoxes, who numbered the stars and fixed their position in the heavens. His catalogue of 10S1 of the priacipal stars was perhaps the most remarkable contribution to astronomical science which the Greek school of philosophers had trans- mitted to posterity. The wonderful labours of Ptolemy, Copernicus, and Kepler, and their results were commented upon. Mr. Leach then described at length the many and important discoveries of Galileo, and concluded by a re- ference to the laws of gravitation, by which all the various phenomena of the solar systehi are beautifully explained.

AN UNSUCCESSFUL PAOSECUTION BY TUE WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. Joseph Turton, fruiterer, West-street, West Bank, Widnes, was summoned to Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of committing a breach of the Feed and Drugs Act by offering decayed fruit for sale. He was represented by Mr. Swift, solicitor, St. Helens. —John Dickson, sanitary inspector to the Widnes Local Board, stated that he visited the defendant's shop on the 27th July. In one window he found a quantity of partially decayed peas, in another a quantity of plums and gooseber- ries also partially decayed. lie seized them, and conveyed them before a justice, who ordered them to be destroyed. They were destroyed. and he produced the order. There were four pecks of peas and 12 quarts of fruit.—Mr. Swift drakw attention to the fact that plums were not mentioned in the information, but Mr. Dickson said he seized a quantity, but could not tell ,the exact amount. In cross-examination, Mr. Dickson stated all the fruit and peas in the windows were not bid, and he allowed the young woman who was in the shop to pick out two pecks of peas and three quarts of fruit which were fit for sale. The woman offered to sell him some of the plums.—Mr. Shepherd, the assistant-ifispector, havieg given evidence, Mr. Swift said his defence was not that the fruit was not bad, hint that it was not intended for sale. The shop had only been opened about three weeks previous to Mr. Dickson's visit, and, as traders generally did at the commencement, the defendant and his brother pur- chased more than they could sell. It consequently decayed, and the back yard was almost filled with decaying vecretable matter and bad fish. The defendant had sent notice of that fact te Mr. Dixon four or five times, but, although the neighbours complained of the nuisance, the stuff was not removed. When Mr. Dixon visited the shop the person in charge told him the fruit and peas were not for sale, but was to be used for manure on the farm of the d,fendant's father, which was really the fact.—Thomas Turton, brother of the defendant, and head of the firm, was called, and said the stuff was not intended for sale.—Mrs. Elizabeth Thompson deposed that on the morning previous to the visit of the sanitary inspector, she purchased a quan- tity of potatoes at the defendant's shop, and he defendant served her. She also wished to purchase some peas, but he would not sell them, saying they were not for sale. She bought some of the plums, which were very good.—A youth was called, and confirmed this statement.—Another witness was being called, when Mr. Earle (the chairman) said the case need go no further ; it was dismissed. GOOD TEMPLARISM AT RIINCORN.—Mr. Thomas Horrocks the converted clown, haying fulfilled his engagement at Widnes, visited Runcorn on Tuesday and Wedneslay. On the evening of each day he delivered a lecture in Bethesda sChool-room, to large audiences. The lectures were under the auspices of the Good Templar lodges of luncorn and Widnes, and many of the brethren from the latter plaoe scurocsoseesdsf uthi.r e ,nbridgeo hotonattend the meetings, w,ehniicnhwernes m verT. Robert Shaw, whose remarks are reported elsewhere. On Wednesday evening Mr. Thomas Norman presided, and in introducing Mr. Horrocks, expressed his pleasure at being present. His views on the temperance question, he re- marked, were so well known, that it was unnecessary for him to occupy their time by making a speech, but he might say that the longer he lived the more determined he was to do all in his power to help on the great and noble work of the temperance reformation. (Applause ) The cause was snaking rapid advances—during his lifetime the drinking habits had undergone a marked change. He had evidence of this a few weeks ago, when he was at a town in North Wales. At the dinner table of the place where he was visiting, something like 30 people took their places, and he did not see one drinking anything but water. (Hear, hear.) Most of them were young men—(hear, hear,)—a band of young men, who would see great things accomplished in the next generation, though he ad many of those present who had passed the meridian of life might not. Travelling about the country, as he did, he had many opportunities of making observations, and the instance he had related was not an isolated one. A few years ago everybody must have beer to their dinner, and it was encouraging to those who supported or worked for the temperance cause to find that this was no longer the case. On every favourable occasion the benefits of temperance, and the evil effects of drink upon the human system ; its blasting influences upon the health and lives of our fellow creatures, should be spoken about—he did so wherever he was—and much good might be thus done. He saw before him in that meeting men who if they had been teetotallers from their youth would have been gentlemen now. (Hear, hear.) There was no doubt about it. He hoped the time was fast approaching when the temperance cause would win its way a thousandfold more than it was doing at the present time. Be impressed upon parents the duty of training their children in the principles of religion, I for if a man was truly religious he would never take much drink—(hear, bear); but at the same time teach them to be teetotallers. He was thankful to say he had seven children, and five out of that number had never tasted drink in their Ilives. (Applause.) Mr. Nor man coecluded by a reference to the intimate connection there was between drunkenness I and pauperism.

div.head: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.

The chief event of next week is the annual election of Runcorn Commissioners, and though, apparently exciting little interest at present, there is an undercurrent of opinion which will find vent, I think, before Thursday. There are certain "quiet moves "on foot, which are likely to have an effect on the result of the election. It will be remembered that last year the candidates of a certain section of the rate- payers were by a strange coincidence all Tories. Of course they had no political aim in view, not at all ; but however that may be they were all elected. Runcorn has it, and not without good grounds, I believe, that similar tactics are to be pursued during the present contest, and under the guise of "neutrality " to win the votes of the ratepayers. Surely a town which boasts of its intelligence and advanced Liberal- ism will not permit itself to be so blinded ; but will at once take such action as will make those at whom I have hinted show themselves in their true colours, and fight the battle openly. The Liberals know their.strength, and they should not hesitate to make use of it under such circumstances.

A very interesting and rather novel point is likely to be raised at the Revising Barrister's Court for the Runcorn parliamentary division, which is to' be held in a few weeks. It is generally understood that no person can have his name placed upon the register in a county constituency unless he is rated at £l2, but Mr. 0. Leak, the Liberal agent for Run- corn, has made 41 claims for householders who are paying a rent of £l2 and upwards per annum, whine the Tories have made eight claims of a similar nature. Somewhat sanguine expectations are held that the votes will be allowed, but the overseers have objected to the whole batch on the ground of ‘, insufficiently rated." Mr. 11. Roberts, the gas and water engineer to the Widnes 1 Local Board, has sent in his resignation, which has not yet, however, been accepted. The reason for this step is is

RESIGNATION OF A WIDNES OFFICIAL Considerable discussion has been caused in local circles at Widnes by the announcement that Mr. Roberts, engineer to the local board, has sent in his resignation. The reason given by him for adopting this course has not been made public.

RUNCORN AND TARPORLEY AGRICULTURAL Sow.—The appeal for subscriptions towards a local fund has been very liberally responded, and it has been decided to hold Tarpor- ley Agricultural Show at Runcorn, and probably early in October. The local committee and the committee of the society will hold a joint meeting, on Monday, to make the arrangements for the event, which will no doubt be success- fully carried out.

RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH. - Tll3 choristers of this church had a free trip to Overton Hills, on Tuesday after- noon. They were conveyed thither in Messrs. Yarwood and Son's large omnibus, and on arriving at Mersey View, were received by the Vicar, Miss Barclay, Miss Rougier, and Mrs. Fitzsimons. Various recreations were indulged in, and the boys were provided with a good tea, a very enjoy- able afternoon being spent.

NEWTOWN MISSION SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCOTiIe scholars attending this school had their annual treat on Tuesday afternoon, when, under the conductorship of Mr Ryan, and headed by the, fife and drum band, they visitec. the yicarage. After a short stay here they proceeded to Weston Point, where, in a field kindly lent by Mr. Thomas Nixon, they disported themselves for several Lours. The procession was then reformed, and the scholars marched to the schoolroom, where tea was provided. The remainder of the evening was spent in various pastiness. WESLETANISNI AT Roca SAVAGE.—Mr. George Marshall, ea-chairman of the Runcorn Baatd of Commissioners, has for some time past been working among the Wesleyans of Rock Savage, and his labours have been so successful that he has decided to erect a building, which it is intended to use as a missioon-room and as a day and Sunday school. The services are at present held in a dwelling-house. The Marquis of Cholmond(dey has leased a plot of land for the site of the proposed building at a nominal rent, and its erection will be commenced at an early date. STRANGE DEATH AT WIDNES.—The police report the death of a labourer named B. Purcell, aged 4S, who resided at 36, Victoria-street, Widnes, which took place on Tuesday last. It appears that the deceased up to three weeks ago had enjoyed good health. About that time a swelling made its appearance on his wrist, of his left hand, and quickly extended to his elbow. It then became discoloured, and the deceased became se weak that be was confined to his bed, and died as stated above. Dr. O'Keeffe refused to give a certificate, and the coroner was communicated with, but he did not think it necessary to hold an inqaest, and ordered the registrar to give a certificate.

A THIEF NICELY CALTG/IT AT RUNCORN. —A young man named George Cooper was brcught up in custody at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, charged with having on the Nth August, stolen one pair of trousers of the value of 9s 6d, the property of Messrs. Marsh and Smith, pawn- brokers and outfitters.—Mr. Marsh said the trousers produced belonged to the 'firm, and were hung up in the shop on Satur- day night at nine o'clock. He did not miss them until eleven o'clock, when two officers brought them. Tne ticket pro- duced was attached to them when the trousers were hung up, and it had upon it the private mark of the firm and the price.—Jane Drury, Water-street, Runcorn, said that on Saturday night last, about eleven o'clock, she was in Mersey- street, when the prisoner called her and showed her the trousers produced. He said "I have given 9s for these, but you can have them for 4s, as I have spent all my money and am hard up." She told him she could not buy them unless he showed her the shop where he had bought them. He said he would, and went a little way with her; then he ran along the fair ground taking the trousers with him. She saw him unfasten the ticket near Spann's, in INlersepetreet. She gave information to the police.—P.S. Whalley deposed to hearing the conversation between laet witness and the prisoner. When the prisoner ran away, he followed, and apprehended him in Penketh-lane. He asked the prisoner • where he bought the trousers. He stated he would show the sergeant, but on his way said "I am properly caught this time. You are sharp chaps here. I was never caught like this before, I Inve stolen them,"--To answer to the ch4rge prisoner said he was drinking all day, and be stole the trousers. He got his living on the sea.—The prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Knutsford Sessions.

INTERESTING CLAM FOR WAGES AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. S. B. Chadwick, Jean Tabourel, a native of Jersey, claimed from Mr. George 11 trvey, master of the schooner Hilda, the sum of £2 10s., balance of wages dice to him for services as seaman on board the Hilda. The plaintiff was represented by Mr. Lake, and Mr. Burton appeared for the defendant. It seemed that on the 2nd May plaintiff shipped as mate of the Hilda, but having for, some time past been insulted by a boy on board the vessel, he decided to leave it on its arrival in Runcorn. On Monday afternoon he gave the captain, in a civil way, the usual 24 hours notice, but instead of listening to him the captain seized. him by the throat and ordered him ashore. Mr. Lake contended that this act amounted to an instant dismissal of his client, and that no further notice was required.—Mr. Barton submitted that the plaintiff was not entitled, to recover the amount of wages said to be due to him. He had been guilty of deser- tion because he had not given the proper notice.—the Bench considered that the act of the captain in seizing the plaintiff amounted to a discharge.—Mr. Burton said the Hilda arrived in Runcorn at the end of July, and was put upon the stocks for repairs. The plaintiff never gave notice then, but remained on board. His duties during that time were merely nominal, but was paid fullwages. Afterwards the 'vessel was loaded and ready for sea, when to the surprise of the captain he declared his intention of going. On Saturday the plaintiff was paid 15s. on account, and did not say a word about leaving, but left the vessel without authority, returning on Monday afternoon, when he demanded a settlement. He bad not given an hour's notice, and the captain thought he was justified in treating him as a deserter, and refusing him wages.—Defendant then gave evidence, and during cross- examination admitted that he took hold of the plaintiff by the collar. He was in a great passion and did not know what he said. He would not swear he did not tell the plain- tiff to go ashore.-1 book was produced showing that £2 Is. was owing to the plaintiff, and the Bench gave a verdict for that amount with costs, amounting to Li 34.

A P'R.ACAB ON RUNCORN BRID4R.—At the Runcorn • Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. C. Reynolds, Archibald Sullivan and Mary Sullivan, man and wife, were charged with having on the 19th inst. un- lawully assaulted John Burton, captain of a flat, and who resided at 34, Shaw-street. Burton was charged with hav- ing at the same time assaulted Archibald Sullivan; and Thomas Reader was charged with assaulting Mary Sullivan. Each defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Burton, solicitor, appeared for the defendants, Burton and Reader, and Mr. Lake appeared for the Sullivans.—Mr. Burton, in opening the case, said the facts were shortly these. On Saturday evening, the 19th August, about nine o'clock, the defendant Burton was on Runcorn Bridge saying "Good night" to a friend of his. Just as he left him the two Sullivans came through the gate, and went down the steps. He followed them, and as he was passing he accidentally knocked against the elbow of Mrs. Sullivan. They were perfect strangers to him, and he said "I beg pardon, Mrs." and went on his way. When they reached the bottom, the husband asked him what he had done that for. Burton told him it was an accident but Sullivan commenced to use some strong language, and the wife, being behincl, struck him on the head; either with a stone or a can, cutting his head deeply and causing the blood to flow. On this the husband started, struck Burton on the forehead and felled him to the ground. Sullivan, his wife, and a third person, unknown, who was with the defen- dants, kicked him. He managed to get up, aimed a blow at Sullivan, and ran in the direction of Ashridge-street. He, however, afterwards thought he would give the defendants in charge, and followed them up Lord-street to get their names. Sullivan returned to him and said "If you don't turn back you will get more than you have got;" follow- ing those remarks up with a heavy blow, which knocked him to the ground; and a scuffle ensued. The wound on Burton's head waA a very serious one, and he went to the Town Hall and showed two policemen, who went to Friar- street and obtained the names of his assailants. Burton after- wards had his head stitched, and since the occurrenee he had been under the care of the doctor and unable to follow his occupation. Reader did not strike a blow, but he saw the disturbance in Church-street. Barton was alone, and it was not probable that he would attack or in- terfere with two men and a woman. Burton, Edward White, of Portland-street; Thomas Reader, Allcock-street, gave evidence in support of this statement. White stated he saw the Sullivans chase Burton, whose head was in a fearful state.—Mr. Lake then addressed the Bench. He said the testimony.would be very_ conflicting. The vans woulcl state that they were leaving the ticket office on Runcorn Bridge when they saw Burton and a friend standing against the wall of the bridge. When they nassed him down the steps Burton made use of some difugreeable language to Sullivan, and threatened to kick him down the steps. He told his friend to come along, and followed them . down the steps, at the bottom of which a scuffle took place- Burton struck Sullivan on the back of the neck and knocked. him down. He got up and went into Lord-street, where Burton whistled for assistance, and Burton, with five other men, amongst whom were Reader and White, Suit- vanattacikted and his wife, who, in defence, struck Burton be • In. n u va int tie side, after he had struck her twice. s Reader side, and she had in consequence been unwell. After t1;-.' ; they Sullivans had got clear ofß.aurr-tsotnre:nt, where c thillnreemai ran to a friend's boos' Frl . in ned all night, being afraid ofgoing home to Westo,n in cons-- (pence of tt threat_by..i,in these men that they wonld.•waylay and attack them. v and his wife were called, and the former admitted Kelly, he had offered Burtori ss. to settle • the ease. Kate of Friar-street, &lie. she washed Sullivan's face on Saturday night. He Its.d a cut which extended from his eye to his jaw, and his r lothes were very • bloody. They stayed in her house nti) Sunday morning. Reader and Burton were waiting on savage's Bridge to attack them.—Mr. Bankes said the Ber.ch'from the evidence produced were satisfied no assault had been committed by the Sullivans, and the case against Vaem would be dismissed. Burton they were certain had comraitted an assault, and he • would be fined 20i. and cost r.tud Reader w0z.1.1 be fined 10s. and cats.

div.head: ptier to the editor.
div.p: ptier to the editor.

ANG-LO-SCOTUS " DISCOURSES ON HARES AND COURSING; ALSO " CORRUPTION." Sir,—My good natured Newton critic (or critics, for Ido not knew whether there are more than one) has or have skirmished or coursed over such wide ground in his, her, or their remarks upon the subject of my first letter to you, that I have in duty bound been obliged to follow them. Bees and ants are to a certain extent—having the advantage of an additional element more difficult to deal with than hares; but having, as I hope, satisfactorily disposed of them, may I crave permission to recur to the statement of Bishop Wilkins anent the hutch the cony is said to have had in Noah's Ark? Fur we know is one of the oldest, if not the most ancient, materials used by mankind as a garment; and it is not my fault that an attempt has been made in your columns to make this skin or case of a hare cover such a wide space outside of what may properly be termed its im- • mediate or cognate connection. However, to resume the original subject, may I ask the writer of the following sen- tence'what animal the term " cony " is meant to describe? " Anglo-Scotus speaks up manfully for the timid animal, e Which, according to Bishop Wilkins (1688), Noah found a separate compartment for in the Ark, a few thousand years ago, and gives a plan showing where it had its " hutch " with the roe, cony, and marmott." Pending a reply I would like to add that the hare will give the reader or student as enjoyable hunting in the domain of literature and folk-lore, as it will in the fields or over the downs. For instance, it was at one time a crime in southern Britain to taste the flesh of the hare, the goose, or the ordinary domestic fowl, though all of these creatures were reared and kept for amuse- ment. The hare is at the present time an object of dis- gust in some parts of Russia, as well as in Western Brittany, where, not many years ago, the peasants could hardly endure to hear its name mentioned. The people of the Swiss lake-dwellings are believed to have shared the superstitious feeling against eating the flesh of tbe hare; whereas the neolithic tribes in Britain used the animal for food. (See Elton's " Origins of English History.") The ancientlrish ate its flesh, and one of the prerogatives of the kings of Tara was to be fed on the hares of Naas. But then the Irish of those days were accused of eating their ancestors. In one part of Wales hares are termed Monacella's lambs; and St. Brendan provided an asylum for them. The at one time sacred character of the hare is ' indicated by the legend of Boadicea, who, according to Dion Cassius, "loosed a hare from her robe, observed its movements as a kind of omen, and when it turned pro- pitiously the whole multitude rejoiced and shouted." At Sheffield the custom of presenting two white hares on St. John's Day has been accepted as a rent equivalent. Eating the "Easter hare," again,: is an old English custom. In Theal's "Kaffir Folk-lore," there is a story relating how, in the attempted execution of a certain task, after the cony, the duiker, the bluebuck, and the porcupine have all in turn failed, and have forfeited their lives in consequence, the hare ;succeeds. "Puss " then kills the fat-devouring inkalimeva, goes for the pot of meat the bushbuck is guarding, helps herself, befools the guardian of the savoury stew, and winds up by cleverly humbugging a number of other animals, the monkeys included, some of which latter she kills, and makes a mantle for herself out of their skins. I may also remind the chronicler of the feats of that wonderful Newton cow that gave butter and sweet-lard for making cakes, that Mr. Theal's interesting book contains the history of" the bird that made milk." It. not only points a moral akin to that contained in the scripture story of "Joseph and his Brethren ; " but also a beautiful allegory in connection with a girl who marries a crocodile,--the account of the apotheosis of which is as enjoyable as is that of the bear in "Beauty and the Beast." In connection with "the most ancient material used by humanteings as a covering, "it may interest children (God bless them all!) to know that the little shoe in which ' the ash-maiden (Cinderella) danced away the heart of the prince was made of " vair "—old French for "fur "—and the word being confounded with " verre," pronounced like I it, but signifying glass, led to the error, which has been per- petuated by poets, painters, and the popular belief. " Miniver " is " mini-vair "—a little far, ; and in the old times of sumptuary laws, could be worn only by nobles of the highest rank, while the " vair," or ermine— the large fur—was used by royal personages only. Hence the great eignificance of ermine in our coats of arms. To take, again, one of the oldest industries in connection with the clothing of the human being, that, of weaving, there is a corrupted saying that few know the origin of. In fact, "First catch your hare" and "the glass slipper" are as Complete errors as the proverb about "Setting the Thames on fire," a feat that can really only b 3 accomplished by an ardently industrious weaver. Yet so widely has the proverb circulated, that,. regardless of its evident absurdity, it has been adopted in all countries, and "He will never set the Seine on fire," or "the Liffey," or even "the Volga," will be said by Frenchman, Irishman, or Russian, with serene faith in its significance, of a person who does not impress himself on the public mind with an idea of capacity. The " temse " is the channel or groove in which the shuttle travels to and fro; hence the significance of the remark or expression, that he or she "will never set the temse on fire " --t.e., work fast enough to create friction. And now as to the subject which was the original cause of these letters of mine—coursing. I presume it is "the survival of the fittest" principle that makes all true Britons passionately fond of sport, especially field sports; at all events, I hope so. And in fairness to those who course or hunt the hare on their own estates or farms, I would record the fact that puss lives al- ways in terror of her enemies, the worst being the slow, pitiless weasel; that once started by the dog the coursing, as a rule, lasts but a few minutes, and when the hare is caught is followed by instantaneous death. There is no escaping wounded, the cruellest fate of all to a hunted animal. Nor can there be a question of doubt about the coursed hare being better for the table than the one that has been shot? But I maintain that there is a difference be- tween hunting an animal in its natural state and habitat, and breeding it for the purpose of destroying it publicly at towing matches, that may possibly be timed to take place on Bank Holidays and Saturday afternoons; to say nothing of their being made the channel for fostering betting and gaming. The practice to me smacks of cruelty, and my opinion is that a public exhibition of cruelty in any shape or form should, in the eyes of the average Briton, be considered bad tone.—l,am, sir, eke., ANGLO-SCOTUS. P.S.—Since penning the foregoing I have received from a I friend a copy of a recent issueeof the St. Janzes's Gazette, from which I quote the following, anent the blue hare of Scotland :—" On the tops of the higher Scotch hills there still linger on among the colder districts a few isolated colo- nies of a very interesting little rodent, known by a large and ' puzzling array of aliases—as the white hare, the •varying - hare., the Alpine hare, and the blue hare of Scotland. In - size it stands about midway between the common hare,and the rabbit; but it differs greatly from both in colour, general appearance, and instinctive habits. Throughout the suit- e's- mer months the blue hare is clad in a suit of tawny-grey fur, with a slight admixture of longer black hairs; and as it runs, the shifting lights upon its back and sides produce a faintly bluish effect to the eye, which has gained for it per- haps the commonest among its numerous popular names. In winter, however, it changes colour, becoming pow-white all over,:except the tips of its ears, which remain a lus- trous black. It does not burrow nor make a form, but shel- ters itself in natural crannies of the rock. It is worthy of observation that where the hares change colour in winter the stoats also usually assume their ermine dress; but where the hares remain of one hue throughout the year the stoats for the most part follow suit under the influence of identical conditions." 243, Beresford-street, Newington, London, S.E.

div.head: MR. ROBERT SHAW ON TEMPERANCE.
div.p: MR. ROBERT SHAW ON TEMPER- ANCE.

• Under the auspices of the combined Good Templar lodges of Widnes and Runcorn, a public meeting was held in Bethesda schoolroom, Runcorn, en Tuesday evening. Mr. Robert Shaw occupied the chair, and there was a large audience. Mr. T. Horrocks, the converted clown, was pre- sent to deliver a lecture.

The CHAIRMAN said before entering the room he had pro- mised Mr. Horrocks he would not take up the time of the meeting by saying many words—only a very few. He knew theyhad come to hear Mr. Horroeks, and that, generally con- sidered, all a chairman had to do was to endeavour to keep order, and his duties at such a meeting as that were very light. They did not expect disorder there—(hear, hear), because they believed that temperance would, of itself, ele- vate and ennoble a man.E(Hear, hear.) The subject of tem- perance was so broad and of such vast importance that a man like himself scarcely knew where to touch it. (Hear, hear.) Those of them who had been in distant' countries, saw one thing which rather tarnished the fair fame of our countrymen, although we thought a great deal of otir own country. We should scarcely be Englishmen if we did not,—we naturally thought a great deal of our own country,—we • thought there was no one in the whole world like an Englishman. Seldom was a drunken man seen in foreign countries, and when the visitor returned to England be reflected and asked himself "How is it that with religions England, with the facilities we had in this country for elevation and for improving the apses, with the amount of money subscribed year by year for the temper- ance cause, and the thousands of men who were giving their time and their energy for the benefit of their fellow- creatures—they might ask how it was that in England they , found men who lived amongst all these privileges and ad- vantages so debasing themselves as to lose entirely that balance of thought and mind, which was the ennobling fea- ture that belonged exclusively to the human _race." Is those countries that we looked down upon we should naturally expect to find drunkenness rampant; yet in many countries that he had visited—in France, Switzerland, and Belgium—it .was the exception to find a man drunk. They might travel a thousend miles and never come across a• man with a rolling pace. While in England it was yery difficult to move along some of the streets without finding a man who scarcely knew which side of the road to walk upon. This was a phase of English character which told against us, and one which it behoved all of them to try and remedy. (Hear, hear.)lt must be admitted that the Good Templar Order and other temperance organisations which were established throughout the length and breadth of the land had done a great deal towards lifting up the population from that which was the cause of almost all the evil in this great and glorious nation. It seemed to him that one source of the drunkenness of the country was the habit of parents constantly using intoxicaftts before .their children. Those of them who had families knew that there was nothing that a lad took such interest and delight in as trying to be like father. His father was his ideal of what a man should be, and they might depend upon it that, if his father was a sober, steady, upright, intelligent man, in 99 cases out of a 100 the son would grow up in the same way. He did not contend that it would be so in every case, because the son might be:taken where home influences would not reach him, and by bad association and contami- nation be lead away. He thought the worse they looked at the question before them, the more they would see and appreciate the influence they had spent upon the young people, and it was important that those influences should be for good. He would not touch more upon that part of the subject; he could only say that teetotalism was the greatest subject but one. (Hear, hear.) Some had thought that it ought even to be placed before that. Well, one could forgive them even for going to excesses when they con- sidered that in some cases those who had the love of God in their hearts had had it taken away because of the great evil of intemperance ;—(hear, hear)—that intemperance had been the means of bringing some of those who had devoted their lives to the service of God from that high position into the basest and the worst,—he said they could forgive those who went to extremes in the matter, and claimed that the temperance movement stood before every other. Mr. Shaw referred to the ill effects produced by temperance re- formers making exaggerated statements, and remarked that the arguments put forth from a reasona'ele standpoint were far more convincing. He had spoken to many drunkards in his own employ, men who had spent pounds in drink. He knew men that spent 20s. to 30s. weekly in drink, a sum larger than they gave their wives to keep on the house with ; and when he had spoken to them about the evil of what they were doing they admitted that what they were doing was wrong, that temperance was a blessing; and in many cases he had prevailed upon the men to save their money. In fact he had saved money for many of them—(hear, hear, and applause,)—and sone of them had really become useful members of society. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Shaw) saw this, that except he would undertake to receive lOs per week from a man he could not save it for the world, and some men in that way had saved ag mush as £2O. (Applause.) When there was about that sum in the bank, the man was stimulated to add to it, and there would not be much fear of him spending it if he were put in possession of the bank book. It instilled in him a little self-respect, which would keep him from falling back. He thonght there were many ways in which a workingman, who was a teetotaller, might do a great deal of good among witilaiosvuefledilileoc awor-mweiot; t rking.men, fer he had a subject which he could all always bring forward. (Hear, hear.) Temperance would ever commend itself to a man, however debased 'he might that talk tiohinweases nesliabilmyeadnd relNr aiso.nllabelnyeacrg, he thought, would have no trouble whatever in putting the case before them. (Applause). Mr. HOAROCKS then delivered one of his characteristic , addreases.

div.head: EXAMINER,, WU-TWA Y, SEPTEMBER 2, 1882. DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER,, WU-TWA Y, SEPTEMBER 2, 1882. DISTRICT NEWS.
ASHTON.

WILFUL DAMAGE TO PUBLIC PROPERTY.—Owing to the serious damage which has been caused to numerous gas lamps in the township by..the dangerous practice of stone throwing, the Local Board have at last taken some steps to put a stop to it. Notices have been posted to the effect that a reward of £1 will be paid to any person who will give , information as will lead to a conviction. A similar reward Is also offered with respect to the running of races, empty- ing rubbish, and discharging firearms on the highways and public places. Aw ASHTON BEERSELLER FINED.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, last week, before F. S. Gerrard and J. Prescott, Esqs., Robert Unsworth, of Ashton, a grocer and holder of an out-door license, was summoned for having his house open for the sale of beer, on Sunday morning, the 13th Inst., and Peter Sixsmith, a painter, a neighbour of Unsworth's, was summoned for aiding and abetting.—Mr. Ellis, of Wigan, appeared for the defence.—Police-constable Adamson stated that at half-past six on the morning in question a man went to the back door of the defendant's house, and was supplied with something which he drank. Soon after that four men came into the house, but in a short time they went to the next house where Sixsmith lived. Unsworth followed them with a quart jug of beer, and subsequently went back to his shop for another quart of seer, A third time Sixsmith was taking some beer from the shop to his own house when witness stopped him. Witness saw Sixsmith pay Unsworth one shilling for the beer-and a sixpence was returned to bim.—Defendant Unsworth was called, and stated that Sixsmith came to his house on the morning in question and asked him to give him a glass of beer. He gave him some beer, but was not paid for it. He denied that he took a jug of beer from his shop to Sixsmith's. —Sixsmith deposed that Unsworth gave him the beer. Unsworth did not bring any beer to witness's house.—The Bench inflicted a.penalty of ss. and costs in each case. -

The result of the working of the half-year has not been satisfactory, as the loss on revenue account No. has been increased by the sum of £415 9s 7d showing a total loss up to the present time of £3,029 lls 2d. It is hoped, however, that when the line into Wigan is opened, and the traffic properly developed, a reasonable return upon the whole capital outlay will be shown." On the preposition of the chairman, the report and the accom- panying statement of accounts sere adopted, and the meet- ing then came to an end. LICENSING MEETING. - The general annual licensing sessions for the borough of Wigan were held on Wednesday. The Mayor (Mr. Alderman Hopwood) presided, and there was a large attendance of magistrates. The chief constable (Captain Kennion) reported that there were within the borough 135 public-houses, 66 beerhouses, 54 outdoor beer- houses, two wine dealers on the premises, two dealers in sweets on and off the premises, one dealer in spirits and liquors, one dealer in spirits, liquor, and beer off the pre- mises, and five wholesale beer dealers off the premises-- total, 226; music hall licenses, 30. During the year five licensed victuallers had been proceeded against, two of whom were fined, one ordered to pay costs, and two dis- missed. Five indoor and six outdoor beersellers were sum- moned, and in eight cases fines were imposed. For the year ended 30th June, 1852, 407 persons had been proceeded against for drunkenness, 308 of whom were males and 99 females, showing an increase of 37 over last year. A depu- tation from a public meeting of ratepayers attended, and presented a memorial praying the benck not to grant any additional licenses, and to use the powers now placed in their hands in dealing with off licenses. All the old licenses were renewed with the exception of six outdoor beer licenses, four of which were refused and two postponed until the adjourned licensing day. There were two applica- tions for spirit licenses for existing beerhouses;three applica- tions for provisional grants, one for beer and wine off the premises, two for outdoor beer licensgs, and two for removal of licenses. The Bench refused the whole of the applies- _ _ _ _
tions with the exception of that of Miss A. Jones for the removal of a beer license connected with her restaurant to new premises, this being adjourned to the next sitting of the Licensing Committee.

div.p: FRODSHAIkt.

Surros WEAVER I.Truorr Clwacw.—The annual Sunday school anniversary was held on Sunday, when two sermons were preached by the Rev. Fitzherbert Rugby, of Shetford. The services were well attended and the collections amounted to £l6 18s. 2d. MR. J. J. STEWAIM'S FAT STOCK SALE.—This sale was held at the Queen's Head Hotel, Frodsham, on Tues- day, when the following prices were realised :—Fat calves, 755. to 95a. each ; stirks, .f 8 17s. 61. to £11; fat heifers, £l3 to £2O lOs •, fat cows, £l5 to £2O; fat sheep, Ms. to 935.; fat lambs 335. to 515.; store pigs, 15s. to 695. There was a very good attendance of buyers from Liverpool, War- rington,Runcorn, and Frodsham. _ _ _
THE 'VOLUNTEERS AT Fox HILL.—The Frodsham Volun-

teer Corps made their annual visit to Fox Hill on Saturday evening by invition of James Reynolds, Esq., J.P., but the previous continuous rain had rendered the ground unsuitable for extensive military tactics. Each man had been supplied with twenty rounds of _blank ammunition, and, under the _ _

command of Capt. R Ashton, they were formed up facing the house, after which they were formed for attack, and advanced gradually to about 200 yards, when they were ordered to re- tire, after which they advanced to 100 yards, and the com- mand given to prepare to charge with fixed bayonets. At the bugle call the company broke into double line, and, after making a desperate charge at an imaginary enemy, the halt was sounded and three volleys were fired in excellent style. The men were liberally supplied with refreshments, after which Captain Robert Ashton thanked Mr. Reynolds for the kind invitation, and gave the time for three cheers, 'which were heartily responded to. Mr. Reynolds in a very suit- able speech highly complimented the men on their discip- line and soldierlike bearing, and said that on behalf of him- self and Mrs. Reynolds they hoped to have the pleasure of welcoming the Frodsham Volunteer Corps on many future occasions,he concluded by asking for cheers for Col. J.Ashton and Capt. Robert Ashton, which were warmly given. The company then marched to the Drill Hall, and, previous to dispersing, the captain thanked the officers, Lieutenants Henry and Harrison, also the non-commissioned officers and the men for their attendance.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

EARLESTONIANS FINED FOE SUNDAY DRINKING AT GOLEORNE.—THE BONA-FIDE TRAVELLER QuEsrtox.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, John Caunce, senior, landlord of the Cross Keys beerhouse, Golborne, was summoned for having his house open during prohibited hours on Sunday, the 13th August; and John Caunce, junior, Richard Brown, Edward Hughes, John Crosby, Joseph Haddonall, and William Caunce, were summoned for aiding and abetting.—Mr. Moore, of Warrington, repre- sented the two Caunce's. All the defendants pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Smith, stationed at Golborne, said that on Sunday, the 13th August, he was in plain clothes with P.C. Whiting watching the beerhouse named. From 8 a.m. to 11 a.m. they saw 17 men and three females enter the house. They saw the defendant's daughter twice go with something under her apron to the-back yard behind the beerhouse, and they also saw several men come from the end of the build- ing wiping their months. John Caunce (the landlord's son), who lived near, went into the beershop four times. and came away each time with something concealed under his left breast. When they saw him coming away at eleven o'clock they went to laim and asked him what he had got concealed in his breast. He at first said " Nothing ; " but after hesi- tating for a moment or two pulled out the bottle produced containing a quart of beer. They took him back to the beershop, and told him that he would be reported for being on licensed premises during prohibited hours. He replied, "You'll make nothing of it." When they got inside they found the other defendants sitting round a table, and John Caunce was stand- ing up. Four of them had pints of beer about _ _ _

half full, and John Crosby had one glass of beer part fu... There were also three empty glasses on the table that had had beer in—a small quantity of beer being at the bottom of each. They asked for the landlord, but were told that they could not see him then as he was ill in bed. They then left but called again about one o'clock and told the landlord that he would be reported.—ln reply to Mr. Moore, the witness said the other defendants were strangers to him. They lived in Earlestown.—Mr. Moore: How far is it from Golborne ? P.C. Smith : We measured it to Earlestown Market-place- -2 miles and 1000 yards. The defendants all live in the immediate neighbourhood or 300 yards of it.—Mr. Moore: Do you know where Earle-street is in Earlestown? The Witness: I have not been in Earle-street.—You know where it is? I was never in Earle-street. I measured from Caunce's house simply to the' Market-place.—How far is the Market- place from the Vulcan? I don't know where the Vulcan i.—How many yards did you make it? • Two miles and 1000 yards.—Was that the high road? That's the highway. We measured the longest way round.—How far does Caunce junior live from Caunce senior? He lives next door.—ln reply to further questions, the constable stated that he believed the old man was about 70 years of age. He did notknow whether he would be surprised to hear that he was 80. All the defendants told him that they came from Earlestown. None of the defendants were drunk; they were all sober.— The Clerk: IS the defendant's house above three miles from Earlestown as the crow flies? P.C. Smith : No, sir, it is not.—Mr. Moore: Oh, yes, it is.—Superintendent Jack- son: Not as the crow flies.—Mr. Moore: It depends which way the crow will fly. (Laughter.)—P.C. Whiting deposed that he served the summonses. Superintendent Jackson: Do you know that it is not three miles from the defendant Caunce's house to where the other defendants live ? P.C. Whiting: Earle-street is just about the same distance as the Market-place. Mr. Jackson: None of them live above three miles away? P.C. Whiting : No, sir. —ln reply to questions by Mr. Moore, the witness added that he knew where the Vulcan and Earle-street were. .From Golborne Farle-street and the Market-place were about the same distance. He did not measure it. Mr. Moore: If Mr. Peake has measured it 31 miles and 200 yards it will not be correct? The witness made no reply. Mr. Moore then addressed the court on behalf of the Caunce's. He pointed out that the landlord was in his 80th year, and unable to appear. He had kept the house for 24 years and neither he nor his family had appeared in a police court before, It had always been their aim and object to conduct their house properly, but, no doubt, the police had a perfect right to bring that case there. The five defendants summoned for aiding and abetting were bona fide travellers to all intents and purposes, and were thought so by the persons who supplied them with drink. It would be for their worships to decide that the distance had been measured from the defendant Caunce's house to where they lived in Earle:street, Earlestown, and that it was 31- miles and 1000 yards. They went to the house and asked to be supplied with beer, „stating that they were travellers and that they had come from Earlestown, more than three miles away. He stated that the landlord had borne an irreproachable character. There was no previous conviction against his client, and if there was any doubt about the case he hoped the Bench would give him the benefit of it.—John Caunce, jun., was then called, and he stated that he had been tapping some barrels for his father, for which he received some beer. He was taking it into his own house when the police stopped him. The distance from Earlrstown had been measured that morning. It was 3i miles and 200 yards.—Mrs. Caunce stated that she served the defendants witß beer. They told her that they had come from Earlestown, and that they had come over three miles.—Several of the defendants said they had nothing to say. They thought they were beyond the distance allowed by law.—The Chairman said John Caunce (the landlord) would be fined 20s. ateil, costs, John Caunce (the younger) would be fined 10s. and cests, and the other defendants would be fined 2s. 6d. and costs each.—The Clerk observed that the mere fact of the men being over three miles away— supposing it was correct—ivas not sufficient. The law said they should not be considered travellers unless they were so. If they went there to drink it was a breach of the law. HOO GREEN.

ATIILETIC SPORTS AT HOO GBEEN.—On Saturday afternoon last, the second annual athletic festival, came off in a field adjoining the Kilton Hotel. Admirable arrangements were made, and there was a magnificent array of prizes; some of considerable value. div.head: KNUT:3FORD.
div.p: KNUT:3FORD.

RELEASE OF MR. W. AIAIR FROM KNITTSFOLD GAOL.— On Monday morning Mr. Mair was released from Knutsford gaol after serving the full period of nine months, to which. he was sentenced on the 29th November last for illegal practices in connection with the last Macclesfield parlia- mentary election. Mr. Mair was the legal agent for the Liberal candidate. Mr. May, the Conservative agent, was sentenced to a similar period of imprisonment, but owing to serious illness was released nearly three months ago. Mr. Mair has been deprived of his office of Registrar of the County Court, but is not debarred from resunaing his general professional business. He does not return immediately to Macclesfield; but will join his friends in the north of Eng- land, in order to recruit his health. He has at times suffered severely from illness, and representations have been made to the Home Secretary; but as the prison doctor could not certify that his life was endangered, Sir W. Harcourt declined to interfere with the sentence. Mr. Mair was met by Mrs. Mair and his business partner, Mr. Bland, and left Knutsford by an early train for Yorkshire. He is the last of the imprisoned bribers sentenced in connection with the last general election.

div.head: LEIGH.
div.p: LEIGH.

TRIENNIAL ELECTION OF GITARDIANS.=A poll has been taken in the Leigh Union by order of the Local Government Board to test the feeling of the ra.tepayers respecting the proposal of the Guardians to adopt triennial instead of annual elections. In the townships of Astley, Atherton, Culcheth, Tyldeslev, and West Leigh, the answer is favour- able to the proposed alteration, the majority being 647. Five other townships, viz., Bedford, Golborno, Kenyon, Lowton, and Pennington. returned a majority of 596 against any change. Of the 10,689 voting papers delivered, 5,262 were either invalid. not filled up, or not returned to the collectors. The votes in favour of triennial elections numbered 2,742, against 2,685, majority in favour 57. LICENSING SEssioNs.—The Annual licensing sessions for the Leigh division took place on Monday. Of the 85 licensed victuallers three had been convicted, being the same as the year previous. There were 149 beerhouse-keepers, and 86 persons held licenses to sell beer off the premises, as compared with 83 last year, but in five cases the premises were closed. Five beersellers had been convicted, being the same number as last year. In 1878, 406 persons were sum- moned for drunkenness; 350 in 1879; 374 in 1880; 387 in . .

...... , 18S1; and in the present year 527, showing an increase of 140 over last year. The apprehensions for drunkenness in 1878 were 270; 186 in 1879; 184 in 1880; 187 in 1881, and in the present year 252, being an increase of 65 over last year. The division comprises nine townships, with a population 0f,51,613. There were no fresh applications for spirit licenses, nor for beerhousea selling on the premises. Of the four applications for beer licenses to sell off, two were withdrawn, and the bench refused the others. • Last year's census showed the population of Atherton to be 12,602, and as, according to the Act of 1840, licensed vic- tuallers must have a ratability of £3O and beersellers £l5 where the population is over 10,000, four spirit-houses and 24 of the 36 existing beza•houses do not come up to the standard imposed by the increased population, and the re- newal of licenses was deferred, the applicants being told that at the adjourned sessions they mast be prepared with evidence to show that their houses are of the required value. A similar decision was given' with referedce to 18 of the 28 off beer licenses in the same township. Renewals were not sought for eight off licenses, and they were struck out, the remainder of these licensee, except where there is a doubtas to the value, being renewed.
