div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

PADGATE WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. —A. preliminary meeting was held in the vestry of the Paigate Wesleyan Chapel, on Thursday last, at 'Which, in spite of the bad weather, there was a good attendance. Mr. Andrew Rathbone was re-elected president, Mr. Frederick Wright was elected vice-president, and Mr. Arthur Bennett was re-elected secretary and treasurer of the society. The committee chosen were Messrs. Joseph Andrews, W. H. Jenkins, Theodore C. London, Matthew Shakeshaft, and J. Wilde. The rules were carefully revised, and arrangements made by which any member might introduce his friends to the ordinary meetings of the society, and also providing for occasional open nights, when the essays might be listened to by the general public of the neighbournood. It was resolved that the session commence with a soiree, to be held the first Thursday in October. A number of new members were admitted. Essays were promised, among other subjects, on " Phrenology,"" Lord Beaconsfield," "The Channel Tunnel and the Tidal Navigation Scheme," " Political Incon- sistency," " Tobacco," "The House of Lords," ." The Boteler family," " Temperance," Sze., and the meeting terminated.

div.head: THELWALL.
div.p: THELWALL.

ENTERTAINMENT TO SUNDAY SCHOOL SCHOLARS. By the kindness of Mr. and Mrs. J. Nicholson, :Uhlman HA!, the Sunday school scholars attending Alt Saints' Church, Thelwall, were,provided with a treat on Saturday last. In the afternoon they 'fere regaled with tea in the schoolroom, and subsequently under the guidance of Mr. Evans, school- master and superintendent of the Sunday school, they were taken to the grounds of Thelwa.ll Hall. Here the evening was spent in skipping, cricket, and race running for money prizes; and the scholars who had been most regular in their attendance were presented with books. Before leaving the grounds Mrs. Nicholson gave each child a bun, and Mr. Nicholson made them each a present of a small bag of sweets.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

~, THE SIIOOTING OP Two POLICE CONSTABLES.—On Monday, the Wigan magistrates committed for trial at the Liverpool Assizes Thomas A. Robison, described as an ".in- dependent gentleman," on a charge of shooting at two police constables with intent to do them grievous bodily harm. The officers went with a tipstaff to execute a warrant from the High Court for the prisoner's arrest, but he resisted for a long time, and when the policemen at last entered his house, he fired shots in their direction from a gun and a revolver, fortunately without injuring them. The prisoner represented that he merely intended to frighten the constables, but "gentlemen," be they never so "independent," cannot be allowed to use loaded firearms in the manner imputed to Mr. Robison. FIRE AT THE WIGAN CORPORATION SEWAGE FARM.— Soon after noon, on Saturday, a large stack of hay was dis- covered to be on fire in the stackvard of the above farm at Newburgh. Information was conveyed to Ormskirk, and the fire brigade, under Superintendent Stuart, were soon on the spot. The stack was immediately cut through, and the fire eventually extinguished before any great amount of damage bad been done. There were several other large stacks in the yard, but the fire was prevented from extending to these.

_ DISTRESSING SUICIDE AT WIGAN.—HEROIC CONDUCT OF A YOUNG GIRL.—On Tuesday, Mr. Drifileld, county coroner, held an inquest at Worsley Mesnes, Wigan, on the body of a young man named Thomas Stephenson, son of Mr. James :Stephenson, Hawkley Hall Farm, who put an end to his life under most distressing circumstances on Saturday night.. Some months ago the unfortunate young fellow, who was 21 years old on the day of bis death, was out with a'cart and horse, when an accident befel him, his head being injured. The accident affected his brain and at times he gave much anxiety to his family.- A careful watch was kept over him, but on Saturday night he succeeded in escaping from the house. He rushed across the farmyard to a gate leading to a pond, and was followed by his sister Alice, but before she could get near him ho had jumped over a wall protecting the pond, and thrown himself in the water at a spot where the depth was from 10 to 12 feet. His sister ran down the embankment to the pond and jumped in after him. In a few moments the father made his appearance, and found both struggling in the water. He was able to grasp the girl and pull her out much exhausted. The deceased sank at orrce, and his body was only recovered two hours afterwards. The jury returned a verdict of "suicide 'whilst temporarily insane." -

THE WIGAN JUNCTION RAILWAY.—The half-yearly meeting of the proprietors of the Wigan Junction Railways Company was held in Manchester on Tuesday. Mr. Nathaniel Eckersley, chairman of the board of directors, presided. The following-report of the directors was taken as read :—" All the heavy works from Strangeways, the point up to which the line is constructed, to Darlington-street, Wigan, are well in hand and approaching early completion. The works of the short branch to connect this cempany's line with the Lancashire Union Railway are making very

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

WHAJITON CHURCII, WINSFORD.—ChriSt Church, Whar- ton, has been for some time undergoing repairs, and as that and the choir need supporting a special appeal was made by two of the most popular church dignitaries of the neighbour- hood. These were the Rev. Canon Hayhurst, of Davenham, in the morning, who has the character of being a most liberal gentleman as well as good preacher; and the Rev. Canon Blackburn, of Warmingham, a great attractor by his style of elognence. The result of the appeal, despite the great attraction of the Salvationists, was somewhat under £ll. SONS OF TEMPERANCE.—This temperance organization, which took up the Primitive Methodist section of a former temperance class of workers who had not a beneficiary tendency as part of their programme, has done well in High- street. Not only has this tenf got many old members, bat also a juvenile section to act as a feeder. On Saturday, headed by the Volunteer Band, amid banners and flags, and', other ensigns of the order, they drew to tea many, who it is hoped will join their ranks, and husband their hard earnings as a result, besides saving health. SALVATION ARMT.—The Army, engrossing as it does so many of the people of the town, seems to be the chief source of attraction, and the observed of nearly all observers. Always there ,seems something up. something to draw attention and excite to a gathering. Some people seem to have a great knack of making friends, and of all the salva- tion officers in this vicinity none have endeared themselves more than Captain Thurman, who lately commanded the Winsford corps. A great holiness convention being called on Monday, of course, Cheshire like, it must have a tea and its following meetin2:. Then, as delegates came from neigh- bouring towns, a dinner must be provided. Thus Monday was a great day, for which Sanday was used as the day of preparation by its knee drill at seven, its mission at AI, its service at 11, and so through the day others. 'But the aim, or one aim, of all mast not be lost sight of amid all the prayer, singing, shouting, Waving of handkerchiefs, and such like performances, a "new barracks." Yes' the col- lections must be made and the home provided for many, who, before the army came here, never darkened any place of worship with their presence. What the amount realised has been we have not yet learned, but no doubt it was hand- some.

div.head: ITEMS OF CHESEIIRE NEWS.
div.p: ITEMS OF CHESEIIRE NEWS.

A few members of the Altrincham Conservative club had a pic-nic to Chester on Saturday. A poll is about to be taken of the ratepayers of Chester upon the proposed Improvement Bill, which a public meet- ing some time ago declared against. The Northwich Floral and Horticultural Society held their nineteenth annual show on Friday and Saturday. There were 550 entries divided among 46 competitors, the competi- tions throughout being very close. The anniversary sermons of the Baptist Chapel, Nant- wich, were preached on Sunday by the Rev. T. Goudby, 8.A., President of Chilsvell College. On Monday the new pastor, the Rev. P. Williams, - Llangollen College, was ordained; the Rev. Hugh Jones, D.D ,delivering the charge. The president of Shropshire Baptist Association and a number of other gentlemen took part in the interesting ceremony. FLOODS.—The heavy rains which prevailed all last week and continued until Tuesday, caused the river Dec to be bank-full this week, and the several streams of Mid-Cheshire and the Welsh borders to be similarly over-charged. A great extent of the low lands was flooded throughout the district, but the fine weather of the last day or two has cleared off the over-supply of water. THE CROPS IN CHESHIRE.—Farmers were generally hope- ful during the wet weather of last week that there would be a change with the full moon of Monday, but there were many long faces when Tuesday morning was as wet as ever. Fortunately, however, the weather changed on Tuesday at noon, and it continued fine until Thursday. On Tuesday afternoon and Wednesday morning many reaping machines were got to work among the ripe oats, and many acres were cut. The crops are generally spoken of as very good, more than an average. Barley also comes out well. Wheat, though above an average crop, is scarcely so well fed as other cereals; a few days' sun would, however, wonderfully imProye the yields. A short spell of fine weather would enable farmers to ingather the little hay that yet requires housing. Everywhere the farmer speaks well of the produce of his meadows.

EDDISEURY LICENSING SESSIONS.—The annual licensing sessions for the division of Eddisbury were held on Monday. Superintendent Naylor reported that there wereB6 licensed victuallers, 41 beersellers, and 12 others who sold off the premises—total, 139—which gave an average of 229 mem- bers of the population to each license. Eleven licensed victuallers had been proceeded against during the year, nine of whom had been convicted. One Iperseller had been pro- ceeded against and convicted. One hundred and nine per- sons had been convicted of drunkenness. The magistrates renewei all the old licenses, and grarted an application for a new license for a house at Mouldsworth Station. An ap- plication for a new license for a house at Banbury Locks was refused.

MEETING OF CREDITORS.—A meeting of the creditors fo Charles Walker, of the Wiltshire House' High-street, Con- gleton, grocer and pinvision dealer, was held on Friday at the office of Mr. Joseph Sampson, solicitor, Manchester. The statement of affairs produced by Mr. A. H. Lamb, the receiver, showed liabilities £759 and assets of £195. Nia. offer of composition being made, the creditors resolved to liquidate the estate by arrangement, Mr. G. H. Russel (secretary of the Manchester Creditors' Association) being appointed trustee, with a committee of inspection. Mr. Sampson was entrusted with the registration of the resolu- tions. Creditors were represented by Mr. Sampson, solicitor, and Igessrs.*Astbury and Eckersley, Mr. G. H. Russell, and Mr. F. Cooper, accountants. THE ACCIDENT AT CHESTER STATION. - Colonel Rich reports the result of his inquiry into the double collision that occurred on the 22nd of July at the south-east end of Chester Station, on the London and North-Western Railway. He says :—" The only conclusion I can arrive at is, that the engine-driver was asleep, or that he was not thinking about his business, and that the fireman was engaged with his fire, or something else, that prevented his -observing the state of the signals and where he was. The collision was caused by the gross neglect of the engine-driver. He has borne an ex- cellent character up to the present time, and I was informed that some time since, when the crank-axle of his engine broke, he showed great activity and presence of mind in preventing a collision and serious consequences, by running forward and stopping a -train which was coming in the opposite direction, although he had been severely cut in the knee when thrown from his engine by the breaking of the crank-axle."

CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY'S ANNUAL SHOW. —The annual exhibition of the Cheshire Agricultural Society was opened in brilliant weather, on Thursday morning, in Mr. Wilbraham Tollemache's charming grounds at Dorf°ld Hall, near Nantwich. The entries show a con- siderable falling off in numbers on preceding years. In fact, it is the smallest show for the past six years. In point of quality, however, the exhibition is very fine. The Duke of Westminster won the premium for a pair of cart or draught horses with his well-known prize-takers Duchess and Lady Whitelock. He was also second in the class for brood mares and foals with Lively Lucy, being beaten for first prize by Mr. Joseph Hill, Smethwick Hall, Congleton. In the class for a pair of agricultural horses Mr. George Rodger, Preston Brook, took the premier honours. Mr. James Crenshaw, of Cheadle, took the first prize for cart stallions, and also the silver cup offered by the local commit- tee, with Congress, a magnificent bright bay animal. Lord Crewe carried off the first prize for bulls over two years with his handsome roan Welford, Mr. Foljambe, M.P., Vyorksop, taking the second with Bright Helm. Mr. Fol- jambe was also second in the class for shorthorn bulls under two years, the first prize being taken by Mr. Charles Brierley, Tenbury. Mr. Brierley took first prizes for a shorthorn cow in milk and a shorthorn heifer under three years. CHESHIRE DAIRY FARMERS' ASSOCIATION.—A meeting of the Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Association was held at the Town Hall, Nantwich, on Saturday, Lord Combermere pre- siding. 'Amongst those present were Mr. H. J. Tollemache, M.P., Mr. G. W. Latham, Mr. Randle Tollemache, Captain Cotton, Mr. Poole, and others. torcl Combermere said that, as cheese was a considerable product of the county, it be- hoved them in every way to try and improve its quality, and not allow themselves to be beaten by the Americans. Cheese-making required a good deal of attention, for it was done by rule more than anything else. Mr. H. J. Tolle- mache, M.P., invited dairy farmers of the district to connect themselves with the association, for he believed it would be ,to their advantage to do so. The objects they had in view were—in the first place to improve the article which they produced, and secondly to endeavour as far as they could to

lessen the expense of bringing the producer and consumer together. Mr. Gouldbourne said that since the association had been formed a marked improvement had been noted in the cheese at Chester fair. -Mr. Mackie suggested that at the forthcoming exhibition of cheese at Chester there might also be an exhibition of the best cheese-making appliances. A petition was signed for presentation to Parliament, point- ing out the great injury that is being sustained by the British dairy interest in consequence of the manufacture of " bosh " butter and lard oleomargarine cheese, and praying the House of Commons to compel mamufacturers of these articles, and those engaged in the sale thereof, to com- pletely describe them by names that shall indicate their real nature.

div.head: MINERS NATIONAL CONFERENCE.
div.p: MINERS NATIONAL CONFERENCE.

A special conference of representatives of the various miners' associations in Great Britain was commenced on Tuesday at the Mechanics' Institute, David-street, Man- chester. Mr. T. Burt, M.P., was elected president, and Mr. B. Pickard (Yorkshire) vice-president. The object of the conference is to discuss the wages question and the laws relating to miners. The meeting was conducted in private. The representatives present were from the following associa- tions, the figures attached representing the number of men at work in the districts indicated :—Ashton-on-Haydock, 7,000; North Stafford, 8,000; Silverdale Lodge, 2,000; Aspull, 3,000; Lancashire Miners' Federation, 15,000; North Yorkshire and Cleveland, 8,120; Wigan, 7,000; Tyldesley and Leigh, 5,000; Northumberland, 18,000; Durham Enginemens' Association, 1,600 ; Durham colliery mechanics, 2,000; Durham Miners' Association, 73,291; South Wales house coal, 8,860; Ashton-under-Lyne and Oldham, 5,000 ; Worsley and Little Culton, 16000; West Bromwich, 10,000; St. Helens, 3,000;. Yorkshire Miners' Association, 45,000; Pemberton, 2,500; Fife and Clackmannan 6,000; South Wales Steam Coal, 50,000; South Yorkshire and North Derbyshire, 8,000; Blackwell, 700; Hindley, 2,000; West Camberland, 5,500; Derbyshire, 5,300; North Wales, 6,500; North Stafford, 6,000; Old Hill, 5,000. Mr. W. Crawford (Durham) was elected secretary, and Mr. John Nixon (Northumberland) treasurer to the Conference. The -credential committee consists of Mr. Daniel Reid (Durham) and Mr. J. Finney (Wigan). Messrs. Wilson (Durham), Ralph Young (Northumberland), and W. Parrott (York- shire), form the business committee; the tellers being Mr. K. Cowie (Yorkshire) and Mr. T. Weir (Fife and Clackman- non). The Conference resumed on Wednesday.—Mr. Burt, M.P., , president, in his opening address, said he could not recom- mend a general strike to raise wages. That was a wild and impractical proposal, but he did approve of the limitation of hours, and would go in for eight hours a day, and a day's holiday every week. They wanted union to achieve the objects they had in view.—On the motion of Mr. Wight (Northumberland), a resolution was passed affirming that the certificated manager of every mine and colliery ought to be the person who has the responsibility, control, and direction of the inine, and should be the person next in charge to the owner. It was also resolved that the under- manager or under-viewer should hold a second-class certifi- cate, and should have served his time as a practical miner for ten Years before receiving his certificate.—On the motion of Mr. head (Durham), seconded by Mr. W. Brown (North Stafford), a resolution was adopted, urging that a workman should not be allowed to enter a mine until it had been examined and reported to be free from any accumulation of gases, such examination to take place not more than two hours before the workman enters. The deputy or fireman making the examination shoulti, prior to work being commenced, make a report in his own handwriting in a book, setting forth the condition of the mine, such book to be kept where the miners can see it before descending. It was stated that in North Stafford, Cumberland, and other districts the collieries are conducted in the spirit of the resolution.—Mr. Cross (St. Helens) moved a resolution to the effect that the use of blasting powder should be entirely prohibited in every mine or part of a mine where gas was given off or was found to exist in such quantities as to be dangerous to the safety of the workmen.—Mr. Finney (Wigan) seconded the motion.—Mr. Abrahams (South Wales) proposed an amendment that blasting should be prohibited only during the time gas is being given off, or so long as it was present in dangerous quantities. In many collieries blasting did not so much affect coal getting as heaving the bottom and bringing down the top. If it was prohibited altogether many col- lieries in England and South Wales would have to be stopped.—The resolution was carried by a large majority, and the conference adjourned. . The Conference discussed on -Thursday a large variety of questions affecting the working of mines and the interests of miners. In addition to a resoltation in favour of the appointment of a Minister of Mines, a motion was passed, after a long discussion, affirming that the power to prosecute under the Mines Act, instead of being exclusively in the hands of the inspector or the Secretary of State, should be granted to a common informer. A resolution was passed pledging the Conference to support Messrs. Burt and Broadhurst in their efforts to amend the Employers' Liability Act. The President (Mr. Burt), speaking on the Employers' Liability Act, said the Conference would recognise the fact that any attempt to reopen this question would be certain to encounter consider,able opposition. There was an indisposition on the part of Parliament to open the question, and but for the fact • that employers had brought pressure to bear upon their workmen to convince them to contract themselves out of the Act, he should have been no party to reopening the sub• ject.—Resolutions were also passed on a variety of other subjects, including the following: The provision of danger signals to make known such atmospheric changes as may • affect the working of mines. The provision of ambulances for colliers at mines. The examination of strangers enter- ing mines. The sinking of extra shafts. The measurement • of air. The provision of safety catchers and hooks at col- lieries, and the carrying out of the Act with reference te , the deductions of coal for dirt.

div.head: ST. HELENS MAN IN ACTION IN EGYPT. . THE BRITISH SOLDIERS' CHARGE.
div.p: A ST. HELENS MAN IN ACTION IN EGYPT. . THE BRITISH SOLDIERS' CHARGE.

Under date Ramleh, Aug. 11, Private Joseph Marsh, of B Company, King's Royal Rifles—a St. Helens man—writes to a friend in St. Helens giving an account of the recon- naissance of the sth August. Speaking of newspaper corre- spondents, the writer says: "You may judge ef our astonishment, when the mail came out, to see that they had sent word home that I Company had run away when on oat- post duty. lam stare the general has a better idea of these thins than the correspondents, and he is perfectly satisfied with the conduct of the regiment in all they have done since their arrival here. In fact, I have found out how most of them get their information. They are generally away out of danger, and when all is over come riding up and run about asking first one and then another how things have gone on, and they make a report as if they were present. As for the outpost affair, there was not one of them present, and how they construed it into cowardice not one of us can understand." Describing the fight on the sth, Private Marsh says: "At 1 p.m. that day we received orders to get two days' rations and fall in, and at 3.30 p.m. we marched off in the direction of the enemy's lines, arriving on the banks of the Canal with the 46th Regiment and half a battalion of the 38th, the Naval Brigade coming down from Alexandria by train, and halting about 4,000 yards from the enemy's trenches. Our battalion crossed the Canal by a foot-bridge, which had been thrown across by the Royal Engineers, the 38th and 46th moving on the left of the Canal. After our regiment had advanced along the banks of the Canal about a mile, B Company extended, sup- ported by C Company and A Company, covered by a 9-pounder gun worked by a ship's crew of her Majesty:s ship Superb, and advanced to within 600 Yards of the enemy, when they opened fire on us. We quickly responded, the Naval Brigade, a mile or more to our right, at once sending shells from the 40-pounders they had brought down with them, and the Marines creeping along the railway embankment under cover until within about 800 yards of the enemy when they opened fire, and we commenced to advance in short rushes. The enemy kept up a rapid fire on us, but they were firing too high, so that their shots took no effect. It was like a band of music to hear the bullets whistle over our heads, and caused your humble servant to duck his head as one or more came much nearer than was pleasant. But this timidity soon passed over, and as we drew nearer we could see the enemy much better, as they were in a trench screened by some tall grass which grew in their rear. The noise was somewhat deafen- ing now with the booming of the cannon and the reports of the rifles. Still we kept pressing on till within 200 yards of the enemy. We halted under perfect &war of a ditch, then ran round a ploughed field and delivered volley after volley into them until within about -a hundred yards, when we batted again and kept up a strong fire. And now happened one of those exploits which has gained for British soldiers such a name for bravery. Fifty men had the courage to charge the trench in the face of overwhelming numbers. Giving a cheer we sprang to our feet and at once rushed over towards them, firing as we ran, when with such a yell—some call it a cheer—we sprang on them. They could not stand the charge and a yell like that, so they turned away and fled, and as they retreated they were met by the cross fire of the 46th on the right. The Marines had kept advancing with us until they had driven the enemy into their forts. During this time the bluejackets had advanced up the line to within a distance of 2,000 yards ivith a Nordenfeldt gun —one of the most murderous things ever invented—and having got their gun into proper range they delivered volley after volley into the forts, and silenced one or two of them. We were now ordered to advance again along the banks of the Canal, which we did for about two hundred yards; and the enemy appearing in large numbers we gave them half a dozen volleys, when the order came for us to retreat, which was done in splendid style. The men we were pitted against were the pick of Arabi's army, and stood well to their posts until we gave them the veil and they could not , stand that.
A legacy of £1,090 has been left to the Liverpool Blue- coat Hospital by the late Senhor Ignacio Veiga, a Portugese gentleman, who received his commercial education in that city.
At the St. Helens Police Court, on Thursday, a woman named Bridget Bolond was fined ed and costs for selling ballads and books without a license.

GOOD TEMPL Al'S' DEMONSTRATION AT AVTDNES. On 'Saturday afternoon last the united lodges of the Inde- pendent Order of Good Template, in Widnes, held an oral- I air demonstration. The weather was rather unfavourable for such an event, and one part of the proceedings was brought to an abrupt termination in consequenee of a heavy downpour of rain, but on the whole the demonstration was very succeseenl. Assembling in Mersey-street at half-past 'two, the members to the number of about 150, there formed in proceseieual order, and paraded the principal thorough- fares, headed by the Star of Widnes Temperance Brass Band. Then followed the members of the Juvenile Temple, the Sunbeam Lodge, preceeded by their handsome two-poled banner. Next came the adult members, who represented the following lodges :—Star of Widnes, Haste to the Rescue, Samaritan, Hope of Appleton, and Hope of Runcorn. The route:taken was up Mersey-street, Oakland-street, down Waterloo-ro el, along Victoria and Widnes Roads to Albert. street, where the procession turned round and returned to a piece of ground near the mirket. Fine weather had so far favoured the demonstration, but whilst the meeting was held here rain fell very heavily, and dispersed the people. A chair did duty as a platform, and upon this stepped Bro. T. Bold, who addressed a few words to the assembled crowd. "Bro. T. Rosy also spoke, and referring to the numerous offensive names applied to Good Templars, said if they could but induce the people to give up that curse against which they had pledged themselves for life, They would be content to bear the most opprobrious epithets. He showed how every man was directly or indirectly a sufferer through the drinking habits of the country. Since he came to Widnes he had witnessed scenes of a most heart-rending description, and so degrading was the love of strong drink, that all sober people might well hate the cursed thing. It was his sincere hope that the words which would be spoken during that demonstration would convince many of the evils of the traffic, and cause them to sign the pledge if not for their own sake, for the sake of their fellows. A few days ago he observed that a large public-house was selling up. That was a good sign—(hear, hear)—for this dark spot on the Mersey. He trusted only a short time would elapse before the next sale in a public-house--(hear, hear)—and that the blighting effects of the trade would cause many to sign the pledge, thus making themselves sober and happy. (Applause). Bro. Hoanocas remarked that be had been delighted with' the procession, and had come to the conclusion that the Good Templars of Widnes were not ashamed to show their colours. (Hear, hear.) The regalia of a Good Templar was an outward sign that he had pledged himself to work against the slavery of drink. If they saw a poor man in the street, they ought not to kick him, but endeavour to get him to be teetotal. He (Bro. Horrocks) did not kick a man, or call him a blackguard because he drank that which did him harm, but ,he spoke as kindly and affectionately as he possibly could to the man. If the working men of -England had to be won from intoxicating drink they would have to do it by love and charity: (Hear, hear.) A Good Templar was working as much for the good of his country as the sol- diers at present in. Egypt; they were fighting one of the greatest foes that ever cursed this country. The meeting was then dispersed in consequence of the rain. An adjournment was made to Lacey-street Wesleyan Schools, where tea had been. provided. About 300 porsons partook of it, and Sisters E. Harrison, J. Reay, Barlow, Gallilee, Hewson, Smith, Roughsedge, Smith, Gallilee, Hughes, Prescott, Wilson, Lamb, Rescorl, Fairclough, and Evans, presided at the tables. ,At half-past seven a public meeting was held in the Volunteer Hall, and was well at- tended, about 500 persons being present. The proceedings were marked with considerable enthusiasm. Bro. Horrocks, "the converted clown," who is a great favourite with Widnes audiences, was present, and he frequently elicited cheers and laughter from the audience, by his earnest con- demnation of the drink traffic and his witty sallies. The chair was occupied by Bro. T. S. Swales. Bros. T. Reay, Shaw, Walley, Ireland, Tomlinson, Barrow, Rescorl, Stayte, and Falkner had seats upon the platform. The band played selections of music during the evening. The CHAIRMAN, in commencing the proceedings, remarked that they were almost celebrating the jubilee of the temper- ance-cause. :He thought Thursday next would conclude the first fifty years of total abstinence organisation—fifty years since those seven grand men of Preston instituted the temperance movement; and he was reminded that day that teetotalism now needed no apology for its existence. (Hear, hear.) He could remember, in his short life, when an apology was expected for the peculiarity of any lady- or gentleman who was introduced into company as a tee- totaller, but now the exception was to find anybody who would stand up for the liquor traffic and its consequences. They were not met that night, then, to apologise for the temperance cause, but to demonstrate what teetotalism had done for those who had become converts to its ranks. The women, men, and children assembled in that hall were as fair samples of humanity as any that could be produced ' from any quarter of the globe. The temperance question had caused a great social revolution, but more work was stilPrequired, locally and generally, for the removal of the liquor traffic from our midst. He liked the motto of the United Kingdom Alliance—" Total and immediate suppres- sion of the liquor traffic." This was no temporising, no half measures suggested ; • but total and immediate sup- pression. Well, they Good Templars had the means for doiag that in our midst. If everybody would join the Order the liquor traffic would be suppressed at once. There would be no buyers, and sellers would soon have to turn their hands to some labour by which they could earn their bread-by the sweat of their brow, which would do some of them good. The publicans knew better than to apply for any new licenses in Widnes, and the townspeople ought to be extremely grateful that they had got a bench of magistrates to whom these men knew it would be useless applying. (Applause.) They had quite sufficient public-houses, being one to every 200 other houses, and when they con- sidered how many of that number contained inmates who did not use strong drink, and bow many used very little, what a tremendous quantity must go into the houses that did use it. There was not the least doubt the community at large was suffering for the benefit of a few. Widnes would be happy, prosperous, clean, healthy, were it not for the drink traffic. The men were earning good wages, and were as good a stamp of men as could be found, considering the work they had to do and the hours they had to work, but as soon as-they left their labour the temptation was thrust right into their faces at every street corner. Before the land was parcelled out for cottages the best sites in the town were set apart for gin palaces; but he believed the time was not far distant when they would have no more right to erect their places than the public had at present to say they should not be. The temperance caese was moving onward; evidences of this were palpable on every hand; and if they would only work, heartily and harmoniously, the time was not far distant when the nation would get what was requifed—the local option resolution. (Applause). He would even go •further than that. He should like to see something in Eng- I land on a par with the constitutional amendment so re- cently passed in the state of Kansas and Ohio, where no liquor had to ,he sold. (Applause). He referred to the work the Salvation Army was doing, of which be said he was proud, and observed that their success in reclaiming the drunkard, was due to the fact that they were un- trammelled by any of the considerations which hindered the minister who was afraid to speak of the subject from the pulpit. Education had greatly aided the temperance move- ment, and the dissemination of temperance literature by Charles Watson had been the means of doing incalculable good. He concluded by urging those present who were not teetotallers to join a temperance society, and took his seat ,amid applause. Brother Saw, who announced that this was his maiden speech, then made a short address, in which he said he became a total abstainer from the sheer force of conviction. He was convinced on three points, when he became a teetotaller :—that be should be benefited financially, physically, and spiritually, and he demonstrated to the audience how this desirable result was brought about. Brother HORROCKS, who was received with applause, said when last he addressed an audience in Widnes a publican got up and said he had made a good speech, but alleged that be (Mr. Horrocks) had previously been in his house. If that gentleman was there that night, and would prove -that statement, he would give £5 to any charitable institu- tion in Widnes—(applause)—and if any of those present knew the gentleman be was alluding to, and should see him after the meeting was over, would they be so kind as to tell him he must not be surprised if "little Tom Horrocks" made him prove that statement. (Applause.) ..His charac- ter was his living, and he had had to work liard to get his character to what it was, and he should never have it blasted by a publican. He always thought there was something wrong somewhere when a man began to speak untruths of another; and he supposed the publican found something ont when he was there before, and it was this: that some of his customers were leaving him. (Applause.) He Was only sorry he had to spend two nights of his time at Run- corn during this engagement—not that he was sorry to go ta Runcorn, but he wished he was to remain a week in If id- nes, and if the publican bl hiked with one eye last visit,Pfther fight or left, he would do his best to make him blink with both eyes this visit. (Laughter and applause.) He wished to bring Mr. Gladstone to task. Some time ago Mr. Glad- stone said in the House of Commons that war, pestilence, and famine were nothing to be compared to the evils caused by intoxicating drink. (Applause.) Now, he (Mr. Hot. rocks) believed that Mr. Gladstone was speaking correctly; and he was sure the chairman believed the same; but if Mr. Gladstone, Prime Minister of England, believed the statement he made, why did he not remain in the House of Commons like a man when the Sunday Closing Bill was leefore Parliament? (Hear, hear, and applause.) When that bill, which the lalies had worked so hard for, went in, the sister of John Bright, Mrs. Lucas—(applause)—and another good lady took up to the House of Commons a petition a mile and a quarter long, and it took two police- men to carry it. (Laeghter.) Mr. Gladstone knew that these ladies had brought that petition. Why, he asked, did not Mr. Gladstone remain in the House of Commons and listen to what Mr. Stevenson had to say with refer- ence to the Bill. Had he done that he would have been able to say with reference to the Sunday Closing Bill for England, what he said about that for Wales: that England wanted Sunday closing, and must have it. But now in consequence of the Bill being talked out it could not come on for another twelve months. He referred to the Sunday Closing Bill for Cornwall. They did not need to wait for Sir Wilfred Lawson to pass his Local Option Bill ; they would pass it for themselves, whether Parliament did or not. In Bristol, during the last twelve months, there had been closed no less than 20 beer-houses and public-houses. What had they done at Newcamtle-on-Tyne ? They had closed 37 public-houses and beershops, so that they were gettjag ctictiy towards having local option. The pabli. '

div.p: cans were passing it for themselves; they were closing up 1 without being compelled to do so by Act of Parliament (Laughter and applause.) Since he was last in Widnes be had seen 3,000 people take the pledge of total abstinence. Mr. Horrocks illustrated in his characteristic manner the evils of -drinking, and the benefits of total abstinence, and he was frequently applauded. The meeting concluded in the customary manner. We ought to state that the arrangements for the day were in the hands of a joint committee, of which the secretary was Mr. T. Baron, and the corresponding secretary Mr. J. May.

div.head: MEETING AT THE VOLUNTEER HALL.
div.p: MEETING AT THE VOLUNTEER HALL.

The Volunteer Hall was crowded with an audience of respectably attired working people, on Monday evening, when a public meeting was held under the presidency of the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar of Widnes. The rev. chairman was supported by Bros. T. Horrocks, Morris Jones (Liverpool), James Lindon (St. Helens), J. Reay, Rescorl, Harrison, and T. Baron; and the children of the Sunbeam and Lily Temple, who wore the regalia of the Order, also occupied seats upon the platform. The CHAIRM&N, after a few preliminary observations, thanked them for asaing him to occupy the chair upon that great occasion in their own annals at all events. (Applause). Naturally whatever concerned Widnes pointedly concerned him, and he took it as a kindness upon their part to lay it in his power to be present with them,—(hear, hear)—for though they were not all regiments with the same markings upon the cloth, they were all regiments advancing against the same enemy, animated with trust in the same high and noble purpose—men who, filled with pity, and women who, filled with love, were ready for a few hours in the day or week to step forward and deny them-selves in their endeavour to raise the fallen, to comfort the weary, to strengthen the weak, and to march shoulder to shoulder, hand to hand, heart to heart, to the haven of rest above. He alluded to

the origin of the Order of Templars, and it object—that of protecting pilgrims who wished to visit the holy places in Palestine—and remarked that the object of the Good Tern- plars was similar, or else they would notliave chosen so great a name. They could not lightly choose so great a name. If he should have the fortune to bear a great and glorious name —although he was not ashamed of his own name —he should feel more than -ever the importance of so demeaning himself that the escutcheon should be handed down not in the least tarnished but with a few fresh marks and a few dints across the face of the shield, which should show that he had not turned his back upon the foe or been a laggard in the strife. Though he had not the privilege of being a Good Templar he bad the great privilege of being a member of a kindred society, a society which they were proud to remember, a society which they were fain to boast of, and whose badge was then upon his coat—(applause)—he meant the Church of England Temperance Society. He urged them to listen attentively, and said whether the result was a large accession to the Good Templars or a large accession to the Church of England Temperance Society—(applause)—they must all have their eye to business; and he had his eye to business as much as anyone—let it be with a combined and hearty union. They would not differ as to whether their colour was blue or red, but let them see to it that it was pure before God—(hear, hear)—that they were as humble, reverent, and single-minded men, warring to the knife against that fell

giant who strode, almost teo triumphantry, through our land. (Applause.) The victories of the past and the laurels upon the brow of the teetotal cause should nerve their arms to work harder, and to labour longer and more trustingly and faithfully. When they saw that Acts were , being passed through the Legislature of our country which should control all licenses in the future—(hear, hear)— , when they saw that the various products of good and, earnest men, though not in all cases passed, were forcing themselves upon the attention of Parliament; when they found men looking forward hopefully and trustingly; when they _found publicans in many cases were
honest-minded men—he maintained that many of the men in the public business in Widnes were honest-

minded, and would welcome as heartily as any in that meeting any measure which should lesson their labours on the Sabbath—then should they not thank God and take courage and go along hand in hand, heart to heart, and say "we will go up with you for victories crown your cause:" (Applause.) Brother MORRIS JONES next addressed the meeting. He remarked that this year they were celebrating the jubilee of the teetotal organisation—(applause)—and he was glad to be present that night if only to commemorate what those few men of Preston did some 50 years ago. In those days people had to make an apology for being teetotal, but now the people who were not teetotal had te make the apology. He thanked God for the rapid strides the temperance move- ment was making. There was now no church of any denomination complete without a branch of the temperance organisation in connection with it; and there was no Sun- day school in England complete without its Band of Hope. He stated that he lived for 21 yeais in a drunkard's home and knew the horrors of drink; and if there was anything that would make him a teetotaller it would be for the sake of the little children. It was said the poor man was being robbed of his beer, but they wanted to save him from being swindled any longer. He asked them to wash their hands of this terrible evil, and appealed to them to join the Order. (Applause.) Bro. LINDON, in a brief address, referred to the Juvenile Templars, and said the pledge they took was four-fold. They promised to abstain from all intoxicating drink, tobacco and other narcotics, from gambling, and the use of bad language. (Applause.) Bro. Hounoms observed that he never thought he should come to stand on the platform with a Church of England clergyman, and proceeded to express his faith in the Church of England Temperance Society. Since the Church

of England had opened its eyes to this great evil the tem- perance cause had made more rapid strides than before. (Applause.) He then pointed out the evils of intemperance and the blessings of teetotalism. The meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks. •

div.head: RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY.
div.p: RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY.

HALF YEARLY MEETING. On Monday afternoon, the half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of this company was held in the Public Hall. Mr. John Brundrit, J.P. (chairm in of directors), presided, I and there were also present Messrs. Thomas Bankes, John I Simpson, William Whittaker William Hayes, E. Timmins, Shaw, Collier, and W. F. Sallreld, secretary. The directors' report states : A. statement of acc,unt is annexed, which shows a steady increase of water enpplied and money received. The balance of £534 5s 46, ineluding £157 lOs lid brought forward from the previous half-year, enables the directors to recommend a divi- dend to be paid of £4 per centum per annum free of incime tax. payable on and after first of September: this will absorb £469 78 Bd, leaving a balance of £6l 17s 8d to be carried forward. It has been considered advisable tio !Rave the water analysed, and a sample of it has been sent (June 25th) to Mr. J. Carter Bell, of Manchester, the County Analyst, who gives the following results, which may interest the shareholders :—Appearance in two foot tube, like distilled water; smell when .heated 100 deg. F, nil; chlorine in chlorides, 8•7 'grains in a gallon; nitrogen In nitrates, very small; oxygen requirel for two minutes, '0056 grains in a gallon; oxygen required for three hours, *0056 ditto; ammonia ditto, 'OOO7 ditto; albuminoid ditto, 'OOO7 ditto: hardness after boiling, 9 9; temporary hardness, 28; poisonous metals, nil. He remarks at the conclusion, "I Con- sider the above to be first-class water." The two directors who retire by rotation are Mr. John Simpson and Mr. William Hayes, but are eligible for re-electims. Mr. R. B Toft is the retiring auditor, and again offers his services to the company. The whole of the buildings, plant, and machinery are in good order, and the water in the well continues as usual." From the revenue account we learn that the water rent I received for the half-year amounted to £1,749 9s. 6d. the total receipts being £2,760 Bs. Bd., while on the contrary I side was placed the sum of £2,760 Bs. Bd., less a balance of £534 ss. 4d. On the debit side of the capital account were 2,000 shares, £lO each; original capital, £20,000 ;93 shares, £lO each; additional capital, £4,031 103. Od. ; depreciation fund, £1,000; debenture, preference stock, and loans, £26,150; total, £52,161 10s. Od. On the credit side was placed gross expenditure to December 31st, 1881, 1 £51,461 9s. 7d.; extension of mains this half- ,year in Leinster and Egerton-streets, £6O 118. lid.; balance, £639 &. 6d.; total, £52,161 10s. OA. The general state- ment showed that there was £464 17s. 9d. in Parr's Bank, less cheques running, £l5 103. 10d. ; £449 6s. 111 The amount owing for water on June 30th, was £632 lie. ; for fittings and meter rents, £lO3 17s. 6d. The statement of accounts was taken as read.

The CHAIRMAN said it was his duty as chairman of the Board of directors to propose that the report and statement of accounts for the half-year ending June 30th, be adopted, and that a dividend as recommended by the directors at the rate of 4 per cent. per annum be paid. In doing so he would call their attention to one or two little matters in reference to the accounts which might interest those shareholders who were not on the directorate. The report stated that the accounts showed a steady increase of water supplied and money received. They might naturally ask if there was a steady increase, how it was that theil was not as large a dividend as was &dared in the June and December half-years of 1880. This was explained by the fact that at that time the alkali works and other large works were doing a very good business and taking great quantities of water. Since that time there had been a great depression of trade, and the receipts which in the half-year ending Dec., 1890, were £1,882 10s. 5d., fell in the following Den-ember to £1,531 10s. 11d, in consequence of a decrease in the con- sumption of water. The receipts for the present half-year, however, showed a very considerable increase—over £2oo— that without any perceptable or material increase in the water taken by the alkali works. There had, however, been one large consumer added to the company's list in the i glycerine work, which had taken a large quantity of water; nt the London and North-Western Railway Company and other large consumers had done little more than previously. 1 There was on the whole a steady increase in the consump- tion. It was an ill-wind that blew nobody good, and the closing of the fountain had had a beneficial effect, as it had compelled numerous ho,useholders, who had not previously used the company's water, to do sot Therefore the recejots were increasing in that respect, and should the commerFal prosperity of the town advance, there would be a still further increase. Since the last meeting, the directors had definitely defined the boundary of the company's property. It would be remembered that when they constructed their works they bought some land on Runcorn Hill and Heath, but there was no defined boundary and when the new quarries started work, they found they were encroaching upon land which at some time might be useful to the Company. They consequently got the agent of the Marquis of Cholmondeley and Mr. Linaker to move in the matter, and the boundary was fixed, so that the quar- ries would not interfere with them in the future: They had room alongside the reservoir to build another of similar

div.head: ELECTION OF RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: THE ELECTION OF RUNCORN COM- MISSIONERS.

ITS ANOMALIES. The approaching election of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners leads is to lay before our readers some features of municipal government which may prove interest- ing. We premise that many are unaware of the differences between Boards of Improvement Commissioners as dis- tinguished from Town Councils on the one hand, and Local Boards on the other- The locale of Improvement Commissioners may be found somewhere betwixt the other two. Like Town Councils,they are called into existence by special Act of Parlia- ment, having force only in the district mentioned therein, Local Boards being under the general acts applicable to the country at large. Unlike Town Councils, they have neither I Mayer nor Aldermen, nor separate control of police. Like Local Boards, a proportion of their number retire annually and are presided over by a chairman. Unlike Town Councils, the ballot is not yet the mode of election ; but unlike either Town Councils or Local Boards, their elections are conducted at varying times, and by a method differing essentially from that required in the election of Local Boards. The Runcorn Improvement Act seems to have been obtained either by or with the active assistance of the trustees of the late Duke of Bridgewater and the Marquis of Cholmondeley, as lord of the manor of Runcorn and Halton, as in the Act there is a special clause securing to them all previous "estate, right, privileges, exemptions, powers, or authorities in all respects as if the Act had not passed." The Special Act was passed on the I 17th June, 1852, the first election taking place in the Octo- ber following. From the preamble we gather that, previously, Runcorn had been formed into a district for lighting and watching superintended by a governing body termed inspec- tors under an Act of the early years ef William IV., but as their powers were limited to the governing of a village township, and as Runcorn claimed to be something more, larger powers were sought and ibtained for "paving, light- ing, watching, draining, cleansing, and otherwise improving and effectually supplying with sewers, and also for establishing and regulating a market within the limit of the Act, comprising the town of Runcorn and certain parrs of the township of Halton." The number of Commissioners is eighteen, two of whom are appointed by the Bridgewater 1 Navigation Company and sixteen elected by the ratepayers. ' Unlike either Town Councils or Local Boards every Com- missioner must reside within the limits of the Improvement Act district, and in addition possess one of three qualifica- tions, either being a ratepayer in the annual sum of 125 or up- wards, or the owner of freehold property of the annual value I of £5O or upwards, or possessed of personal estate to the value lof £l,OOO over and above all debts and engagements. Unlike either Town Councils or Local Boards, nomination of candidates for election is unnecessary, and such is the i glorious uncertainty of the system, that up to five minutes before the close of the poll any person possessing any of I the above qualifications may be voted for. The voting paper 1 is entirely blank so far as candidates are concerned, the I ratepayers being at full liberty to fill in any names they 1 . choose. As towns rise in manufacturing importance the 1 1 inevitable tendency is for the wealthier portion of the I inhabitants to reside in some suburban retreat, but U) , matter however fitted or qualified in other respects such an one may be, if a member already, he must vacate his seat, , or if the ratepayers are ever so desirous of honouring him I by electing him to a seat on the Board they cannot do so, because of this now-a-days absurd indispensable qualification. We venture to predict that Runcorn would gain much and I lose nothing by putting herself in harmony with modern usage and obtain such an amendment of their act as would allow of persons otherwise qualified to reside any- where within seven miles of the, at present, ()harmed circle known as the Improvement Act district of Runcorn. Cases \ have occurred in which Runcorn has lost the valued ex- perience and sterling worth of members of the Board and the services of others who were but residing at a distance of scarce more than five minutes from the centre of the , town. Runcorn would also do well to take a step nearer a Town Council.by seeking to adopt the Ballot. Seldom does an election occur but whispers of strange doings and of active interference with the freedom of electors fill the air. There is little indication in the town that the annual election of Commissioners is to take place on Thursday next. Of the retiring Commissioners Mr. Wm. Handley has, we understand, declined to stand for re-election, and Mr. Samuel Collier, who has been unwell for some months, will probably follow the same course. The other retiring members are Messrs. G. S. Hazlehurst, T. Norman, Peter Briscoe, and Joseph Williams, and so far as is at present known, intend to again seek the suffrages of the ratepayers. When elected in 1879, Mr. Norman was at the head of the poll with 900 votes, Mr. Hazlehurst securing 818, Mr. Wil- liams 790, and Mr. Briscoe 478. Various rumours are afloat with reference to the " works list," which has not yet been issued. The names of Mr. James Dobson and Mr. Marshall are mentioned as probable candidates, but the latter declines any wish for the honour. A placard signed "A Ratepayer" was posted on the walls of the town on Thursday morning, in which the ratepayers are advised to vote far Messrs. Robert Wright, Richard Oldbury, John Williams, William Mellor, Henry White, and John Jances Waterworth. The present Board of Commissioners is charged with "frittering away "the money of the ratepayers in "false and useless " litigation, and with taking no action to prevent, if not con- niving at, a nuisance awhich threatens to bring upon the town an epidemic of infectious fever. The claims of the candidates are based upon their ability to prevent such "abominable mismanagement." The voting will com- mence on*l'hursday morning at nine o'clock, and close at four.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board-romn, Victoria-road, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. T. Suttcen Timmis, the chairman, presided, and there were also present the Revs. Father Clarke, Father Finigan, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Bradshaw, J. Brack, H. W. Deacon, H. Brunner, R. Shaw, J. H. Davies, and G. H. Daaby (clerk).

NEGLECTED CHILDREN.—SCHOLARS IN THE STREET. Mr. DEACON proposed the passing of the minutes of the District Education Committee, vita° reported that during the month of July (four weeks), 118 applications for the pay- ment of school fees were made, and 223 persons were sum- monelto appear before the committee for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 100 gases. Twenty-one cases were taken before the magis- trate, and convictions recorded in 20, one being withdrawn. —Rev. Father FINIGAN drew attention to the fact that although 223 cases had been before the committee there was still a great number of children running about the streets. —Mr. DEACON replied that there was a less number of children en the streets than there was the previous year. The figures presented at the last meeting showed that the Education Committee had done something during the past year. There were about 150 children absent from school who ought to have been present, against about 330 the pre- vious year. He explained the method adoptelby the com- mittee in dealing with parents who neglected to send their children regularly to school.—Father FINIGAN said he was net complaining of the committee, but asked them to remem- ber that they had about 300 children in the district not on the rolls, who ought to be on. Ire the Board's district there were over 5 000 children of school age, but they would find that 23 per cent. of these were not at school; and he really felt that there was a very large number on the streets, and to a great extent uncared for. He had been asked to mention one case by Di. Cooper, who found in one house three children so badly cared for that he was compelled to call in the nuisance officer. He (the speaker) could mention other cases. He had told the names to Mr. Deacon.—The CHAIRMAN: Why has not the school attendance officer found these children ?—Rev. Father FINEGAN : That is the question, Mr. Chairman. You had perhaps better address it to the chairman of the committee. —Mr DEACDN said the mother of the children had no money, and if the Board paid the school fees they could not send the children to school. The woman received no relief from the Guardians, and the Board must either send her to prison or leave the case alone. There was no other course open. In some cases the committee determined to prosecute, and had several persons sent to prison, the children going to the workhouse in the meantime. There had been several instances of that kind. Some of these people had been fined eight times, and they could go on fining them month after month, but it made no difference. It was severe on a man, but he did not care and it did not seem to have the least effect on the attendance. The average attendance this year would be better than last by, perhaps, four per cent.—The CLERK remarked that several young children had been com- mitted to an iadustrial school.—Mr. DEACON was under- stood to say that in some cases the magistrates would not send them unless the parents Consented._ The CHAIRMAN suggested that a free ragged school would solve the difficulty.—Mr. DEACON said the committee were trying to get children in the Industrial School, which was the cheapest thing for the ratepayers.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 2. 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 2. 1882.

The charge was is. per child per week to the ratepayers, the reminder of the cost being made from general taxation, and sometimes the magistrates made an order on the parents. This was a cheaper method than going to the workhouse, and the moral effect on the child was also much better.—The discussion closed and the minutes were passed. SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.

The following recommendations of the managers of the board schools, having been approved by the committee, were submitted to the F oard for confirmation, viz. :—That J. H. Heacock be appbinted caretaker and cleaner of the West Bank., Schdbls (vice James Chu:lie, deceased), at a salary of £1 is. per week, with residence, taxes, water, coal, and gas free : he to provide all materials and labour requisite for the thorough cleaning o‘the school, and to perform such other duties as the managers may direct. That Mrs. M. H. Todd be appointed head mistress of the infants' department of the West Bank School (vice Mrs. Davies), at a salary of £75 per annum, rising according to the scale of the Board, and with the ad- ditional payments, if earned, as detailed in resolution of the Board No. 1,061. That the fees for teaching the central classes of female pupil teachers shall be for masters ss. per -evening of two hours, and mistresses 3s. 6d. for the sable. The committee reported that the Simm's Cross managers had let a class-room to the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar of Widnes, for the purpose of holding a Band of Hope meet- ing, on the 21st and 28th August, for the sum of ss; and that the West Bank managers had let the infants' room to the Wesleyan Sunday School Committee for the sum of ss: both in accordance with the scale of hire laid down by the Board. -

ought to enrol himself amongst the ranks of the Rechabites to help forward the cause of sobriety, thrift, and morality. Brother H. ROPER, who was received with applause, next addressed the meeting. He said he had for 40 years been labouring in the cause of temperance in connection with Rechabitism, and he hoped the movement in Runcorn, although it had maderapid strides, would go on increasingly for years to come. During the past five years they had obtained a fair number of members, but when the large population of Runcorn was considered the members had not made that advance which they might have done, had they put forward greater efforts. What he was saying they must take in the kindliest manner, because he did not wish to be offensive to the members or officers of the tent, but he be- lieved in plain speaking. The tent had been established nine years, and now possessed 75 members, and looking at that from a moral point of view it was a good thing. The probability was that these members had sober, happy homes that night, and although they might have been total ab- stainers before Rechabites they might have violated their pledge had they not been supported by their connection with the Order, which was a stay to all total abstainers. (Hear, hear.) He very much questioned whether he should have been a total abstainer himself that night had he not been so intimately connected with the work of Recha- bitism, so that he should advise all new members to get in harness at once, and the old members would do all they possibly could to help them in the good work. The funds of the tent must only be looked upon as a sick fund; the funeral fund for the members and members' wives was pro- vided in what was called the district; that was a- sub- scription levy made on each member was put in a central fund in the district to meet all deaths in the various teats in the district, so that the worth of the Rancorn tent was very good, when they took into consideration the low rate of sick- ness they had in connection with the Order. It would, indeed, average more favourably than many of the existing old societies. Referring to the holding of clubs in public- houses, the speaker said they knew too well that there were not only scores, not only hundreds, but thousands of the brightest young men of the land being ruined through their connection with those societies which were held in public- houses; and it was his earnest wish that they could do more good in that direction but he was pleased to say that up to the present they had done a great deal, because be could point to many lodges of Oddfellows, Druids, and other societies that formerly held meetings in public-houses now held them in temperance meeting rooms or Sunday schools (hear, hear); to his (Mr. Roper's) mind a very much more fit place for the purpose. (Applause.) He found that some of these societies had not increased during the last year; and he thought it a bad sign when a society that numbered over 500,000 members °Ale increased something like 58. (Hear, hear.) The Rechabites numbered 40,000, and they found that, although they could not go into the same high- ways and byeways for members that the other societies that were not total abstainers could do, they found that last year the membership increased by about 3,000. (Applause.) Whatever might be said about teeto- talism it was spredding, and spreading more rapidly. Rechabitism in the past had been sneered at, but it haa stood the storms of seventy winters, and the Registrar ot Friendly Societies said it was by far the best society; that it was the wealthiest and healthiest in existence. Its sick- ness in fact, was very little more than half of those held in pudic-houses. (Hear, hear.) The death rate of the Recha- bites was only one in 141, while the death rate of those held in public houses was one in 41. There was no society worked on such economical terms as the Rechabites. Mr. Roper showed the necessity of becoming a member of a friendly society if a working man would escape a pauper's grave ; and the manifest advantage of the Rechabites' Order. The juvenile order numbered about 20,000 members at pre- sent, and he could not for the life of him see why it should not number 200,000. He appealed to the parents to enrol their children, who would have instilled into their minds the principles of teetotalism, and it was a remarkable fact that after the sound training in the lodges only one per cent. violated their pledge. He announced that he had been requested by a. member of the Order to say that he would give a handsome present to that boy who proposed the most members from then to Christmas as a sort of encouragement. Mr. Roper resumed his seat amid applause. Brother Maas then spoke on the manifold advantages presented by the society, which he said was the wealthiest in existence. Ps members could claim to be in the front rank of the great and grand temperance societies of the kingdom in trying to benefit their fellow men. Not only did they help the members financially, but the Rechabite society was a great moral elevator, supporter, and streng- thener of those who joined its ranks. (Applause.) Brother H. HINDE made a vigorous speech on behalf of the principle of teetotalism. On the motion of Brother WARBURTON, seconded by Brother LAME, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chair- man, to the gentlemen from Manchester, and Brother Hinde for tbeir kindness in coming to address the meeting. The motion was carried with acclamation, and the doxo- logy having been sung the meeting separated. '

div.head: SITES AND BUILDING COMMITTEE.
div.p: SITES AND BUILDING COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this committee, which were confirmed on the motion of Mr. Brock, contained recommendations that the closets at the West Bank Schools be converted into trough closets by the Widnes Local Board, at a cost to the School Board of a sum not exceeding £l6; and that the tender of Messrs. Lea and Sons for the cleaning and paint- ing of the caretaker's house, West Bank Schools, for the sum of £2 10s. 6d. be accepted.

div.head: FINANCE.-THE BOARD AND THE OVERSEERS.
div.p: FINANCE.-THE BOARD AND THE OVERSEERS.

The Finance Committee recommended for payment accounts amounting to £517 15s. 10(1.; and stated that since their last report the following sums had been paid into Bank :—Schools fees for July from Simms Cross Schogi, £54 88. ; Warrington-road, £23 28. 6d.; West Bank, £47 16s. Bd.; from the parish authorities, £4 195.; total £l3O Bs. sd.—Mr. SHAW, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said he was sorry to again have to say that the overseers were a long wNy behind in collecting the rate, of which the Board had only received about half. It placed the Board in a very awkward position, because the fact was that they had uo money to pay the present orders of the Board. He thought it most extraordinary that the Hoard should have to press the overseers so much for the reasonable rate they asked for, and that they should place the Board in the posi- tion of overdrawing at the Bank.—The CHAIRMAN : I think, Mr. Shaw, that you should instruct the clerk to write them a very strong communication immediately.— The CLERIC: I wrote a very strong letter long ago.—Mr. SHAw : We have done it fora long time.—The CHAIRMAN: They have got to find the money.—Mr. SHAW: 'And they have the power of collection.—The subject dropped, and the motion was passed.
THE NEW SCHEME.-A COMMUNICATION.
The CLERK read the following communication :

Widnes, August 14th, 1882.—T0 the Chairman and Members of the Widnes School Board.—Gentlemen,—We, the under- signed, beg to draw your attention to the payment for the in- struction of pupil teachers under the "new scheme," and to point out that when we accepted the said sch4ne we under- stood that pupil teachers were to be instructed in classes, and that a special payment was to made for the same. We now learn that it is not intended to form classes for male pupil teachers for the present, and that the masters are to instruct their own pupil teachers as heretofore and we therefore beg to recommend that until the new arrangements are completed, the old scale for payment for instruction of pupil teachers shall be cintinu'd.—JA.3lES 8. SHODDY, THOMAS SHOWAN, DAVID W. HUNTER.
The communication was referred to the School Manage- ment Committee on the suggestion of the Chairman.
THE COST OE -BOARD SCHOOLS.

The CLERK presented each member with the report of the Committee of Council on Education for the year ending August, 1881, which has just been issued. He drew the attention of the Board to a table which gave the means of comparing the financial results, measured by the expendi- ture and grant, of the working of the day schools of certain classes and localities. It showed that the income per scholar in average attendance at Board Schools was-In Birmingham, 63. 5d.; readfard, 153. 811.; Widnes, 12s. 11P. ; whilst the average for England and Wales was 93. nd. The grant earned per scholar in average atten- dance was-In Braiford, 15s. lid.; Birmingham, 163. 411. ; WidneS, 17s. Op.; England and Wales, 15s. 9P. We may state that Bradford had the largest expenditure in the places given in the table from which we made these extracts, and Birmingham the lowest, and it will be seen that Widnes occupies a very favourable position. div.head: RECHABITES' DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: RECHABITES' DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN.

A very successful demonstration and meeting, in connec- tion with the Independent Order of Rechabites, took place at Runcorn, on Monday. The members of the Union Tent, No. 215, who are adults, and of the Excelsior Tent, who are juveniles, met in Bethesda school-room at half-past two. Having here been formed into processional order, they paraded the town led by the Widnes Star of Temperance brass band, after which was borne aloft the large banner of the Order. Bro. S. Lamb, P.D.C.R., was the marsball. The procession stopped at Dr. Robinson's residence, where the band played a selection. Seventy-five members took part in the demonstration. The route taken was from the school, along Bridge-street, to Delph Bridge, where the procession wheeled round and went along Church-street, Queen-street, Lord-street, and Duke's-field. Then tip Shaw-street to a field on Runcorn Hill. The younger members engaged in numerous games, but the weather, which had favoured the proceedings so far, became very threatening, and a heavy shower of rain descended. Shelter was taken in a-large barn, but those who wern unfortunate enough not to be able to enter, received a tnost uncomfortable wetting. Afterwards a tea meeting was held in Bethesda school-room, and was well attended, about 150 persons being present. In the evening a public meeting and entertainment was held. Tne room was crowded, and many were compelled to stand. In the absence of Mr. W. Farish, Bro. W. Dutton, D.S., of Norley, occupied the chair, and he was supported on the platform Ly Bro. Councillor H. Roper, H.D.R. (Manchester), Bro. —. Ellis, P.D.C.R. (Manchester), Bro. Hinde, D.T., Bro. Evans, P.C.R., Bro. J. E. Warburton (secretary.) During the evening the following programme was creditably gone tbrough,and the audience demonstrated their appreciation frequently :—Selection by the band; \song by members of St. John's Band of Hope • recitation "Drunkard's little boy," Bro. Jno. Leach ; selection by the band ; recitation, Bro. Wm. Gerard; song, "Love at home," Bro. E. Owen; song, "Where is my boy to-night," Bro. F. Leach recita- tion, Bro. A. Kennon. The CHAIRMAN said he was very sorry Mr. Farisb, ex- Mayor of Chester, was dot present to give an address, but be was unwell, and, therefore, unfit to be present. He (the Chairman) happened to know a little of Mr. Farish's life and career, and consequently he felt very highly honoured in being asked by the secretary to take the chair in his absence. Long life yet be given to Mr. Farish ! He had been a bold pioneer in the temperance work, and if everyone of them had worked with the same energy in the Order as Mr. Farish had done England would be better to-day than it was. He (the Chairman) happened to represent the Wins- ford and Norley diatrict of Rechabites, and be was one of the gentlemen who ofened it. It was launched with fear and trembling, and some people said that the tents would not exist many days. This, he thought, was in the year 1864. Since then they had advanced onward and onward, r and last return he made out for the Board of Directors there were 1,999 members. (Loud applause.) During this year they had had the pleasure of opening three new tents, and if the Order advanced at this speed, next June, or in a few years, they would be a very large district indeed. Out of the 1,999 members he last reported to the Board he was surprised and delighted to find that only 27 had violated their obligation to the Order. These, however, had seen the error of their ways, ceased to do evil and learned to do well, and came back to the Order, finding they could not mend themselves, go wherever they would. (Applause.) The SECRETARY then read a report, in which he gave some interesting particulars. He said the tent was opened on the 23rd October, 1873, with 23 members. It had now therefore been in existence nine years, and at the end of June quarter, 1881, they had 60 members with funds amounting to £lB7. At the end of June quarter this year they bad 89 members, but since then there had been initiated seven, and the Order now numbered 76, with funds amounting to £221 in money, and about £2O worth of pro- perty. In June, 1881, the juveniles numbered seven; at the present time they numbered 47. Mr. Warburton then enumerated some of the benefits of the Order, remarking that before a person could join he must sign the pledge of total abstinence from all intoxicating liquors. This was, indeed, the chief requirement of the Order. The entrance fee was regulated acoording to the age of the applicant, who could become a member up to the age of fifty, and from the date of entrance each member was entitled to medical aid free of charge. The contribution was 2s. per month, and a member who bad been in the tent twelve months was, when he became sick, entitled to 12s. per week for 26 weeks; 6s. per week for a further 26 weeks; and then 4s. per week so long as his illness continued; while if any member 60 years of age. who had been in the society 20 years, was unable to follow his regular employment, he would be allowed 3s. irr week on application. When a member died, his widow would receive the sum of £10; or if his child died, the sum of £2 would be paid. Half of these amounts would be paid when the member had only been connected with the society six months. In the juvenile tent the antrance fee was 6d. and is., according to the age of the applicant, and each member paid the sum of 7d. per month. If a member became sick after being in membership twelve . months, he was entitled to 3s. per week and if death ensued the sum of £3 would be paid. These advantages, Mr. Warburton remarked, were equal to those given by any other society in the country, and it was a fact that the average life of a Recbabite was greater than the members of those societies which were connected with public:houses.
