TILE WEATHBR.—The very unsettled weather of the past and present week has considerably interfered with the suc- cess of the harvest operations. The showers which have repeatedly fallen almost each day have caused some anxiety among the farmers and a few weeks' run of fine and season- able weather is ardently wished by all. ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM A WIDNES PAWNBROKER'S SROP.—Yesterday, at Widnes Police-court, before Mr. John Brock, John Butler, aged 11, and Mary Cullen, his mother, were brought up in custody, charged with stealing, on the 20th ult., a woman's dress, of the value of 103., from the pawnshop of Annie Jameson, Ann-street, West, Widnes.— Prosecutrix said the dress wap safe in her shop on the morning of the day named. It was at the far end of the shop, lying on the table. About six o'clock in the evening she missed it, and gave information to the police. She did not remember seeing the boy in her shop, but the female prisoner was in about four o'clock in the afternoon on which the dress was stolen.—George Ingram Neild, of Farnworth, said he kept a pawnshop in Widnes-road. On Monday, the 28th ult.' the male prisoner went to his shop and offered the dress produced in pledge. He (witness) advanced him 4s. 6d. upon it. To the best of his recollection, the boy said his mother had sent him to pledge it. On the previous day, when in custody, the boy told him his mother had told him to say he was turned 12 years.—P.C. Tinwerley deposed to apprehending the male prisoner on Thursday morning at his father's house, in Kent-street. He then stated that a strange woman, who he met at Simms Cross, had given him the dress to pledge. From something he afterwards said in the cells, his mother was apprehended, and they were together charged with the robbery. The boy replied, "My mother sent me with it." The female prisoner replied, "I never took it. Never in my life. I was in the shop between four and five o'clock in the afternoon. Jack was there in the morning."—The prisoners were remanded until Monday.

THE. CHANNEL ISLANDS VINERIES AND EARLY PRO- DrCE COMPANY (LIMITED).—We would direct the atten- tion of investors and others to the formation of this com- pany, the capital of which is to be £50,000 in shares of £1 each. Briefly summarised, the objects of the company are: Ist, the purchase of land and erection of vineries and glass- houses; 2nd, the distribution of produce by the appointment of agents in every town of importance throughout the United Kingdom; and 3rd, the receiving on consignment from growers generally, and distributing same among the various agencies. The investment may be recommended bnause of the soundness of the undertaking; the suit Ability of the Channel Islands, where grapes and edibles are grown in perfection ; and the fact that the exports last year amounted to £BOO,OOO, of which £50,000 was paid in commission. This surcharge on the growers' profs will be saved by this com- pany, who will consign to their own agents in all the large towns. Lastly, the directors will not receive payment until the shareholders receive a dividend of 10 per cent. The share list will remain open until the 9th September next.

div.head: LATEST NEWS. THE CAMPAIGN IN EGYPT.
div.p: LATEST NEWS. THE CAMPAIGN IN EGYPT.
RECONNAISSANCE AT KASSASSIN.

The Daily Telegraph's second edition, published at noon, yesterday, contains the following abstracts from special messages received in the morning :—Kassassin, August 31 (via Port Said), September 1, 9-55 a.m.) During the recon- naissance yesterday, Major-General Drury Lowe discovered a new entrenched camp ten miles from here across the desert. It is possible the cavalry will make an attack as soon as the horses are rested. No news has been received as yet of Lieutenant Gribble, reported to be missing. Nearly all our advanced forces are under canvas in tents captured from the enemy. The heat is very great, and there are many suf- ferers from sunstroke. Last night it was considered likely that the enemy would attack our cavalry camp situated on the banks of the canal between Mahsatnen and Kassassin. Major-General Drury-Lowe and Colonel Baker Russell were quite ready to receive him, but nothing occurred, although Arabi's cavalry were seen hovering about all day, and mounted Bedouins were continu- ally observing our positions. The cavalry division is now complete, and comprises a formidable force. Our cavalry charge on the 28th is pronounced by military men here as a most splendid performance. The Household Cavalry and the Foot Guards continue to discharge their duties under circumstances of the most trying nature in the most exemplary manner. Their behaviour has totally dis- pelled some illusions that have hitherto been entertained at home with regard to the fitness of these troops for the most active rough-and-ready service. We have now at Kassassin 4,000 troops, 800 cavalry, and 20 guns. Nearly all the Indian troops have now landed. The construction of the railway to the front is making rapid progress. A large • quantity of supplies were sent forward to-day. The stream of the sweet water canal is rapidly falling. Our wounded are doing well. DARING ACHIEVEMENT NEAR ALEXANDRIA.

A telegram from Alexandria at 3-10 a.m. yesterday, says: —For a long period a house situated on the,bank of the canal, near the enemy's camp, has afforded constant cover to men whose fire has been tiresome on all occasions of ad-

vance. General Wood last night determined no longer to permit this to be, and entrusted the work of abolishing the nuisance to Captain Slade. The officer obtained forty blue- jackets from the Minotaur, who landed close to the red house near Ramleh, and marched forward under his guidance to the canal pontoon, where they were joined by a company of the 53rd, who accompanied them quietly to the bank of the canal, with all the necessary means for blowing up the house in question. They arrived at the position, which is well under the enemy's, fire, without attracting attention, and the party proceeded to lay cartridges, gunpowder, and gun cotton' to which was attached an electric wire carried from the

battery. On firing the charge a portion only exploded and it was necessary to rearrange the whole, which was success- fully done, and the entire building reduced to ruins. This adventurous achievement probably to9k the enemy by sur- prise, for he might have done us great damage. By the gallant behaviour of the men under Captain Slade a serious obstacle has been removed, and future reconnaisances will be facilitated. Telegraphing at 'a later hour the same correspondent says,— Lieutenant Smith, Dorrien's corps of mounted infantry, reconnoitred right up to the enemy's position at Millaha last night. All is quiet here this morning. The marines were landed to-day to garrison the forts at Gabarri. Sir Evelyn Wood is now in command here and at Ramleh.

div.head: MILITARY CONVENTION.
div.p: THE MILITARY CONVENTION.

A Constantinople correspondent telegraphed yesterday : —This morning, at the expiration of the time fixed for the Porte to give its final reply on the question of the Military Convention, Lord Dufferin received a cpmmunication from the Porte proposing a compromise in regard to the landing place of the Turkish troops. According to this proposal the Turkish troops would either be permitted to land at Alex- andria on condition of marching immediately upon Aboukir, or it would be stipulated:that they should land at Alexan- dria in the event of bad weather. Lord Dufferin has tele-
graphed to Earl Granville for instructions, and will pro- bably postpone his departure for Prinkipo.

There have only been two fatal cases of scarlet fever at Accrington this week, compared with five last week and 14 the week previous. During August the deaths from this disease numbered 29, 81 deaths from all causes having been registered during the month. The new cases, too, are few in number compared with last week.

The body of Jane Ann Riley, aged 25, a dressmaker, of Blackburn, was found floating in the river Ribble at Mytton, near Clitheroe, about six o'clock on Thursday even- ing. She left home at noon, and it is supposed that she threw herself into the river. A letter was found upon her which led to her identification. This is the third case of drowning in the Ribble in the Clitheroe district within ten days. An unusual incident has just cccurred at a village near Coventry. A young couple presented themselves at the church to be married, but the clergyman forgetting his engagement was from home. The clerk suggested a post- ponement, but the bride insisted on the wedding taking place, and the clerk had to seek the services of a clergyman two miles away, who attended and tied the knot. On Thursday night a paoic occurred at the Theatre Royal, Oldham. A disturbance arose in the pit, and some one called out, "A fight ! " Some one then raised a cry of "Fire!" causing great alarm. Many rushed for the doors, and some mounted the stage. The performers came on the stage and calmed down the alarmed people. Those in the boxes and galleries remained in their seats. A shocking accident occurred on Thursday afternoon on the Lancashire and Yorkshire line near Bolton. Whilst three platelayers were at work a coal train came np, and the 3 men stepped out of its way not observing the approach of the Fleetwood express. One man, John Bolling, aged 60, Chew Moor, was struck by the engine of the express and dashed to pieces. The other two men narrowly escaped. The deceased was the father of 21 children, nine of whom are living. LETTER FROM THE DUKE OF ALBANY.

Yesterday morning the Mayor of Preston received a letter from the Duke of Albany expressive of his deep regret at being unable to visit Preston during the Guild week, in con- sequence of a slight indisposition. He hopes at some early date to be able to visiLLancashire, and especially the town of Preston., Lord Derby or Lord Lathom will be asked to lay the foundation stone of the Free Public Library.

div.head: STEAMER SUNK: TWO MEN SUFFOCATED.
div.p: A STEAMER SUNK: TWO MEN SUFFOCATED.

Severs./ of the crew of the steamer Guy Minnering have arrived at Liverpool, and redorted the necessity to neat their vessel at Tripoli. The steamer caught fire shortly after leaving Tripoli and returned thither. A Turkish War vessel assisted the crew to subdue the flames but without effect, and she finally had to be scuttled. The boatswain and an able seaman were suffocated in the chain docker. THE DUBLIN POLICE AGITATION.

A company of Rifles marched into the Green-street Police Barracks yesterday morning and it is stated that they are to perform the ordinary duties of the police there. This, it is alleged, is in consequence of the meeting of policemen on Thursday night, and it is believed that the Lord-Lieutenant has decided upon dealing with the disaffected men in a most resolute manner.

div.head: HIGH TIDE IN THE ISLE OF MAN.
div.p: HIGH TIDE IN THE ISLE OF MAN.

An Isle of Man .correspondent telegraphs :—According to anticipation, the south-easterly wind raised the height of the the tide at midnight considerably over that of Thursday at noon, and the promenade was swept from end to end by seas. Beyond slight floodings no damage was done. The new steamer Mona's Isle after making the passage from Liverpool in four hours, landed passengers in Douglas, and sheltered in Ramsey Bay all night, leaving there at six this morning, to return to Douglas. The wind is moderating con- siderably. AFFRAY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND IRISH HARVESTMEN.

On Thursday evening,Jas. Bates and Joseph Bebbington, labourers, were brought before Mr. Torakinson, at Tarporley, charged with murderously assaultin4 Thos. Sharkey, an Irish labourer. A number of Irish labourers are engaged by the Cheshire farmers at Wettenhall, between whom and the Englishmen bad blood has arisen. On Monday night-, about ten o'clock, the Englishmen assembled for. an attack on the Irishmen, who were drinking at the Little Man plichouse When the Englishmen charged the publichouse, the Irish bolted through the back. Sharkey, however, was seized by his assailants, and most brutally beaten with sticks. He received a number of scalp wounds, one of his ears was nearly cut off, and his jtw was completely smashed. He now lies in a very critical condition. The prisoners were remanded till the injured man is able to appear to support the charges.

div.head: DEPARTURE OF CETEWAYO FROM LONDON.
div.p: DEPARTURE OF CETEWAYO FROM LONDON.

Yesterday morning the Zulu King, accompanied by his aousin, Uncongewana,the chiefs Umkosana and Ungobozana, Mr. Shepstone, Mr. Dunn, and Mr. Fynney, left London and proceeded to Southampton, where he embarked on board the steamship Nubian for Africa. In the early morning the weather was gloomy and threatening, but subsequently brightened up, and when the King and his suite left the residence in Melbury Road, shortly after ten, the sun was shining pleasantly. Notwithstanding the fact that the hour of Cetewayo's departure had been kept a profound secret a large crowd had assembled in Melbury Road and the imme- diate vicinity to witness the departure of the royal party. The appearance of Cetewayo and his chiefs in travelling attire was the signal for an outburst of cheering, and the display of enthusiasm on the part of the spectators was continued until the cat riages had reached the main road. The King, who looked remarkably well and in excellent spirits, seemed to be greatly pleased at the warmth of the reception, and bowed several times in acknowledg- ment to the crowd. The cheering wascontinued along High- street, Kensington, where the royal equipages and their occupants were speedily recognised. Waterloo Station, from whence Cetewayo and his companions travelled by the London and South-Western Railway to Southampton, was reached shortly after eleven. On arriving at the station the King was received by Mr. Verrinder, superintendent of traffic, and other officials of the company, and conducted to the train which was to convey him to Southampton. It was not generally known by what train the King would start, and hence there were comparatively few spectators on the platform, but ,those who were present gave a cheer as the train slowly steamed out of the station punctually at a quarter past eleven.

WINWICK GRAMMAR SCHOOL—This SCHOOL RE-OPENS (DV.) on September 7th. Intending foundation pupils from the old parish of Winwick should be at the school at nine o'clock. September 6th, provided with a testi- monial of conduct from their teacher.—For particulars address, The HEAD MASTER.

OST IMPORTANT TO THE LIBERALS OF WARRINGTON. ALL LIBERALS who have received Objections should THU (SATURDAY) EVENING, bring them to the LIBUDAL CLUB, BEITSEY-STREET, any time from Seven to Nine pm. By making a declaration in the presence ef a magistrate, who will attend for the purpose, the trouble and annoyance of attending at the Revision Court may be saved. • H. ROBERTS, Liberal Agent.

NOTICE.—In the matter of composition of creditors of Re JAMES READE, grocer, Earlestown. I HEREBY GIVE NOTICE, that any person or persons having any CLAIMS against the estate of the above James Reade, who have not previously done so, must SEND IN THE SAME to me, the under- signed, on or before the fourth day of September, 1882. Also all persons INDEBTED or OWING any account to the above estate must forthwith pay the same to the undersigned liquklator.— Signed this 24th day of August, 1812. WILLIAM MILLS, Auctioneer, Atc., Earleetown. Liquidator of the Estate.

A SOUND BUSINESS INVESTMENT. THE CHANNEL ISLANDS VINERIES AND EARLY PRODUCE COMPANY, LIMITED: Capital, ZO,OOO, in shares of £1 each. Payable 2s. 6d. per share on application, 2s. 6d. on allotment. 2s. 6d three months, bs. four months, ss. six months respectively, from date of allotment. Bankers: The National Provincial Bank of England, Bishopsgate-street Within, and Branches. Summarised objects of ' the Company: 1. The purchase of land and erection of vineries and glass- houses. 2. The distribution of produce by the appointment of agents in every town of importahce throughout the United Kingdom. 3. The receiving on consignment from growers ' generally, and distributing same among the various agencies. The Share List will remain open until the 9th day of Septem- ber next. Company's Offices, 18, Adam-street, Adelphi, London. FRODSHAM AND HELSBY DRAINAGE BOARD.— NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that a GENERAL MEET- ING of the Ratepayers within the District of the Frodsham and Helsby Drainage Board wtll be held at the Towtt HALL, FRODSHAM, on MONDAY, the 11th day of SEPTEMBER, 1882, at 7 o'clock in the evening, for the purpose of Electing New Mem- bers of the Board. The number of members to be elected is 15, and the qualifications are as follows :—The proprietor of not less than 20 statute acres within the district. The heir appar- ent of the proprietor of an estate of not less than 20 statute acres within the dlstrict. The occupier, yearly or otherwise, of not less than 30 statute acres within the district. The agent of a proprietor of an estate of not less than 20 statute acres within the district, such agent acting under a written appointment. JAMES REYNOLDS, Returning Officer. Frodsham, 28th August. 1882.

TO CONSUMERS OF GAS.—The Warrington Corpora- tion Gas Committee, being desirous of further en- couraging amongst their consumers the use of GAS FOR COOKING and other purposes, are now prepared to Sell, Let out on Hire, or Parchase, Lease, GAB COOKING STOVES at a small half-yearly rent charge. All the stoves will be selected from the best makers for economy in consumption of gas, perfection in cooking, and constructed on the best scien- tific principles. The Gas Committee, in order to make cook- ing by gas a success, will lay all extra services and connect the stoves, whether supplied by the Corporation or anyone else, ready for use free of all expense to the consumer.—By order, JAMES PATERSON, Manager. Gas Works, Warrington, 26th June, 1882.

COWLEY'S MIDDLE SCHOOL—These Schools will be OPENED for tuition on MONDAY the 9th OCTOBER NEXT, M. E. J. SIMPSON. M.A., Trinity College, Cembridge, Head- -master of Hinckley Grammar School, has been appointed Head Master of the boy's school, and Miss Kate Jurgenson, 8. Andrews, late assistlnt mistress at Norwich High School, Head Mistress of the girls' rehool. Tuition fees boys, LS per annum; girls, £7 per annum ; entrance fee, £l. To enable the governors to determine the number of assistant masters and mistreeses required, intending pupils are requested to apply for admission to the schools without delay. Applications for ad- mission must be made on forms to be obtained from me, the undersigned. Pupils applying for admission before the 7th September next, will not be charged the entrance fee of £l. Private proposals for purchase of either or both lots will be received by the solicitor having-carriage of the sale up to the 20th day of September, 1882, and, if approved of, will oe sub- mitted to the Judge without further notice. Dated this 3rd day of August, 1882. JOHN MARTLEY, for Examiner. DESCRIPTIVE PARTICULARS. Lot I.—The Maidenmount Salt Mine. This Mine is situate within a short distance of Carrickfergus, and has been working for abdut 10 years. There are two shafts, adjoining each other, for the purpose of working the Mine; the depth of each shalt Is about 90s feet, and the workings extend over a large area. the rock running ndrth. There are about 40 men and 18 horses in constant work. The annual output of rock is about 15,000 tons ; about one-third of tilts goes to the Carrickfergus Works (Lot 2 described below) for manufacture. The working plant consists of one horizontal engine, 30 H-P., winding belts and pulleys; one grinding naill and engine, 10 11-P., grinding 50 to 60 tons per day; weigh- bridge, trucks, buckets, and the usual quarrying tools. The Shafts are 4 feet square, timbered with pine, and guides for ropes. The Buildings on the premises consist of an Engine House, the foundation of which is of stone and brick, the structure wood, and a felt roof, rock loft being a wooden shed; offices, powder store, engine driver or caretaker's house (mood) and a small stable. Lot 2.—Carrickfergus Salt Works. These Works are situate In the Town, adjoining the Harbour; they consist of the usual boiling and melting pans, small engine 8 H-P., pumping gear, Ac.. &c. The premises being all in Mr. Dalway's possession, immediate possession can be obtained. The sale of Lot 2 is subject to the Landlord's approval. The terms upon which the Landlord's consent to a sale has been given are. t,e approval by him of the Purchaser, and that, the premises shall be used solely for the purposes of the busi- neoi heretofore carried on therein. The deed of Conveyance will not pass to the Purchaser any Wade fixtures on the premises, but such trade fixtures may be taken by the Purchaser, at a valuation ta pa agreed upon between him and the Official and Tradig„.ssignees of the Court of Bankruptcy in the matter of MarriClE Robert Dalway, an Arranging Debtor, who are willing to sell the same. Lot 1.- These premises, including the machinery, bade fixtures, &c. (which will not, however, pass to the Purchaser) as a going concern, has been recently valued by Mr. Edward Allworthy, valuator, at £6,250. Lot 2 has been also recently valued by same gentleman at £750. PARTICULARS APPLICABLE TO BOTH LOTS. The demand for Salt Rpck and Salt has increased of late years. The Commissioaers of the town of Carrickfergus have lately borrowed £12,000 from the Board of Works, for the pur- pose of making a new Pier and Harbour at that town. , These works are expected to provide a depth of 18 feet of water at high tide, and of 10 feet at low water thus affording accommodation for vessels of large tonnage. The Works are under contract to be finished on let May, 1883. A Bill is being promoted in the present Session of Parlia- ment for the purpose of connecting the above-mentioned new Pier and Harbour ith the Belfast and Northern Counties Railway. It is expected that the above scheme will largely increase the coal carrying trade to Carrickfergus, and from thence to inland Districts, and thereby the export of Salt from that port, vessels discharging ceal being likely to reload with Salt or Salt Rock. The Salt export is expected also to be largely increased directly the improved Harbour accommodation, enabling vessels of a larger tonnage than heretofore (which previously took in ballast at Belfast) to take in ballast or cargo of Salt Rook or Salt at the Carrickfergus Harbonr. . For Rentals, Maps, and further particulars apply at the Registrar's Office of the said Land Judges, Chancery Division, Inns quay, Dublin. OMAR C. NELSON, Esq., Solicitor, 69, Donegall-street, Belfast; or to BOUCHIER EATON, Solicitor having carriage of the Sale, 42, Fleet-street, Dublin.

Mr. BANKES seconded the motion, which was carried. Mr. John Simpson and Mr. W. Hayes, the retiring 4irectors were re-appointed on the motion of Mr. BANES, seconded by Mr. COLLIER. Mr. R. B. Toft Was re-appointed auditor on the proposi- tion of Mr. COLLIER, seconded by Mr. SHAW. Mr. COLLIER moved that the thanks of the meeting be tendered to the Chairthan for the able manner in which he had carried out the duties of chairman of directora during the past year. The motion was seconded by Mr. SHAW, and carried. The CHAIR-MAN, in making his acknowledgments, assured the shareholders that he felt it his duty, as well as his pleasure, to do all he could for the Company. Backed up as he was by such a body of directors, and so efficient a secretary as Mr. Salkeld, he found his work was very light. Mr. SHAW moved, and Mr. WHITAKER seconded a vote of thanks to the secretary for the very efficient manner in which he had discharged his duties. The motion was carried, and Mr. SA.LKELD said it had been his endeavour in the past to advance the interests of the Company and it should be no less so in the future. The proceedings then terminated.
